title: Bundlepose
pitch: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart.
about_excerpt: Agents propose. People compose. Shopify bundles. You and your AI agent co-compose a bouquet that doesn't exist yet — and a Cart Transform Function makes it one real, purchasable line in the cart. Like Comment Story Updates top Basic Use Case Co-Compose System Inspiration E-commerce lets anyone sell 24 hours a day — but an online store is really an unmanned roadside stand. Nobody greets you, nobody asks who the flowers are for. We build Shopify apps for a living (Theme App Extensions, Shopify Functions), and florists are a vertical where this gap hurts most. Custom bouquets ARE sold on Shopify today — but the "custom" part still happens over phone calls, LINE messages, and free-text note fields. The composition, the price, the stock — none of it is structured. When WebMCP arrived, we saw a chance to put a clerk back in the store: an agent that listens to "something warm for my mother's 60th birthday, under $40," knows the flowers (meanings, occasions, pet safety), and builds the bouquet with you. Shopping agents are good at finding products that already exist. We wanted the harder thing: turning agentic commerce from product discovery into product creation. What it does Bundlepose is a Shopify app where a shopper and an AI agent compose a product that doesn't exist yet — and turn it into a real order. The agent proposes. Through 11 bouquet_* WebMCP tools registered on every storefront page, the agent reads the florist's rules (slots, stem limits, budget) and today's flowers — real Shopify variants with metafields for role, color, flower meaning, occasions, and pet safety — then drafts a bouquet within the budget. The person composes. The draft appears in a composer panel on the same page. The shopper adjusts quantities, removes a stem, picks the wrap, restores something — by hand. The agent sees those hand edits on its next bouquet_get_state call and rebalances. One shared workbench, edited from both sides. Shopify bundles. bouquet_commit — the only tool allowed to touch the cart — validates the draft and adds it. A Cart Transform Function (Rust) merges stems, wrap, and arrangement fee into one cart line, priced as the exact sum of its parts , carrying its recipe through checkout. Three bouquets? Three clean lines, not thirty loose stems. Why this needs WebMCP: Shopify's built-in storefront tools already let agents search products and fill carts — but they can only sell what exists. A bouquet that was just invented in conversation isn't a product; twelve loose stem lines don't tell the merchant "this is one bouquet," and two bouquets in one cart are indistinguishable mush. Page-level WebMCP tools + a Cart Transform close exactly that gap: the agent works inside the store's own rules and inventory, hands off to Shopify's standard tools for checkout, and the human approves on the same page they're browsing. The UX win is concrete: what used to be a phone call, a LINE thread, and a free-text note field becomes a structured, priced, stock-checked bouquet built right on the product page — and one clean line in the cart instead of a dozen loose stems. The tools: bouquet_get_rules , bouquet_list_components , bouquet_create , bouquet_get_state , bouquet_add_items , bouquet_remove_items , bouquet_set_wrap , bouquet_set_note , bouquet_validate , bouquet_commit , bouquet_discard . How we built it Storefront (Theme App Extension, app embed): registers the 11 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() — imperative API, top-level document (ChatGPT does not detect tools inside iframes). Tools and the composer panel mutate one shared draft store (persisted to localStorage), so agent calls re-render the panel instantly and human edits are readable back through bouquet_get_state , including a per-stem diff against what's already in the cart. Backend (React Router 7 + TypeScript on Fly.io, SQLite/Prisma): tools call the store's own domain via Shopify App Proxy ( /apps/composer/* ) — signed, same-origin, zero CORS. We verified WebMCP execute runs in the normal page context (not a sandbox), which makes this possible. The catalog endpoint reads the Admin GraphQL API, exposing composer.* metafields (role, color, meaning, occasions, pet-safe) as the agent-facing florist knowledge. Cart write: Shopify.actions.updateCart (Storefront Actions API) with hidden _bundle_id / _bundle_name line attributes, Ajax Cart API fallback — then navigate to /cart , which is always correct regardless of theme. Bundling (Shopify Function, Rust → WASM): groups cart lines by _bundle_id and emits a LinesMerge operation under a "Custom Bouquet" parent variant ( requiresComponents: true , price $0 — the merged line's price is the components' sum). Config lives in a metafield on the Cart Transform; missing config = no-op, so checkout never breaks. Fixture-tested with @shopify/shopify-function-test-helpers . Merchant setup: an idempotent admin setup page — one click seeds the demo florist (14 stems with metafields, 2 wraps, an arrangement fee, the merge parent kept UNLISTED: purchasable by direct variant reference for the merge, hidden from search), another activates the transform after shopify app deploy . Challenges we ran into Exposing WebMCP tools on a Shopify store. A Theme App Extension turned out to be the right surface: its app embed runs in the storefront's top-level document, which is where agents such as ChatGPT discover tools. We then named and scoped the bouquet_* tools so they complement — rather than overlap with — Shopify's standard storefront tools, which already handle search, cart and checkout. Staying in sync with the store's theme. Writing to the cart from a tool succeeded on the server, but the theme's cart icon and drawer did not reflect the change. The theme owns that state and only reacts to its own events, so we moved the commit path to Shopify's Storefront Actions API, which fires those events, and navigate to the cart page after a commit so the result is always visible. Co-composing with the agent, not through it. Our first approach drove every cart change through WebMCP alone, and the shopper ended up doing more work — each small tweak became another round of conversation. So we built the embedded composer: the agent's proposal lands in an on-page panel that the shopper can edit by hand, and the agent reads those edits back. Splitting the work this way is what finally made the experience feel good. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end from ChatGPT: conversation → draft → hand-edit → agent rebalance → commit → one merged bouquet line → checkout. The math is exact. Five lines (3 roses, 4 tulips, 2 eucalyptus, wrap, fee) merge into "Warm Birthday Bouquet — $39.50", precisely the sum of its parts; a second bouquet stays its own line, and checkout expands each into its recipe. A real shared workbench. Remove a stem by hand and the panel shows "Removed / Restore", the agent sees changes_since_cart , and "Update cart · +$3.00" shows the delta before you approve. It's a product, not a rig: idempotent one-page seed of the demo florist, graceful fallback in browsers without WebMCP, and a Rust Function with fixture tests. What we learned Chat is not always the best interface. When you build with WebMCP, it's tempting to think of every interaction as a conversation. But some things — like removing one stem or trying a different wrap — are faster to do by hand than to describe in words. To give customers a good experience, we learned to combine chat with other kinds of UI, rather than force everything through the agent. WebMCP tools have to coexist with other apps' tools. Publishing tools with WebMCP turned out to be easy. That is exactly why it needs care: on a platform like Shopify, our tools run on the same page as Shopify's own tools and, in the future, tools from other developers' apps. Tool names, descriptions and responsibilities need to be designed so that agents can tell them apart and use them together. Explaining this to customers is hard. Our demo store shows a banner inviting shoppers to try the new experience with their AI agent. In practice, it is still difficult for a non-engineer to understand what that means or how to start. Until WebMCP-capable browsers are common, even a careful explanation will only go so far — as app developers, we need to keep working on how this is introduced to real shoppers. What's next for Bundlepose Let the agent sell, not just build: add upsell_suggestions[] to bouquet_validate / bouquet_get_state returns — "for $3 more, satin wrap," "your budget fits one more focal stem" — so upselling happens in conversation, the way a real clerk does it. More templates for the same engine. The Cart Transform's grouping logic is product-agnostic and the shop rules already ship as a profile object (noun, unit, slots) — generalizing the tool names and copy is the next step: coffee blends, cookie assortments, spice mixes, gift kits. title: Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI
pitch: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you.
about_excerpt: A privacy-first toolbox where every tool is a WebMCP capability - so an AI model on your own device, or any agent, can do real multi-step tasks for you. Like Comment Story Updates AI to AI data transfer Lora adapter for better MCP use List of all WebMCP tool on the website Multi-step task can be compressed to single webmcp call Agent using actual webMCP calls to use tools from the website Inspiration I run mentria.ai, an extensible toolbox: 34 tools, 8 games, user-installable extensions and an AI-learning feed, all running in the browser, including language models of up to 27B parameters executing on the visitor's own GPU through WebGPU (smaller models cover low-end devices). The core of the site never sends your data anywhere. A few features, like the comms chat or the peer swarm for model downloads, talk to a server or to other people, and only when you turn them on. Every tool already registered its abilities on an in-page "capability bus" so my on-device model could operate them. WebMCP is a browser API that lets a web page publish its functions as tools that any AI agent (a browser's assistant, an in-app browser, an extension) can discover and call. It is the same idea I had built for my own model, now as a standard that any agent understands. So the question became: what happens when outside agents get the same doors my local model already uses, and what can the local model do for them? What it does One bridge, whole site agent-ready. mentria-webmcp.js registers every AI-safe capability with document.modelContext , picks up tools that appear later, and marks the read-only ones so agents know what is safe to call. Because the bus announces across tabs, an agent sitting on the notes page can also spin the decision wheel, start a timer or create a story in Story Studio if those tabs are open, all from where it is. Agents operate the real UI. Spin the decision wheel and it visibly spins in your tab; ask for a QR code and it renders in the tool; start a timer and the tab title counts down. An on-page "Agent activity" panel lists every call an agent makes with its arguments and result, so nothing happens out of sight. The person watches, interrupts, or takes over at any point. The on-device model as a privacy layer. Capabilities that read private data are never exposed to agents. Instead the site exposes a tool backed by the model running on your device: an outside agent that needs something from your notes calls notes__summarize_private , the local model reads the notes, and only the summary goes back. local_ai__ask generalizes it, so any agent can hand any prompt to the model on your GPU, and an on-page panel streams the local answer so you always see what your model said. The agent gets what it needs; the data never leaves. Extensible by anyone. Extensions are single HTML files that register capabilities on the same bus. The bundled Story Studio, Unit Converter and Dice Roller installed from the Extensions page (/tools/extensions/) show up to agents automatically, and anyone can add a tool without touching this repo. The same tools, from the inside. The site's own agent at /tools/console/ is a 27B model in a browser tab, fine-tuned for tool calling with a LoRA trained on our own machines. Ask it to "create a story from @notes.1" and it reads my private note, makes one call, and a titled five-slide story appears in the studio. The homepage prompt answers from the same local model. How we built it Every capability is described once on the bus (name, description, JSON schema, ai and read-only flags), and one bridge file turns those descriptions into WebMCP tool registrations. It is feature-detected, so browsers without WebMCP pay nothing, and an origin-trial token is served so testing needs no flags. The site is Eleventy plus plain JavaScript, no bundler, hosted as static files; models are downloaded once from our mirror and cached on the device. The tool-call LoRA was trained in about fifteen minutes on our in-house pipeline and hot-swaps at runtime. Only one model instance runs at a time: tabs coordinate over a broadcast channel, so a tab that already holds the model answers on behalf of the others instead of loading a second copy. The on-device agent also tests the site: a console__test capability lets any agent commission a QA run of a tool, and the model reports what worked, what was awkward and what broke. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is per-document. An agent on one page could not see the tools of another, so I built a cross-tab announce layer on the bus. Now one page exposes the tools of every open tab. Agents hit bugs people never do. Chrome throttles animation frames in background tabs, so an agent working in one could wait forever on an animation. Tool calls now settle deterministically. The model faked success. On tasks it could not do (opening another website, for example) the base model substituted a tool it did have and reported success 84% of the time. I trained an adapter that teaches it to name what it cannot do instead, which also makes its WebMCP tool-call decisions better. Accomplishments that we're proud of The privacy layer works end to end. An outside agent asked for the gist of my notes and got a summary computed on my GPU, in seconds, without ever seeing the notes. An adapter that makes the agent honest. False success on impossible tasks went from 84% to 0%. Live, on the same task, the base model substitutes the site's own search for the website it cannot open and reports on that instead; with the adapter it answers "I cannot open Google or any other site" in under half a minute, without a single click. In a longer rehearsal the base model went further: eleven typing attempts into a dead field over five minutes. One request, one call. Asked to turn a private note into a story, the agent did not click its way through the app: it made one tool call and a finished five-slide story appeared, title and all. One page, every tool. An agent on one Mentria tab can use the tools of every other open tab, through one standard interface. An agent that tests the site. The same on-device model QA-tests Mentria's own tools and reports what it finds, so agents are first-class users here in more than one sense. What we learned A real model you own, that can operate real tools, is a better product than 34 tools or "privacy" alone, and a web standard is what lets outside agents join that same surface without a server in the loop. Agents are first-class users: testing with them finds bugs humans never trigger. For tool-using agents, honesty about which tools exist beats cleverness; that is what the adapter really taught. And a local model is not just a feature, it is the place to put the parts of a task that should never leave the device. What's next for Mentria.ai - an extensible toolbox with on-device AI The privacy layer grows from summaries to actions: a cloud agent filling in an invoice can ask the local model for the details that live in a locked note, and once you have unlocked it, the local model answers with only the fields needed, no copy-paste and no human in the loop for every step. Beyond that, a single conversational surface for all the AI tools, and an Extension Studio where the on-device model writes single-file apps that compose these capabilities instead of rewriting them, so anyone can grow the toolbox in a sentence. Provenance and the judged build: the site predates the challenge; everything WebMCP above was built during the submission window (commits from 2026-09-01, listed in WEBMCP.md). MIT licensed. Submitted as a frozen snapshot: webmcp.mentria.ai and the webmcp-demo repo hold the exact judged build and will not change during judging; production continues at mentria.ai (main repo github.com/mentria-ai/website, tag webmcp-submission ). title: Budget Bench
pitch: Plan your household budget with your browser agent — every change is a proposal you approve
about_excerpt:
Plan your household budget with your browser agent — every change is a proposal you approve
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Budgeting a household is a shared decision between people — and increasingly, between a
person and an AI agent. Handing an agent full write access to your money is wrong. Making it
scrape and click a human UI is worse. WebMCP offers a third path: give the agent real tools
and keep the human in the loop at the only moment that matters — approving the change. 

 What it does 

 Budget Bench is a household budget workbench where the browser agent and the human work on
the same live page: 

 
 The agent reads the whole budget with get_budget_summary (income, category budgets,
spend, what's over/tight, pending proposals). 
 The agent acts through five proposing tools: find_savings (trims discretionary
categories and moves the difference to savings), set_category_budget ,
 add_category , record_spend , and propose_plan (full rebalance to hit a savings
target, fixed costs untouched). 
 Every mutation is a proposal. Tool calls never write to the budget. Each one lands in
the human-visible Proposal Tray with a plain-English summary and the agent's reason. 
 The human approves or rejects each proposal (or the whole tray). Approvals apply
atomically; every proposal and every decision is written to the activity log. 
 

 Why WebMCP is the strong fit 

 
 Agent tools, not agent autonomy. Household money is exactly the case where an agent
should propose and a human should decide. WebMCP tools carry structured schemas, so the
agent gets a reliable contract instead of DOM scraping; the tray guarantees the human veto. 
 What people + agents can do together that was hard before: a two-minute conversation —
"energy bill's up £35, find the money from discretionary" — becomes three reviewed,
reversible, explained edits instead of a spreadsheet session. The same shared page also
means the agent always sees the effect of its own proposals before the human decides. 
 Shared context, not replicated state. The page state is the app: no backend, no
accounts, no auth replication. That's only possible because WebMCP runs tools where the
state already lives — in the tab the human is looking at. 
 

 How we built it 

 One static page (vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, zero dependencies, zero build step) with a single
state object and one render function. Six tools registered via
 document.modelContext.registerTool({name, description, inputSchema, execute}) per the
WebMCP draft. Proposals carry apply closures, so approval is atomic and the tray doubles
as a transaction log. Tool logic is covered by an automated Playwright suite (27 checks:
registration, schema behaviour, proposal isolation, approve/reject application, error
paths) which stubs only the browser side of modelContext — the app's tool code runs
unchanged. Hosted on Surge. MIT licensed. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Designing tools that are genuinely useful to an agent while guaranteeing the human veto:
every mutating tool needed to become a proposal generator rather than a writer, which
reshaped the whole state model. Also pacing propose_plan so fixed costs stay untouchable
and the plan lands as ONE reviewable decision instead of a barrage of edits. 

 Accomplishments we're proud of 

 The proposal tray pattern: six tools, one hard invariant — the agent proposes, the human
decides — and the activity log that proves it. 

 What we learned 

 That "agent-accessible" and "human-controlled" are not a trade-off if the tool layer is
designed as a proposal system rather than a command API. 

 What's next for Budget Bench 

 CSV import of real bank data (local-only), per-category proposal bundles, and a
"what-if" tool that compares two plans side by side in the tray.

title: gpuiXwebmcp
pitch: A native developer debugger for WebMCP—inspect tools, execute calls, and trace browser-agent interactions.
about_excerpt:
A native developer debugger for WebMCP—inspect tools, execute calls, and trace browser-agent interactions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 I wanted to explore how WebMCP could be used to make websites easier for AI agents to interact with. While working with WebMCP, I felt there was a missing developer tool for seeing what tools a webpage exposes and what happens when those tools are called. 

 So I built gpuiXwebmcp, a native debugger for WebMCP using Rust and GPUI. It connects to a WebMCP-enabled Chrome tab and lets you see the available tools, inspect their schemas, execute them, and view the execution results. 

 The main idea is simple: instead of guessing what an agent is doing inside a browser, developers should be able to see the tools and their execution clearly. 

 I built the project to learn more about WebMCP, GPUI, browser communication, and building native developer tools with Rust. One of the main challenges was connecting the browser environment with a native GPUI application and keeping the tool and execution state synchronized. 

 This project is still an early experiment. The next things I want to explore are agent execution, tool-call replay, better debugging information, and connecting local AI models to the WebMCP tools.

title: Synspace
pitch: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds.
about_excerpt: A 3D workspace agents can actually operate. WebMCP exposes the world as structure, not pixels — an AI measures, simulates and proposes; you approve. One world, two minds. Like Comment Story Updates screenshot-city screenshot-workspace Inspiration Agents should not have to infer meaning from pixels and click coordinates. SynSpace explores a better model: give an agent structured access to a spatial world while keeping the human in control of every consequential change. What it does SynSpace is an agent-native 3D spatial workspace. A person and an AI agent work on the same room, office, or city layout. The agent can inspect objects and zones, measure walkways and clearances, check constraints, run isolated what-if scenarios, and propose changes. Nothing is applied until a human approves it; approved changes are attributed, logged, and undoable. How we built it We built SynSpace with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Tailwind, and Zustand. The app centers on one versioned world document shared by the UI, spatial-reasoning engine, scenarios, and WebMCP tools. It exposes 30 typed tools through document.modelContext, with the W3C WebMCP polyfill used for live testing today. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making AI collaboration safe and trustworthy instead of merely impressive. We needed deterministic spatial checks, isolated scenario forks that cannot mutate the live world, stale-proposal detection, and explicit human approval before any agent change can land. Native WebMCP is not yet broadly available in browsers, so we also had to ensure the polyfill path exercises the same real tool handlers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A genuinely shared world document—no drift between the human’s view and the agent’s model. Deterministic constraint evaluation for collisions, spacing, egress, clearance, and walkway width. Human-gated proposals with before/after metrics, revision-based staleness checks, and single-step undo. Runtime asset definitions: an agent can create a new primitive-based asset type without changing application code. 82 automated checks across spatial logic, scenarios, proposals, persistence, custom assets, and WebMCP integration. What we learned Structured tools change the quality of agent interaction. When an agent can query real objects, dimensions, and constraints, it can reason in terms people care about rather than guessing from a screen. We also learned that good agent UX needs visible boundaries: simulation before modification, evidence before approval, and reversibility after action. What's next for Synspace We want to add multi-user collaboration, server-backed persistence, richer geometry and asset import, continuous constraint feedback while dragging, and support for native WebMCP as browsers adopt it. Longer term, we see SynSpace becoming a practical workspace for layout planning, facilities design, retail environments, and other spatial decisions where humans and agents need to reason from the same source of truth. title: daymaker.fun — DayOps for real life
pitch: Your day changed. Your plan should too — a shared DayOps board where people and agents recover disrupted plans together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your day changed. Your plan should too — a shared DayOps board where people and agents recover disrupted plans together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Plans do not fail inside planning apps. They fail in the real world: an activity runs late, the group gets tired, weather changes, or a fixed commitment constrains everything else. An agent can research alternatives, but its answer normally becomes another block of chat text that someone must manually copy into notes, maps, and a schedule. We wanted to close that loop. The human should report reality. The agent should handle the research and replanning. Both should work on the same live artifact. What it does daymaker.fun is a shared DayOps board for humans and agents. A person describes or edits the real needs of the day. The agent reads the same live state, researches appropriate places, and uses five focused WebMCP tools to structure the brief, add source-backed stops, update statuses, and reorder the proposed schedule. Each accepted change appears immediately in the interface. Fixed requirements stay visible, stale writes are rejected, and each revision can be shared with another device through a self-contained portable link. Unlike a traditional itinerary generator, daymaker.fun is designed for recovering a plan after reality changes. The person keeps direct control of requirements; the agent handles the tedious restructuring and research. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent can describe a revised day but cannot reliably read the current board or apply structured changes to the exact artifact the person is viewing. DOM clicking would be brittle, and the chat answer would drift away from the plan. daymaker.fun exposes five focused tools: get_mission_state reads the live brief, Needs, schedule, locks, sources, revision, and portable URL. update_day_context structures or updates the planning context. update_mission_stop changes an existing stop by stable ID. add_mission_stop adds one researched, source-backed stop. reorder_mission_stops reorders future stops while preserving locked commitments. These tools call the same typed domain transitions as the human UI. WebMCP is therefore the shared state and action layer that makes the product possible, not an add-on. How we built it daymaker.fun is a local-first React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite. Mission is the single domain source of truth. Human controls and the WebMCP adapter dispatch actions through the same pure transition layer and store. Strict Zod schemas validate every tool input, and optimistic revision checks prevent stale agents from overwriting newer human changes. The top-level page registers five imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(), feature-detects support, and owns their lifecycle with one abort signal. In browsers without WebMCP, the normal human interface remains usable. Each tab holds one mission in memory. Portable links serialize the validated mission as UTF-8 JSON, gzip it, encode it as unpadded base64url, and place it in the URL fragment. The recipient gets the exact point-in-time plan without an account or backend, and the fragment is not sent to the host. Codex helped build, debug, test, deploy, and document the application, including the cross-device portable-link hotfix. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was choosing a small tool surface that gives the agent enough control without overlapping actions or hiding consequential changes. We also had to preserve fixed requirements, make agent changes immediately legible, reject stale revisions, and make long portable links reliable across devices and Safari. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human–agent loop from editable real-world Needs to a visible, source-backed schedule. Five narrow WebMCP tools backed by one shared domain model. Runtime validation, invariant checks, and revision-safe mutations. Cross-device plan snapshots without a backend. A responsive interface that remains useful without WebMCP. 102 unit/component tests and 8 Playwright end-to-end tests passing in the final preflight. What we learned Agent-native UX is not chat placed next to an app. It is a well-designed shared state model, a small set of precise actions, and immediate visual verification. The most useful WebMCP tools were the ones that cleanly connected reasoning to existing product behavior. What's next for daymaker.fun Consent-based live location, collaborative missions, weather and transit adapters, richer route evaluation, and reusable DayOps templates for families, events, road trips, and field teams. title: WebTrace Atlas
pitch: See what any website loads, uncover hidden risks, and test dependencies with an AI agent using real browser evidence and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: See what any website loads, uncover hidden risks, and test dependencies with an AI agent using real browser evidence and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Modern websites quietly load dozens - or hundreds - of scripts, trackers, APIs, and third-party dependencies. Existing developer tools expose the raw data, but investigating it is still slow and highly technical. We built WebTrace Atlas to explore a web where people and AI agents can investigate that complexity together using shared, verifiable evidence. What it does WebTrace Atlas opens any public website in an isolated Chromium session and maps what it loads, who it communicates with, and how those dependencies affect performance, privacy, security, and accessibility. Through 12 WebMCP tools, an AI agent can launch analyses, inspect measured findings, trace dependency paths, focus resources in the visible dashboard, and run real before-and-after experiments with selected dependencies blocked. Every agent action updates the same workspace the person sees. How we built it The frontend uses React, Vite, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and React Flow. A Fastify API controls isolated Playwright browsers and collects network and runtime evidence through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Axe provides accessibility checks, while DuckDuckGo Tracker Radar helps identify known trackers. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Their handlers share the frontend’s Zustand state, allowing human and agent interactions to remain synchronized. The production application runs on AWS ECS Fargate behind CloudFront. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was translating noisy browser telemetry into bounded, reliable information an agent could use without exposing raw page content or encouraging unsupported conclusions. We also had to preserve request initiator relationships, safely analyze user-provided URLs, coordinate long-running browser jobs with cancellation, and ensure agent actions visibly updated a dense interactive dashboard. Block simulations required resolving only resources from the current analysis and launching a genuine second browser run rather than estimating the result. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that WebMCP is central to the product rather than an added demonstration layer. The agent can initiate the complete workflow, investigate structured evidence, manipulate the human-visible interface, and perform real counterfactual experiments. We also implemented SSRF protections, bounded untrusted outputs, cancellation support, stable resource identifiers, explicit tool annotations, synchronized activity tracking, and automated unit and end-to-end tests. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most powerful when tools expose meaningful product capabilities - not merely existing buttons. Giving agents structured data improves accuracy, but sharing visible application state is what creates genuine human-agent collaboration. We also learned that trust depends on transparency: users should see what the agent selected, what it changed, and which claims come from measured evidence versus inference. What's next for WebTrace Atlas Next, we want to add authenticated and multi-page analysis, saved and shareable investigations, historical comparisons, richer dependency-path visualization, and team collaboration. We also plan to expand the WebMCP workflow with deeper diagnostics and approval checkpoints, allowing agents to propose experiments while people retain control over consequential actions. title: CRM Health Doctor
pitch: A deterministic CRM reliability audit with three read-only WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT and humans co-review the same prioritized evidence on the page.
about_excerpt: A deterministic CRM reliability audit with three read-only WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT and humans co-review the same prioritized evidence on the page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents and CRM automation are only as reliable as the data they act on. A CRM can appear operational while still containing missing ownership, stale deals, weak activity signals, or malformed fields that undermine routing, reporting, automation, and eventually agent behavior. CRM Health Doctor started as a deterministic CRM reliability diagnostic: evaluate known conditions, calculate health scores, and produce a prioritized review queue rather than asking an LLM to guess what is wrong. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: What if an AI agent and a human reviewer could inspect the same deterministic CRM evidence directly on the page, without giving the agent write access to the CRM? That became the WebMCP human-agent co-review layer. What it does CRM Health Doctor evaluates a synthetic CRM dataset using explicit deterministic rules and produces: an overall CRM health score category-level scores a prioritized issue queue record-level evidence deterministic review guidance For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended that report with three browser-native, read-only tools: get_crm_health_summary list_priority_issues explain_priority_issue Instead of asking the agent to infer findings from visible HTML, the page exposes bounded structured state through WebMCP. The most important interaction is the synchronization between agent and human. When the agent prioritizes or explains a record such as C-008 , the corresponding row is automatically focused and highlighted on the report page. This creates an observable co-review workflow where the agent and the human are reviewing the same evidence. Who this is for The immediate audience is CRM administrators, RevOps teams, and automation/AI practitioners preparing CRM systems for agent-assisted operations. These teams already depend on ownership, activity, lifecycle, and pipeline data for routing, reporting, automation, and AI workflows; unreliable CRM state makes every downstream system less trustworthy. Why WebMCP changes the interaction Without this WebMCP layer, the human can inspect the report visually while an agent must either infer state from the rendered interface or receive a separate backend integration. Here, the page itself exposes a governed structured interface to the agent and simultaneously shows the human which evidence the agent selected. The browser becomes a shared review surface rather than two disconnected experiences. How I built it The diagnostic layer is implemented in Python using deterministic normalization, rules, scoring, prioritization, and remediation mappings. The generated report is a self-contained static HTML page containing safely embedded synthetic report state. The WebMCP browser layer is implemented in JavaScript and registers three tightly scoped read-only tools. Tool inputs are validated, outputs are bounded, and CRM-derived strings are treated as untrusted evidence rather than instructions. The architecture is deliberately simple: Synthetic CRM fixture → Deterministic Python diagnostic engine → Precomputed safe report state → Static HTML report → WebMCP tools → Agent + human co-review The public challenge deployment is hosted on Render as a static site. It requires no backend, database, authentication service, or live CRM connection. CRM Health Doctor existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing work includes the deterministic diagnostic engine, scoring logic, fixtures, and original report UI. The challenge-period contribution adds: structured WebMCP-safe report state three browser-native read-only tools strict tool input contracts bounded structured outputs deterministic remediation mappings visible synchronization between agent selection and the report UI graceful behavior when WebMCP is unavailable public WebMCP deployment and validation The repository includes explicit provenance documentation, a challenge-delta document, and a tagged pre-WebMCP baseline. Challenges I ran into Making agent behavior observable Returning correct structured data was only part of the problem. I wanted the human reviewer to see exactly what the agent was reasoning about. That required connecting tool execution to deterministic visual behavior on the page, including scrolling, row focus, highlighting, and an accessible status update. Keeping the trust boundary narrow It would have been easy to turn the demo into an autonomous remediation agent. I intentionally did not. The public challenge version has: no live customer CRM data no CRM write path no raw HubSpot record IDs no network calls from the deployed page strict tool inputs bounded outputs deterministic remediation guidance explicit human-review requirements Working with an evolving WebMCP environment WebMCP is still evolving and browser behavior remains experimental. I validated the implementation through both ChatGPT's in-app browser and a WebMCP-enabled Chrome build. During testing, I encountered a difference in how the experimental Chrome build expected tool arguments to be passed. Rather than hiding that implementation detail, I documented the exact validated invocation flow in the public repository. Accomplishments I'm proud of I am most proud that the final challenge build is small, explainable, and observable. The project successfully demonstrates: three working WebMCP tools on a public deployment deterministic CRM health evaluation bounded structured agent access visible synchronization between agent actions and the report UI explicit human review instead of autonomous writes validation in both ChatGPT and WebMCP-enabled Chrome a reproducible synthetic demo with no customer data The strongest moment in the demo is simple: the agent identifies C-008 as a priority issue, and the same record is immediately highlighted for the human reviewer. That interaction is the core idea behind the project. What I learned The biggest lesson was that agent UX is not only about giving a model more context. A stronger pattern is: deterministic evidence → bounded tool → agent reasoning → visible human review WebMCP makes the browser itself a useful coordination surface between the agent and the user. Instead of asking an agent to scrape or visually interpret a dashboard, a page can expose exactly the structured state the agent is allowed to reason over while keeping consequential decisions under human control. I also learned that deterministic systems and AI agents do not need to compete with each other. Deterministic logic can establish the evidence and operating boundaries, while the agent provides interpretation and interaction on top of that trusted layer. What's next for CRM Health Doctor CRM Health Doctor is still a narrow prototype, not a production CRM auditing platform. The next logical direction is an agent-readiness layer for CRM operations . The broader workflow is: CRM evidence → Deterministic reliability assessment → Prioritized review queue → Governed agent analysis → Human approval → Controlled remediation Future work could include: broader diagnostic coverage authenticated multi-portal assessment historical reliability trends richer evidence sources configurable policy thresholds controlled remediation workflows with explicit approval gates integration with CRM and operational MCP tools after reliability checks pass The larger opportunity is not simply to let an AI agent operate a CRM. It is to help determine when the CRM data and operating controls are reliable enough for an agent to act safely in the first place . title: Co-Presence
pitch: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no.
about_excerpt: We build agents we talk at, not ones we work next to. Co-Presence is a shared board where humans and outside agents edit at once, and the tools that matter are the ones that say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent usage keeps growing, but the shape of it generally doesn't change; go to a chat window, describe the thing, then wait until it comes back. This means the agent is never working in the room with you. That's what I wanted to experience: where the agent and user are on the same surface at the same time, simultaneously reaching for things. And more specifically, when the agent isn't the app's own. Notion's AI works, but it still doesn't feel like you're working together with it. What it does It's an infinite sticky-note canvas. Open it in multiple windows, and now you have several people each with their own agent, all editing the same board live. There's no server holding state, the tabs sync directly, and the board lives in the browser. Any agent with WebMCP capabilities can join by calling the eleven tools the page puts up. It can read the board, ask what's changed since it last looked, ask what the humans are doing right now, arrange things, draw links between them, annotate, collapse a cluster into a summary, add notes, or propose reorganizing the whole thing. An important part is that it can refuse agent actions, taking into account interactions between humans and other agents. How we built it Some brainstorming and then AI building tools. Stack was React 19, Vite, TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for scene state, and Yjs with awareness for peer sync over BroadcastChannel. Also, agent actions all go through one wrapper that gives them a body on screen, which includes a cursor, a visibly held note, and motion that takes time. Without that, an agent taking actions just looks like notes teleporting. Challenges we ran into The biggest one was realizing that a refusal has to be a return value and not an error. If you throw at a model it just tries again. If you tell it what it ran into and who got there first, it usually does something sensible instead. That changed the shape of every tool. WebMCP also has no way for a tool to ask the user anything, which is awkward when your whole thesis is asking permission. The handler for the destructive tool ends up just sitting there and waiting while a dialog goes up in every tab. Deciding that silence should count as a refusal rather than approval took longer to settle than the code did. Then there was a bug where the two tabs weren't in the same room at all. The room was keyed off the whole URL, so a tab carrying an extra query parameter quietly joined a room of its own. Both windows looked perfect on their own, which is what made it bad. Every cross-tab guarantee was untested and I didn't know it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I think this is a good exploration into how multi human-agent interactions working together in the same room would look like in the future. It doesn't run with a server, and you can actually see multiple agents working side by side with humans. What I learned Notion's last write wins policy works for now, but what'll happen when dozens of agents are working on the same thing at the same time? I think that's what the future holds and it makes me realize that the current systems are not built at all for that kind of scale. Why WebMCP Fits This is about an agent being outranked; by a hand, by the room, or by the board moving while it thought. None of that exists outside the page: a hand on a note lives 300ms and never reaches a database. A server can't see it, and automation is the user, so there's nobody to yield to. WebMCP is the only shape where the agent is a guest. What's next for Co-Presence Not too sure to be honest, but I can envision this system being used for other applications as well, not just note taking. title: Threadline — Debug the Argument
pitch: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical.
about_excerpt: Your agent researches. You decide what becomes canonical. Like Comment Story Updates A contested claim becomes an inspectable graph; three agent proposals wait for human review. Nine dated source records preserve provenance before synthesis. Two proposed groups and one atomic verdict stay staged—not canonical—until reviewed. What Threadline is Threadline is a provenance-preserving argument debugger for contested online claims. A browser agent reads the same investigation a person is reviewing and uses eight in-page WebMCP tools to stage sources, atomic claims, typed relations, non-destructive groups, and a bounded verdict. Agent-authored proposals are visibly noncanonical until a person accepts them. If a person rejects a proposal with a reason, that rationale returns through get_workspace so a later agent call can revise its approach. The result is not another feed summary. It is an inspectable collaboration in which the agent does the expensive work of researching and structuring an argument, while the person retains authority over what becomes durable truth. The problem Fast-moving technical discussion on X and the wider web flattens primary evidence, repetition, interpretation, prediction, and contradiction into one stream. A claim can look independently corroborated simply because many posts repeat the same underlying source. An autonomous summary hides those dependencies and can quietly become the next person's “fact.” Threadline makes the evidence lineage visible. It separates what a source directly establishes from what people infer, predict, amplify, or dispute. What people and agents do together The agent can: inspect bounded canonical workspace state and deterministic structural analysis; inspect full source evidence inside explicit untrusted-data boundaries; research and stage public sources it actually accessed; propose atomic claims and typed supports , contradicts , qualifies , or amplifies relations; propose non-destructive groups for repeated claims; propose one bounded verdict and its evidence relations as an atomic patch; and focus the visible graph on unresolved or primary-evidence work. The person can: inspect every source trail and staged graph entity; accept a defensible proposal; reject a weak proposal with a recorded rationale; decide which verdict becomes canonical; reopen saved investigations after reload; and export portable JSON or a Markdown evidence brief with the decision receipt. Why WebMCP is essential Threadline registers eight imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Purpose Authority get_workspace Compact canonical state, structural analysis, recent human decisions, and rejection rationale Read only inspect_sources Full evidence records inside explicit untrusted-data delimiters Read only stage_sources Propose public evidence the agent actually accessed Review queue only stage_claims Propose small evidence-grounded claims Review queue only stage_relations Propose typed claim-to-claim relations Review queue only stage_merge Propose non-destructive repeated-claim groups Review queue only stage_verdict Propose one verdict and its relations atomically Review queue only set_focus Change reversible presentation focus Presentation only This is more than “chat with my site”: The registered tool surface enforces proposal-only authority. There is no registered accept, reject, reset, import, delete, rename, or case-switch tool. Acceptance is available only through the person-facing UI. This is a capability boundary, not authenticated proof of personhood. The agent and person share one live object. Stable source, claim, relation, group, proposal, and case IDs refer to the exact graph on screen. The agent does not reconstruct graph meaning from pixels. Optimistic concurrency prevents silent cross-talk. Every non-discovery call requires expectedCaseId ; every staging call also requires expectedRevision . A stale staging call or cross-case call returns structured recovery output before any proposal or canonical mutation. Rejection becomes protocol feedback. get_workspace exposes up to eight recent human decisions, including rationale, for later agent calls. Schemas and trust boundaries are explicit. Inputs are closed and bounded. Read tools carry read-only and untrusted-content hints, and full third-party evidence is returned only inside named untrusted-data delimiters. Staging is idempotent. Equivalent proposals reuse a stable ID, and pending entity IDs are reserved so competing proposals cannot present different content under one identity. Because the tools live in the page, Threadline needs no backend, database, account, API key, or bundled AI runtime. A complete product, not a proof of concept The primary interface is a responsive, keyboard-accessible provenance graph and review queue—not a chatbot. Pending graph entities are visibly marked STAGED — NOT CANONICAL and open their owning proposal. Amplification is first-class: repeated claims can be grouped without deleting original wording, relations, or sources. A verdict is an atomic patch. Its conclusion and evidence relations enter canonical state together, while only direct claim-to-verdict edges become its basis receipt. Up to eight investigations can be created, opened, renamed, reset, removed, imported, and exported. When exclusive Web Locks are available, cases labeled Saved survive reload. Otherwise they remain clearly labeled Memory only and exportable before reload. Screenshot transcriptions are explicitly labeled human-supplied evidence; Threadline never fabricates a public URL or treats an attributed statement as proof of its underlying claim. The deterministic preview is visibly labeled as a checked-in fixture replay, never as a live model response. Threadline uses dependency-free browser ES modules, semantic HTML, CSS, functional SVG, and Node's built-in test runner. It is hosted on ChatGPT Sites and released under the MIT License. The bundled challenge case The main investigation asks: Will WebMCP replace browser automation? Nine dated public records include Chrome documentation, the WebMCP explainer, a pinned WindTunnel benchmark result, and WebKit and Mozilla standards-position records. The graph separates a large demonstrated efficiency advantage on instrumented sites from task-level parity, explicit fallback guidance, and unresolved cross-browser implementation. The evidence supports a narrower verdict than the feed does: WebMCP is a semantic fast lane on instrumented sites, not a replacement for browser automation. The walkthrough deliberately stages one defensible group, one weak group, and one atomic verdict. The person accepts the first, rejects “Adoption and fallback” with the rationale “Same topic, different claim,” inspects the verdict evidence, and accepts the verdict. The unresolved standards claim remains visible after resolution. Verification npm test : 226 passing tests covering all eight registrations, phase prompts, prompt-boundary injection, case and revision guards, screenshot provenance, proposal identity, human review, atomic verdicts, reload-safe storage behavior, import/export, evidence briefs, and registered-callback/preview parity. npm run evals : 3 passing deterministic workflow evaluations . Seven live-agent journey definitions are checked in and deliberately marked not-run until observed in a compatible live session. npm run smoke : deployable static entrypoint, 2 local assets , 25 JavaScript modules , metadata, accessible landmarks, interaction sizing, responsive guards, and module syntax. Judge testing instructions No credentials are required. Open https://threadline.jameswirths.chatgpt.site in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. Open Investigations , select or load the bundled WebMCP example, and choose Reset case . Confirm 8/8 Site tools ready , Saved , Unresolved , 0 pending , and 09 sources. If the case says Memory only , do not rely on the reload check. Paste the Exact live fixture prompt from docs/demo-runbook.md into Site tools. It reads both guidance pages, verifies the case and revision, calls stage_merge once and stage_verdict once, then stops. Expect exactly three pending proposals while canonical state remains unchanged. Accept Performance amplification . Reject Adoption and fallback with Same topic, different claim. Inspect the verdict evidence, then accept the verdict. Confirm Resolved · human accepted , 0 pending , four installed verdict relations, and three direct basis-receipt relations. The Ask card now advances to Investigate what remains . Use Focus unresolved and confirm the cross-browser standards claim remains unresolved. Reload the saved case, then export the Markdown evidence brief. If Site tools are unavailable, Preview example pass provides the same checked-in three-proposal fixture through the production store. It is clearly disclosed in the UI as a deterministic preview and must not be described as a live agent call. Built With chatg

title: My Project Desk
pitch: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled.
about_excerpt: A local-first project workspace where people and AI plan, create, reconcile evidence, and review work together, while consequential decisions and completion remain human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates The Project Desk Dashboard Workspace Options: manage portable copies, local references, and this browser's workspace data. Tasks the agent and human have added to the project Decisions the agent identified the human needs to make Deliverables the agent created based on the tasks and decisions A working record of facts, assumptions, and missing information. Human, agent, and system actions in a shared history. About Project Desk AI agents can create plans, recommendations, and drafts quickly, but the work often remains scattered across chat. People have no durable shared surface for seeing what is verified, what is inferred, what is still unknown, what needs their judgment, and what has actually been approved. Project Desk was built to make that collaboration legible. It gives a person and an agent one project workspace with tasks, decisions, evidence, deliverables, and activity history. What it does A person creates a browser-local workspace and describes an objective. They may add tasks or references themselves, then ask ChatGPT to plan through the open app. The agent inspects the workspace, creates only necessary tasks, records clearly classified evidence, and requests human decisions where judgment is required. After the person answers, the same reusable handoff starts another work pass. The agent reads the latest decisions and references, reconciles stale or answered evidence, and saves substantial plans, briefs, checklists, drafts, or other work products directly into the relevant tasks. The person can request changes, accept a deliverable while keeping the task open, or accept and complete it. Project Desk is local by design. Workspace data stays in the current browser unless the person deliberately exports it, restores a backup, uploads a bounded reference, or asks ChatGPT to work with the open page. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, the agent would have to guess at page meaning from buttons and layout, rely on coordinate clicks, or return work to chat where it becomes detached from project state. Project Desk exposes eleven typed domain actions against the same live workspace the person is reviewing. The agent can inspect state, read references and approved decisions, add necessary work, submit deliverables, record and reconcile evidence, and request judgment. The tool boundary deliberately withholds workspace selection, deliverable acceptance, unrestricted task editing, and human completion. The linked GitHub repository includes the WebMCP tool reference, implementation details, and testing documentation. Instead of repeatedly copying plans, decisions, and revisions between ChatGPT and a separate project tracker, the person and agent can keep the work in one shared workspace. After the person supplies decisions or references, the agent can inspect the updated project, reconcile outdated evidence, advance multiple tasks, and save reviewable deliverables, while the person retains control over acceptance and completion throughout repeated work-and-review rounds. That creates a safer and more useful human-agent loop: the agent can contribute work to a structured application, while evidence, uncertainty, decisions, and final authority remain visible to the person. How it was built Project Desk is a React and TypeScript application packaged for ChatGPT Sites. It uses imperative document.modelContext.registerTool registration for eleven WebMCP tools, explicit JSON schemas for tool inputs, and browser-local storage for project state. Vitest covers workspace isolation, prompt behavior, evidence reconciliation, deliverable review, stale approvals, backup validation, and progress calculation. Challenges The hardest design problem was defining where the agent power should stop. The workflow went through repeated usability tests to remove circular approval steps, distinguish task review from completion, make unanswered evidence actionable, reconcile stale claims after a person supplies information, and explain how repeated work passes are started. Accomplishments Eleven discoverable WebMCP tools with meaningful project-level actions. A complete planning, decision, work, reconciliation, review, and completion loop. Substantial agent deliverables saved in the app rather than stranded in chat. Evidence classifications and history that distinguish verified facts, reports, assumptions, and open questions. Explicit human control over workspace selection, acceptance, and completion. Local backup, restore, export, reset, and bounded reference-file support. What I learned I learned that effective WebMCP tools require more than connecting an agent to an app. The tools need clear descriptions, predictable state changes, visible feedback, and thoughtful approval boundaries so people understand what the agent did and what still needs their judgment. The importance testing by humans still plays in this world where AI can do much of the coding and testing themselves. Testing Project Desk also showed me how important guided onboarding and shared, reviewable work products are for making agent-assisted workflows feel trustworthy and useful. I would not have gotten there without human testing being in the process. What's next for Project Desk After the challenge, Project Desk will become a free Everyday AI Made Simple resource. I have a free resources hub where I provide thoughtful resources to people learning how to use AI tools. Future work may include a version with optional account-based synchronization and templates while retaining the current local-first mode and human-approval boundaries. I also created the branding, onboarding, human-approval safeguards, documentation, and demo video. title: AgentBridge
pitch: The control layer for the agent-ready web.
about_excerpt:
The control layer for the agent-ready web.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web is rapidly moving from websites designed only for humans toward a web where humans and AI agents can work together. 

 WebMCP makes this possible by allowing websites to expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But while experimenting with WebMCP, I saw another important problem: how does a website owner stay in control of what an AI agent can actually do? 

 A merchant may be comfortable allowing an agent to search products or check inventory, but actions such as adding items to a cart, submitting a request, or changing data may require more control. 

 That inspired AgentBridge — the control layer for the agent-ready web. 

 What it does 

 AgentBridge helps website owners make their websites agent-ready while maintaining control over agent access. 

 A website can expose capabilities such as: 

 
 search_products 
 get_product 
 check_inventory 
 add_to_cart 
 

 as structured WebMCP tools that compatible AI agents can discover and invoke. 

 AgentBridge then adds a merchant-controlled layer around those capabilities. Website owners can: 

 
 Discover capabilities that could become agent tools 
 Control individual tool permissions 
 Enable or revoke Agent Access 
 Require human confirmation for sensitive actions 
 Inspect WebMCP tools exposed by websites 
 

 For example, an AI agent can search a merchant's products and check inventory automatically, while an add_to_cart action can require explicit human confirmation before it is completed. 

 How I built it 

 I built AgentBridge as an end-to-end WebMCP prototype consisting of a merchant portal, a WebMCP-enabled demonstration storefront, a backend policy layer, and a Chrome extension that acts as a WebMCP Inspector. 

 The Northstar demo storefront exposes commerce capabilities as structured tools. AgentBridge manages which of those capabilities are available to agents and applies policies for actions requiring confirmation. 

 I also built the Inspector to discover WebMCP tools registered by websites. I tested it not only against my own storefront but also against an independent Google Chrome Labs WebMCP implementation, which helped demonstrate interoperability beyond the AgentBridge demo environment. 

 The project uses JavaScript, Node.js, Express, Chrome Extension APIs, WebMCP, HTML/CSS, and Railway for deployment. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was moving beyond simply exposing tools and designing a practical permission model around them. 

 I had to think about questions such as: 

 Who controls agent access? Which capabilities should be available? What happens when an action changes something? How can access be revoked immediately? 

 This led to per-tool permissions, a global Agent Access switch, and human confirmation for higher-impact actions. 

 Another challenge was making the system work across different websites rather than designing everything specifically for one storefront. Building and testing the WebMCP Inspector against an independent implementation helped validate the broader approach. 

 Website ownership verification, runtime policy synchronization, extension-to-website communication, deployment, and keeping tool state consistent also presented interesting engineering challenges during development. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making the web agent-ready is not only about giving AI agents more capabilities. 

 It is also about giving humans control over those capabilities. 

 WebMCP provides a powerful foundation for structured agent-to-website interaction. Building AgentBridge showed me how permission management, confirmation, discovery, and access control could complement that foundation. 

 What's next 

 I see AgentBridge evolving into infrastructure that helps businesses adopt the agentic web without giving up control. 

 Future versions could support more website platforms and capability types, richer policies, production-grade ownership verification, activity analytics, and developer tooling for testing WebMCP implementations. 

 As more websites become accessible to AI agents, I believe there will be a growing need for a layer that sits between websites and agents and answers a simple question: 

 What is this agent allowed to do? 

 That's the role AgentBridge is designed to play. 

 AgentBridge — The control layer for the agent-ready web.

title: CoAuth
pitch: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature.
about_excerpt: Most prior-auth denials that get appealed are overturned. CoAuth lets an AI agent do the filing and a clinician keep the judgment and the legally required signature. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 01-intro 05-compare-tools-vs-baseline 03-blocked-at-gate 02-agent-filling 04-submitted-confirmation 06-webmcp-tools-panel CoAuth - an agent-native prior-authorization cockpit Inspiration Prior authorization is where American healthcare loses time it cannot afford - and it loses it to paperwork, not to medicine. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, 80.7% of appealed prior-authorization denials were fully or partially overturned, yet only 11.5% of denials were ever appealed ( KFF ). Read those two numbers together: most denials that get contested turn out to have been wrong, and almost no one contests them. The clinical decision is usually fine. The filing is where it breaks. That is an unusually clean fit for WebMCP, and not just because forms are tedious. Browser agents are weakest exactly where this work lives - long, write-heavy, multi-step forms full of coded fields (ICD-10, HCPCS J-codes, NPIs) that a pixel-clicking agent has no way to get right. And in this domain a human is not optional: a licensed clinician is legally required to attest. So the task splits along a natural seam. The agent is good at the mechanics; the human is mandatory for the judgment. That is what human-plus-agent collaboration is actually supposed to be - not an agent doing everything while a person watches a progress bar, but two participants each doing the part only they can. What it does CoAuth is a single live page that registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . An agent loads a patient record, reads a payer's coverage rules as structured data, fills every non-judgment field, attaches clinical evidence, scores denial risk, detects contraindications and unmet step-therapy criteria, and drafts the medical-necessity narrative and an appeal letter. What it cannot do: fill a clinician-judgment field, resolve a critical contraindication, or submit. Those belong to the human, and both halves are enforced in code rather than described in prose. The demo case is Marcus Lee, a psoriatic-arthritis patient requesting Humira through Aetna. The agent fills the form cleanly and then catches what a rushed clinician might miss - a positive TB screen, a contraindication for this drug - flags it, tries to submit, and is stopped. It drafts the medical-necessity language from the chart but cannot adopt its own draft. From there the clinician signs in, makes the call on the TB screen and documents why, accepts the drafted wording as their own, attests, and signs. Only then does the submission go through, with a server-verified audit trail in the clinician's name. Two details make that boundary real rather than cosmetic. The signature is minted only for an authenticated clinician who re-enters their own credential at the moment of signing - each clinician has a distinct secret, so the name and NPI in the audit trail belong to the person who actually signed, not to anyone who knew a shared password. And the filed submission is rendered as an X12 278 - the HIPAA-mandated Health Care Services Review transaction payers actually receive - so every value the agent filled and the clinician signed maps to the real prior-authorization EDI, not just our own JSON. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, and Zustand on the front end; Vercel Edge Functions and Upstash Redis on the back end. A 15-rule clinical engine drives conflict detection, denial-risk scoring, and validation. The architectural decision that carried everything else: the WebMCP tool surface is the application's only write path. Every click in the interface calls the same invokeTool an agent calls, tagged with the actor - there is no parallel code path for humans. So the tools cannot rot behind the UI, attribution is a property of the call path rather than something each component must remember, and the built-in "with tools vs. without" comparison drives the real tools rather than a re-implementation. Tool schemas are generated from the seed data, so the patient, payer, drug and field enums cannot drift stale - an early bug had a payer hint still reading "uhc or aetna" after a third payer was added. Every property carries a description; write tools declare destructiveHint / idempotentHint so a runtime can require confirmation before submit ; and a get_submission_state tool lets an agent joining mid-task see what is filled, who filled it, what is unresolved, and whether the clinician has signed. Correctness is proven by 127 checks that run against the deployed system - not unit tests, and nothing mocked. They attempt to submit without a signature, with a forged approval, with a form edited after signing, with a clinical override swapped after signing, and with one approval replayed twelve times concurrently , requiring exactly one acceptance. They drive the registered WebMCP tools through a real model-context surface and try, as an agent would, to set the attending attestation. They drive every clinician control the way a hostile script would and require that none of them takes effect. And a meta-check reads the clinical rules table and fails if any rule is not exercised by a test. Challenges I faced The entire pitch is that an AI agent cannot file a prior auth without a real clinician signing off, and the hard part was making that actually true instead of just looking true. Every time I thought I'd locked it down, I'd poke at it and find another way around my own gate. My first gate was a browser check, which is useless against an agent that lives in the browser. I moved it to the server, then found the sign endpoint would hand a signature to anyone who asked, under any name they typed. I fixed that, then found a script could still sign using the logged-in doctor's own session, no click required. Turning on the database to stop replays silently rejected every submission in production. And the safety rules were reading tea leaves, so a note saying "no adverse events" got written into a letter to the insurer as a treatment failure. The real enemy was never a single bug. Every time I fixed the exact thing in front of me, the same kind of bug was sitting one layer over: I'd guard the button and leave the API open, guard one tool and leave its twin open, protect the signature and forget the reasoning behind it. What finally worked was to stop patching the specific hole and close the whole category at once, with one shared check instead of five copies I'd never keep in sync. What I learned Stop trusting the moment something starts working. Every real hole showed up after the feature looked done, and I only made progress once I started trying to break my own product on purpose. A passing test can also be a lie: I had one proving an approval couldn't be reused, and it passed while the live site happily accepted a burst of the same token, because the test wasn't checking the thing I was actually afraid of. And the big one, about the product itself: the interesting part of a human-plus-AI tool isn't making the AI capable, that part is easy. It's drawing the line the AI cannot cross, building the wall around what belongs to the human, and proving it holds when someone is actively trying to climb it. For something that touches patient care, that wall isn't a feature. It's the whole point. I came up with the concept - use WebMCP to let an AI agent and a clinician fill a prior authorization together, where the agent does the mechanics and the human keeps the parts they're legally required to own - and I made every design and engineering decision behind it. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.
