 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'm currently training for my first ever marathon. Having come from a competitive running background back in high school, I recognise the importance of having a bespoke training plan and a coach that truly understands your needs and circumstances. 

 Typical training apps do a basic Q&A to take a low-res "snapshot" of your current fitness levels, then spit out a workout structure that assumes you progress the same way as everyone else. It's no wonder people often get injured from following these rigid regimes! Also, subscription costs add up quickly, and I didn't want to stack yet another $20+ monthly subscription on top of all the ones I already have (like ChatGPT whoop whoop!). 

 As someone who's keenly interested in tinkering and building with agents, I got the idea to build an agentic coach to go through this marathon training journey with me. While this definitely would've worked adequately with other primitives like Google Sheets, I realised WebMCP could shift the paradigm and enable me to a beautiful, interactive workspace that both my coach agent and I can collaborate on together. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Good coaching is more than just generic advice generation. A coach needs access to the runner’s current training plan, recent workouts, personal constraints and preferences; the runner needs to understand why the coach proposes a certain training regime (i.e. provenance). Therefore, a bespoke training regime should be transparent and collaborative. 

 WebMCP enables the web app itself to be the shared interface between runner and agent. The agent can read canonical context and propose tweaks through purpose-built tools, while the runner can see the same evidence and review those changes in the workspace. Neither side has to rely on invisible state and/or context held only within a conversation. 

 How this creates a better training experience 

 Conversation remains the best way for a runner to describe subjective experiences such as fatigue, discomfort or a workout that was given up on. The workspace is better suited to displaying calendars, evidence and before-and-after comparisons. Your Last Coach lets each interface do what it does best. 

 A fresh coach agent can retrieve a structured Coaching Briefing, inspect the relevant workout(s) and preserve the runner’s feedback in their own words. Its recommendations then appear as an interactive review inside the training calendar rather than as a wall of text in chat. The runner can compare the options and explicitly approve one before anything changes. 

 Taken together, these make for a more collaborative and grounded coaching experience, where the runner can have full confidence that they are receiving a training plan that's truly personalised for them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 I built Your Last Coach as a client-side React and TypeScript application with one authoritative workspace state shared by both the visible interface and the WebMCP tools. This prevents the agent and runner from looking at separate versions of the training plan. 

 The page exposes six tools covering the coaching journey: 

 
 Retrieving the Coaching Briefing 
 Reading the workout plan and any completed workout results 
 Recording the runner’s feedback 
 Opening a window for the runner to review plan changes 
 Retrieving the runner’s decision. 
 

 A structured interaction contract helps a fresh agent discover the intended workflow without requiring a custom prompt or skill. 

 Recommendations are validated by the application and presented as two ranked options in a native review window. The plan is updated atomically when the runner presses “Adapt my plan”. The new plan version and an adaptation receipt are then available to both the runner and agent. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 As WebMCP was completely new to me at the start of this project, the main challenge was in learning about how it worked, and brainstorming how I could build my product around this emerging framework. This also forced me to consider the various trade-offs between using WebMCP versus other methods (e.g. for providing my agent with the necessary context so a fresh session can hit the ground running). 

 Other related challenges were around figuring out the limitations of WebMCP, particularly where it's supported at the moment, since it's still a new concept. For example, I stumbled a little when working in Codex Cloud sessions, as I did not realise that WebMCP wasn't supported in the cloud browser at the time of working on this. 

 Miscellaneous challenges would be, of course, managing the scope of this submission despite my lofty goals for the final product. I wanted to showcase the key features of WebMCP, without creating an overly convoluted demo product. Time was also a limiting factor here, as I had to compress most of the work into a weekend. For the challenges I faced throughout this experience, I'm pretty proud of the outcome and of myself :) 

 What's next for Your Last Coach 

 This demo currently contains synthetic data, so the obvious next step would be to incorporate real health and workout data from my fitness tracker using the COROS MCP. This will require architectural considerations around automating data egress/ingress, storage, security, etc. 

 In terms of features, I will likely expand the idea of "monitoring topics" as valuable slowly changing context. An early example visible in the demo app today is a topic on an ongoing shin injury. These are important for coaches to know about, but also requires careful planning around mutability, since the state of these topics changes over time, and we would not want our agent coach to plan around topics that are no longer relevant, but still are useful to keep in mind down the line. 

 Longer-term extensions could be around running-adjacent parts of training, such as nutrition and strength exercises. I firmly believe agent coaches are more than capable of performing at close to the level of human coaches when given the right context about the runner, and I hope to build an agent coaching system that gets me there.

title: MCPx
pitch: A reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows, giving AI agents durable execution, uncertainty-aware recovery, and human-approved compensation across web applications.
about_excerpt: A reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows, giving AI agents durable execution, uncertainty-aware recovery, and human-approved compensation across web applications. Like Comment Story Updates MCPx — a reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows. A real AI Operations Agent observes application state and delegates consequential multi-service operations to MCPx after human approval. Every workflow transition is persisted in a PostgreSQL-backed transaction ledger for inspection and recovery. After approval, MCPx compensates completed operations in reverse dependency order and verifies remote resource removal. Routing recovers from an uncertain write, Frontend fails before commit, and MCPx pauses before destructive compensation for human approval. Inspiration While building with WebMCP, I kept thinking about one question: What happens if an agent performs an action, the application successfully makes the change, but the response never gets back to the agent? For example, imagine an agent creates a routing rule. The route is successfully created, but the acknowledgement gets lost. From the agent's point of view, it looks like the request failed. But did it actually fail? If the agent simply retries, it could create the same resource twice. If it assumes the action worked, it could continue a workflow based on something that may not exist. The problem gets even harder when an agent is working across several applications. Maybe the first three actions succeed and the fourth fails. Now you have resources left behind and someone has to figure out what actually happened. That was the idea behind MCPx . WebMCP makes structured agent actions possible. MCPx makes those actions reliable. What it does MCPx is a reliability runtime for multi-step WebMCP workflows. The main idea is simple. For consequential actions, MCPx thinks about three things: Execute → Inspect → Compensate For example: create_route → get_route → delete_route Execute performs the action. Inspect asks the application for the actual state of that action. Compensate provides a way to safely undo it if the larger workflow fails. This becomes especially useful when something goes wrong after an action has already been sent. Instead of immediately assuming failure, MCPx can put the operation into an explicit state called IN_DOUBT . It then asks the application that owns the resource for ground truth. If the resource actually exists: IN_DOUBT → RECONCILING → RECOVERED The workflow continues without blindly performing the original mutation again. If something later fails for certain, MCPx stops the workflow and asks the human operator before performing destructive rollback. Once approved, it compensates the completed operations in reverse dependency order and checks each application again to confirm that the resources created by that transaction are gone. Why WebMCP? This is where WebMCP became particularly interesting to me. The applications involved in a workflow should remain the source of truth for their own resources. MCPx should not need direct access to every application's database just to determine whether an operation succeeded. Instead, each application can expose structured capabilities through WebMCP. In MCPx, the reference applications register tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The MCPx Browser Runner discovers tools from the authorized applications using: document.modelContext.getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) It then executes the native browser tools through: document.modelContext.executeTool(...) So MCPx coordinates the workflow, while each WebMCP application still owns and understands its own state. That separation is a big part of the project. The demo I built a four-step reference workflow to show what happens when things don't go perfectly: Database → Compute → Routing → Frontend Database succeeds. Compute succeeds. Routing is where things get interesting. For the demo, I intentionally inject an acknowledgement-loss fault after the Routing service commits its resource. MCPx doesn't know yet whether the write happened, so Routing becomes IN_DOUBT . Instead of blindly calling create_route again, MCPx calls get_route . The Routing application confirms that the route actually exists, so MCPx marks the operation RECOVERED and continues. Then Frontend deliberately rejects before committing its operation. This is a confirmed failure, so the transaction stops in AWAITING_COMPENSATION_APPROVAL . The human operator can see what happened and approve the rollback. MCPx then compensates: Routing → Compute → Database After every compensation, it calls the application's inspection tool again to verify that the resource created by this transaction is actually absent. The transaction finally reaches COMPENSATED . Humans and agents working together I didn't want MCPx to become another AI agent. I wanted it to solve a different problem. The way I think about the architecture is: The agent decides what should happen. The human controls important safety boundaries. MCPx makes sure the multi-step operation is executed reliably. WebMCP gives MCPx structured capabilities to work with across the applications. To test that idea outside the MCPx dashboard, I integrated MCPx with FileFlow , a distributed file-processing project I had already built. During the challenge, I extended FileFlow with an AI Operations Agent. The agent can observe real information about the FileFlow pipeline, including queue state, worker heartbeat and failed jobs. For low-risk situations, such as an eligible failed job, the agent can take a bounded recovery action itself. But when it wants to perform a consequential multi-service workspace operation, it asks for human confirmation and then delegates the actual workflow to MCPx through @mcpxx/sdk . That separation became one of my favourite parts of the project: the agent doesn't need to reinvent retries, reconciliation, rollback and transaction durability every time it wants to do something consequential. How I built it MCPx is a TypeScript monorepo containing: a Next.js coordinator and control plane a browser WebMCP Runner a PostgreSQL-backed transaction and event ledger a DAG workflow engine execute / inspect / compensate reliability contracts explicit IN_DOUBT , RECONCILING and RECOVERED states human-approved compensation post-compensation verification four independent WebMCP reference applications the @mcpxx/sdk package for external applications and agents One architectural rule was particularly important to me: MCPx should not secretly bypass WebMCP for the actual reference-service mutations. The SDK can submit a workflow to the MCPx coordinator, but the work waits for an active browser runner. The Browser Runner discovers the appropriate WebMCP tool from the application's origin and executes it through the browser. The result is then reported back to the durable coordinator. Challenges I ran into One of the hardest bugs came from RegisteredTool . At first, it seemed reasonable to discover a WebMCP tool, store it and execute it later. That didn't work. A native RegisteredTool contains browser-owned context associated with the page or frame that registered it. Treating it like normal serializable data caused execution to fail. The solution was to store only the tool's metadata. When MCPx actually needs to execute something, the Browser Runner discovers the tools again and passes the fresh native RegisteredTool directly to executeTool(...) . Another challenge was changing how I thought about failure. I initially thought mostly in terms of success and failure. But after a request has been dispatched, there is a third possibility: we simply don't know yet. That is why IN_DOUBT became such an important state in MCPx. The final challenge was rollback. Calling a delete operation isn't enough to prove cleanup happened. MCPx therefore inspects the owning application after compensation and only considers that step compensated when the resource is confirmed absent. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from building MCPx is that reliable agent systems need to be comfortable saying: "I don't know what happened yet." Agents are getting much better at deciding what actions to take. But once those actions have real side effects across multiple applications, another set of problems appears: partial success, lost acknowledgements, duplicate operations, recovery and cleanup. I don't think every AI agent should have to solve those problems itself. MCPx is my exploration of what a reusable reliability layer for consequential WebMCP workflows could look like. Challenge work disclosure MCPx was built from scratch during the WebMCP Challenge. This includes the coordinator, Browser Runner, transaction engine, reliability contracts, WebMCP reference applications, control plane and @mcpxx/sdk . FileFlow existed before the challenge and is used here as an external application consuming MCPx. During the challenge, I extended FileFlow with i

title: Cobweb - WebMCP enabled Micropython IDE
pitch: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval.
about_excerpt: Cobweb is a zero-install browser IDE bringing WebMCP to physical hardware: AI agents can probe microcontrollers, edit device files, run MicroPython code live, and debug boards with human approval. Like Comment Story Updates 💡 Inspiration Physical computing and IoT have always promised an exciting world of creativity—turning code into blinking LEDs, motor movements, robotics, and environmental sensors. Yet for beginners, educators, and even seasoned makers, the onboarding experience is plagued by toolchain friction: Hunting down and installing OS-specific USB-to-UART drivers (CH340, CP2102, FTDI). Configuring desktop IDEs like Thonny, Arduino IDE, or heavy VS Code toolchains. Juggling serial baud rates, COM port drops, and manual file transfer scripts. With modern browser capabilities like the Web Serial API and File System Access API , we realized that the entire embedded development lifecycle could run 100% inside the browser with zero installation . When WebMCP was introduced as an open standard for agentic web applications, we asked a fundamental question: Why should AI agents only interact with web forms, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools? What if an AI agent had physical hands on hardware? Cobweb was born to bridge this divide—creating a zero-install MicroPython IDE where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly to probe, code, execute, and debug physical microcontrollers. ⚡ What it Does Cobweb turns any Chromium browser into a full-featured MicroPython development environment that connects directly to microcontrollers (such as Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32, or BBC micro:bit) over Web Serial at $115{,}200\text{ baud}$. Key capabilities include: Zero-Install Python IDE : Code editor powered by CodeMirror 6 with syntax highlighting, automatic indenting, and multi-file local storage. Interactive xterm.js REPL : Direct serial connection with live terminal streaming, ANSI color rendering, and raw-paste mode. Device Filesystem Management : Browse, read, write, edit, and delete files stored on the microcontroller's onboard flash memory. Deep WebMCP Integration : Exposes 15+ fine-grained, structured tools to external AI agents via document.modelContext.registerTool . Human-in-the-Loop Safety : Every mutating agent action (flashing files, modifying code, running hardware commands) triggers an interactive approval modal with live side-by-side diff previews before anything touches the physical board. Board Hardware Notes : Persistent scratchpad where the agent and user track pin mappings (e.g., $I^2C$ SDA/SCL pins, SPI buses, ADC channels, and sensor addresses). 🛠️ How We Built It Cobweb is built as a pure client-side Progressive Web App (PWA) with no backend servers or cloud dependencies: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ External AI Agent │ │ (ChatGPT / Chrome with WebMCP) │ └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ │ WebMCP JSON-RPC / Tools API ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Cobweb WebApp │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ WebMcpBridge.tsx │◄─────►│ Tool Registry │ │ │ │ (use-webmcp-tool) │ │ (15+ Structured Tools) │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ └───────────┬────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ CobwebApproval Modal│ │ ReplInterface (TS) │ │ │ │ (Live Diffs) │ │ (Raw REPL State Mach.) │ │ │ └─────────────────────┘ └────────────┬───────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┘ │ Web Serial API ▼ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ Physical Board (Pico) │ └───────────────────────────┘ 1. The WebMCP Bridge ( WebMcpBridge.tsx ) We utilized use-webmcp-tool to dynamically expose our tool registry to the browser's model context: useWebMCP({ name: def.name, description: def.description, inputSchema: def.parameters, async execute(args) { if (def.requiresApproval) { const approved = await requestApproval({ id, name: def.name, args }); if (!approved) throw new Error('Tool execution rejected by user.'); } return await tool.call(args, {}); } }); 2. High-Performance Serial Communication ( ReplInterface.ts ) MicroPython communication relies on a custom finite state machine implementing the raw-REPL protocol : Raw Mode Entry : The host sends \x01 ($\text{Ctrl-A}$) to enter raw REPL. Raw-Paste Windowing : To prevent buffer overrun on microcontrollers with constrained RAM ($\approx 264\text{ KB}$ on RP2040), we implement dynamic flow control: $$\text{Chunk Size} \le W_{\text{window}}, \quad \text{replenished by } \text{\textbackslash x01 bytes}$$ Execution & Stream Separation : Code is executed via \x04 ($\text{Ctrl-D}$), returning structured stdout and stderr delimited by end-of-transmission bytes: $$\text{Banner} \longrightarrow \text{OK} \longrightarrow \text{stdout} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04} \longrightarrow \text{stderr} \longrightarrow \text{\textbackslash x04}$$ Queue Serialisation : An AsyncBlockingQueue<Uint8Array> safely decouples serial reads from async execution promises while mirroring bytes to xterm.js . 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 1. Single-Channel Serial Contention The Web Serial port is a single, non-multiplexed stream. If a user is typing in the REPL while an AI agent attempts to run get_board_info or read_device_file , raw bytes interleave and corrupt the state. Solution : We built a single-slot promise lock chain for all read/write/eval calls ( send , sendRaw , reset ), ensuring strict atomicity without blocking UI rendering or serial event dispatching. 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 100% Client-Side Architecture : Zero backend servers, zero telemetry, zero credential relay. Everything runs directly between the user's browser and their USB port. True Agentic Physical Computing : An AI agent running in ChatGPT or Chrome can inspect the board identity ( os.uname().machine ), write sensor drivers, execute test snippets, and diagnose hardware errors in real time. Rich Human-Agent Co-Pilot Experience : Instead of replacing the human, WebMCP in Cobweb creates a fluid dialogue where the human handles breadboarding and hardware wiring, while the agent handles MicroPython syntax, pin registers, and driver debugging. 📚 What We Learned WebMCP is a Game Changer for Browser Capabilities : Traditional desktop agent tools require complex native MCP servers (stdio/SSE over localhost). WebMCP brings tool calling directly to the browser DOM and Web APIs, making cutting-edge capabilities like Web Serial, Web Bluetooth, and File System Access instantly accessible to AI agents. Structured Tools Beat Vision/DOM Scraping : Prior to WebMCP, agents navigating web IDEs had to guess button positions or scrape xterm canvases. With WebMCP, tool calls are typed, deterministic, and instant. title: Vitals Incident Room
pitch: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together.
about_excerpt: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vitals Incident Room Dashboard Vitals Incident Room Agent Capabilities Vitals Incident Room Architecture Inspiration Vitals started with a simple frustration: when a production incident happens, engineers rarely investigate it in one place. They jump between dashboards, logs, traces, deployment history, alerts, and remediation tools, manually connecting the dots under pressure. While exploring WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to rethink that workflow. AI agents are increasingly capable of reasoning about complex engineering problems, but traditionally they have had to interact with web applications through the UI or through completely separate integrations. That creates a gap between what an agent can reason about and what it can actually do. So I asked: What if the observability application itself could expose its capabilities directly to an AI agent, while the engineer and agent remained in the same workspace? That became Vitals Incident Room , an experiment in what an agent-native incident-response workflow could look like. I wanted to go beyond "add a chatbot to a dashboard." The goal was to make the agent a genuine participant in the incident lifecycle while keeping the human in control of consequential decisions. What it does Vitals Incident Room is a WebMCP-powered incident-response workspace where engineers and AI agents investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. For demonstration, a checkout-api service experiences a severe latency and error-rate regression shortly after deployment v2.8.3 . The agent can discover and invoke structured WebMCP tools to: inspect service health, query metrics, compare deployments, inspect distributed traces, search operational logs, analyze the gathered evidence, prepare a remediation, apply an approved remediation, verify recovery. The investigation can look like: get_service_health ↓ query_metrics ↓ compare_deployments ↓ inspect_trace ↓ search_logs ↓ analyze_incident The agent correlates those signals and identifies the most likely cause: a database query regression introduced in v2.8.3 . It can then prepare a rollback to the last known-good version. However, the agent cannot authorize its own action. prepare_remediation ↓ HUMAN APPROVAL ↓ apply_remediation ↓ verify_recovery ↓ RESOLVED The remediation changes the application's simulated system state, and the final verification checks that both latency and error rate have actually returned to acceptable levels. The result is a shared workflow rather than a chatbot sitting beside an observability dashboard. How I built it Vitals Incident Room extends existing Vitals observability work with a focused browser-based Incident Room designed specifically around WebMCP. The application is built with TypeScript and React, with a deterministic simulated observability environment so the complete workflow can be reproduced without requiring real production credentials or infrastructure. The architecture separates the WebMCP layer from the application domain: Architecture Layer Component Responsibility Human Engineer Reviews evidence and authorizes consequential actions Web App Incident Room Presents shared incident state and workflow Agent Interface WebMCP Tool Surface Exposes structured capabilities to the AI agent Agent AI Agent Discovers tools, gathers evidence, analyzes the incident, and executes approved actions Observability Metrics · Logs · Traces · Deployments Provides the signals used for diagnosis Analysis Evidence Correlation Combines signals into a ranked root-cause hypothesis Remediation Prepare → Approve → Execute Proposes and safely applies the remediation Verification Recovery Checks Confirms latency and error-rate recovery before resolution Core flow: Engineer → Incident Room → WebMCP → AI Agent → Observability Data → Evidence Analysis → Remediation Proposal → Human Approval → Execution → Verification The WebMCP layer exposes nine focused tools with explicit schemas and annotations. Read-only investigation capabilities are separated from state-changing operations, and operational logs are explicitly treated as untrusted content. I also made the demo stateful. A rollback doesn't simply change a label from "failed" to "resolved"; it changes the simulated deployment, latency, error rate, and database-query performance. Verification then reads that new state. This gives us a deterministic cause-and-effect loop: v2.8.3 ↓ latency regression ↓ agent investigation ↓ rollback to v2.8.2 ↓ metrics recover ↓ incident resolved Most importantly, I designed the human approval boundary outside the WebMCP action surface. The agent can prepare a remediation, but only the engineer can authorize it. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding how much of Vitals to expose. Vitals already covers a broad observability workflow, and my first instinct was to make everything agent-accessible. That quickly became the wrong direction. A large collection of loosely connected tools would demonstrate API coverage, but not why WebMCP fundamentally changes the product. I narrowed the project to one complete incident-response journey and treated everything else as secondary. Another challenge was making an agent-driven workflow believable without depending on real production infrastructure. I solved that with deterministic metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and mutable runtime state. This lets us make the entire experience reproducible while preserving realistic relationships between the signals. I also had to think carefully about authority and safety. An agent that can investigate an incident and then immediately authorize its own rollback creates a dangerous feedback loop. I separated proposal, approval, execution, and verification so the human remains responsible for the consequential decision. Finally, WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, so I had to pay close attention to tool schemas, browser support, registration behavior, tool annotations, and the difference between a WebMCP-capable webpage and the agent consuming those tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that the project evolved beyond a conventional "AI + dashboard" demo. The agent can actually compose multiple capabilities exposed by the webpage: Health + Metrics + Deployment history + Traces + Logs ↓ Evidence-based diagnosis I'm also proud of the human-in-the-loop safety model. A consequential action cannot be executed until it has been explicitly authorized by the engineer, and recovery is not declared until the post-action state passes verification. Another accomplishment is that the demo is completely deterministic. I can reset the environment and reproduce the same incident, investigation, remediation, and recovery sequence without relying on external production systems. Incident Room also deliberately treat operational log data as untrusted content. That distinction matters in an agentic environment because data discovered by a tool should not automatically become an instruction to the agent. Most importantly, Vitals Incident Room gave us a concrete answer to a question the project started with: What does an observability application look like when an AI agent is a first-class participant rather than an add-on chatbot? What I learned My biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most interesting when it changes the workflow, not when it merely exposes functions. A collection of tools is easy to demonstrate. Designing a workflow in which an agent can discover, compose, and act on those tools while sharing state with a human is much more interesting. I also learned that tool design is effectively part of product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, output structures, side-effect annotations, and error behavior all influence how reliably an agent can use an application. Another important lesson was to separate: Evidence ↓ Analysis ↓ Authorization ↓ Action ↓ Verification That separation made the application easier to reason about and gave us a much clearer safety model. Finally, I learned that the best agent experiences are not necessarily fully autonomous. In many engineering workflows, the strongest design is agent speed + human judgment . What's next for Vitals Incident Room This challenge version is intentionally focused on one incident-response journey. The next step is to connect that workflow to real observability infrastructure. Future versions could support real Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, production log providers, deployment systems, and runbooks while preserving the same WebMCP interaction model. I also want to explore richer agent collaboration, including: incident timelines that agents can continuously update, safer remediation strategies such as canary changes, richer evidence graphs and dependency analysis, post-incident report generation, agent permissions based on risk and environment, multiple engine

 Inspiration
We’ve all watched AI agents struggle with simple web tasks. An agent might successfully navigate a site, but when it comes to e-commerce, it often hallucinates product specs, misreads prices, or gets completely derailed by dynamic DOM elements. We realized that asking agents to "guess" their way through a UI is a fundamentally flawed paradigm.
When we discovered WebMCP, it was a lightbulb moment. Instead of forcing agents to scrape and interpret UI, what if the website explicitly defined how it could be used? We built GiftGenie to prove this paradigm shift. E-commerce requires high accuracy and reliability, making it the perfect testing ground to show how an agent-native web app creates a vastly superior experience when humans and agents collaborate.
What it does
GiftGenie is a micro e-commerce platform designed from the ground up for human-agent collaboration. Instead of a human endlessly scrolling and filtering, they simply state their intent (e.g., "Find a $50 gift for my dad who loves gardening"). 

 The AI agent then takes over, utilizing three structured WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_gifts: Instantly filters the catalog based on interests, budget, and relationship. 
 get_gift_details: Fetches exact shipping times, reviews, and specs (guaranteeing zero hallucinations). 
 reserve_gift: Securely holds the chosen item for 15 minutes. 
 

 The agent presents the best options and handles the tedious research, but the human always retains the final creative and financial decision. 

 How I built it:
We wanted a lightning-fast, highly responsive frontend to showcase the WebMCP integration. 

 
 Frontend: Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS. We used a split-screen layout: a chat interface on the left for the agent, and a dynamic product/reservation panel on the right. 
 Data: To keep the focus on the interaction model, we used a locally hosted products.json file with 12 highly curated items. 
 WebMCP Integration: The core magic lives in src/webmcp/registerTools.ts. On app mount, we use the native browser API to register our tools: 
 

 document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_gifts",
 description: "Search the curated gift catalog based on recipient interests, budget, and relationship.",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 interests: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } },
 budget_max: { type: "number" },
 relationship: { type: "string" }
 },
 required: ["interests", "budget_max"]
 },
 execute: async (input) => { /* Filters and returns structured JSON */ }
}); 

 I tested the entire flow natively using Google Chrome with the chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag enabled, ensuring seamless communication between the in-browser agent and our exposed tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Schema Precision: Initially, our inputSchema was too loose, causing the LLM to occasionally pass strings instead of arrays for the interests parameter. We had to rigorously tighten the JSON schema and improve the tool descriptions to enforce strict typing. 
 Agent-UI Synchronization: We wanted the visual UI to update in real-time when the agent called a tool in the background (e.g., visually adding an item to the "Reserved" panel while the agent was still typing its response). Bridging the gap between the background WebMCP tool execution and the React state required careful event handling. 
 Description Engineering: We learned that the description field of a tool is just as critical as the code. We had to iterate on the natural language descriptions to ensure the agent understood exactly when to use get_gift_details versus just summarizing the initial search results. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Zero Hallucinations: Because the agent relies strictly on the structured JSON returned by get_gift_details, it never invents product specs or prices. The reliability is 100%. 
 The "Handoff" Experience: We successfully created a fluid loop where the agent does the heavy analytical lifting, but seamlessly hands control back to the human for the final creative choice. 
 Flawless WebMCP Execution: Getting the document.modelContext API working perfectly in the Chrome testing environment on a tight 48-hour deadline. 
 

 What we learned
Designing for AI agents is fundamentally different from designing for humans. Humans will forgive a clunky UI or a confusing layout; an agent will just fail completely if the data structure is ambiguous. We learned that building for the "agent-native web" requires a shift in mindset: Tool descriptions are prompts. Writing clear, boundary-defining descriptions for WebMCP tools is just as important as writing the execution logic itself.

title: Roomwright
pitch: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In September 2024 I moved to a new country, into an empty apartment I'd only seen in photos. A year later, almost to the week, I moved again. Different place, same problem. Both times it went like this: you stand in the middle of a bare room with a phone full of furniture tabs and no real sense of scale, you order things that don't quite fit, and you spend evenings pushing an imaginary couch around in your head. It isn't just me. Every fall a wave of people do exactly this: new students, new arrivals, first apartments, furnishing a room they can only picture in fragments. What you want in that moment is simple: what do I need, how would it look, what will it cost, and once it's all in, is there any floor left to stand on? That's a planning problem, and planning is exactly what an agent should be good at. But a chatbot can only describe your room back to you. It can't move anything in it. WebMCP changes that: a page can hand its own capabilities to an agent as tools. So I built the page worth handing over. What it does Roomwright is a 3D room planner that runs entirely in the browser. You draw a room, set the doors and windows, and place furniture from a catalogue of parametric pieces. Every item has real dimensions and required clearances. Orbit it, drop to a floor plan, resize or recolor anything, and it keeps a running shopping list with a total. Every one of those actions is exposed to an agent as a WebMCP tool . There are 19 of them. So instead of clicking, you can say: "Studio apartment, 4.6 by 7 metres, door on the south wall, two windows on the east. Bed against the back wall, a sofa splitting off the living area, a small dining set by the window." The agent reads the tools the page offers and builds the whole thing: resizing the room, cutting the openings, furnishing three zones, running the planner's own clearance checks, catching its own overlaps, and fixing them. Then you take over: "turn the sofa toward the TV, lose that chair." Same room, same undo history, you and the agent trading turns on one canvas. How WebMCP powers it The key decision: the UI and the agent mutate the exact same state. There's a single store, and a button click and a tool call go through the same action. So undo/redo, autosave, shareable-URL persistence, and live layout validation all just work for the agent. There is no agent-specific code path for any of them. Tools register against document.modelContext using the spec's AbortSignal lifecycle, in four groups: Read : get_room , list_catalog , get_shopping_list Build : add_item (resolves a product by id, name, or fragment, so the agent never has to guess), create_custom_item , duplicate_item (with an east-west / north-south mirror so "a chair on each side" is actually symmetric), remove_item Arrange and check : move_item , rotate_item , resize_item , set_variant , set_room_dimensions , set_opening , remove_opening , suggest_spot (grids the room and returns candidate positions), check_layout (overlaps, blocked doors/windows, clearance failures, walkways under 0.75 m, narrowest gap) Show : select_item (highlights a piece, opens its inspector), set_view , reset_layout suggest_spot and check_layout matter most. They give the agent a feedback loop, not just setters. It places, checks, notices a conflict, and re-plans, visibly, in the activity log. How I built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite React Three Fiber + drei + @react-three/postprocessing for synthetic image-based lighting (no HDRI file), real shadow-mapped shadows, screen-space AO, and a restrained post pass Parametric furniture : every piece is authored geometry keyed on its kind, not a glTF download, so the bundle stays small and every dimension is real Zustand for the single shared store, Tailwind CSS v4 for the UI Device-aware quality tiers (High / Medium / Low, auto-detected from the GPU string and core count, with a live framerate monitor that steps down) so it runs on a laptop, not just a workstation Deployed on GitHub Pages Challenges The spec is still moving. Early references used navigator.modelContext ; the current spec uses document.modelContext and has no unregisterTool . You unregister by aborting an AbortSignal . I probe both and use the signal lifecycle, with a short retry in case the host injects the API after first paint. Shared post-processing broke drei's ContactShadows. EffectComposer sets gl.autoClear = false , and ContactShadows relies on autoClear to wipe its render target, so moving a piece smeared shadow trails across the floor. Fixed by dropping ContactShadows for a directional shadow map plus per-frame screen-space AO. The agent kept guessing product ids. It saw sofa-halden and tried coffee-milo (the real id is table-milo ). Fuzzy resolution plus returning the full catalogue on a miss fixed it in one step. Symmetry. duplicate_item offset copies by a fixed diagonal, so "a lounge chair on each side" never mirrored. Added a real mirror across the room's centre line, and floor lamps now auto-aim at the room centre so a mirrored pair points the right way. Testing WebMCP is hard today. Only ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser exposes document.modelContext (plus Chrome 149 behind a flag), and it's gated by account type. What I learned The leverage in WebMCP isn't the tool calls. It's the shared state . The moment the agent and the human mutate the same model, everything the app already does (undo, validation, persistence) becomes something the agent does too, for free. Design the state model well and the agent integration is almost nothing. And tool descriptions are the API. Fuzzy product resolution, mirror options, and full-catalogue errors did more for reliability than any prompting. The agent behaves well when the tools let it. What's next Real glTF furniture and user uploads, photo-assisted room capture, L-shaped and multi-room layouts, a path-traced render mode. And a retailer-facing version: drop these tools onto product pages, and every shopping agent can lay out a real room instead of guessing. title: Mechanism Canvas
pitch: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner.
about_excerpt: An organic chemistry canvas where WebMCP agents test competing mechanisms, show their evidence, and leave the final move to the learner. Like Comment Story Updates Mechanism Canvas lets agents test competing chemistry paths while the learner keeps control of the final answer. The learner sets agent permissions, hint limits, and commit authority before any agent work begins. The agent explores competing mechanisms in isolated branches while the learner’s draft stays sealed. A deterministic validator rejects the incomplete path and approves the complete SN2 mechanism. The Observatory reveals available tools, agent actions, validator results, and the full proof trail. The agent can return a checked proposal, but only the learner can move it onto the canvas. After reviewing the evidence, the learner commits the approved electron-flow mechanism. An interactive 3D inspector connects curved-arrow reasoning with molecular geometry and lone pairs. About Mechanism Canvas Inspiration I kept coming back to a mismatch between how students solve organic chemistry problems and how AI tutors usually communicate. Reaction mechanisms live in diagrams. The important details are the atoms, bonds, lone pairs, curved arrows, and the order in which electrons move. A separate chat window sees almost none of that unless the student stops and translates the drawing into prose. Giving an agent broad control of the drawing surface creates a different problem. It can finish the exercise before the learner has worked through it. I wanted to see whether an agent could help inside the real mechanism canvas while the student still controlled the consequential part: what actually gets added to the answer. That became the central idea behind Mechanism Canvas. The agent gets a safe place to explore. The page checks the chemistry. The learner decides what comes back. What I built Mechanism Canvas is an organic chemistry workspace where a student and a WebMCP agent can work with the same structured mechanism. The page exposes meaningful chemistry objects instead of screen coordinates, so the agent can refer to a particular atom, bond, lone pair, or revision without guessing from pixels. The main demo is a counterfactual (S_\mathrm{N}2) lab. The agent tests two electron-flow paths away from the learner's draft. In the first branch, it forms the new bond but forgets the coupled leaving-group cleavage. The production validator rejects that attempt. The second branch contains both moves, so the validator approves it. The checked branch then reaches a visible proposal gate. It still does not change the learner's mechanism. The learner can inspect the evidence, add the proposal to the draft, request one more check, and make the final commit. An incorrect agent attempt becomes useful evidence instead of damage that has to be undone. The site also works as a complete manual tutor when WebMCP is unavailable. Direct agent collaboration is an extra layer on top of the same interface rather than a separate agent-only experience. How I built it I built the app with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The mechanism canvas is backed by a structured graph with stable IDs for atoms, bonds, electron sources, and curved-arrow moves. A deterministic chemistry engine evaluates proposed steps against six reviewed fixtures. The model can suggest and explore, but it does not decide whether a mechanism is chemically valid. The WebMCP layer registers 26 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool uses a closed JSON schema and calls the same TypeScript store commands as the visible interface. Mutating calls re-read live state and check the current revision, scope, and learner-granted permissions before they run. Tool discovery changes with the task. Coach mode begins with 16 available tools. Opening the two-path lab adds the branch controls. Starting a six-action comparison session narrows the surface to the capabilities needed for that job. Once the action budget is used, the work tools disappear and only four evidence controls remain. A cached tool cannot restore access that the learner has already closed. I also built a Collaboration Contract where the learner sets the agent's maximum role and hint level. An intent-bound session freezes the job, problem, revision, and action budget. The Live Run Observatory shows which capability batches the host accepted, and a Proof Ledger records privacy-minimized before-and-after receipts from the actual tool callback boundary. Around that core, I added keyboard-operable SVG structures, local persistence, reversible commits, state diffs, electron-flow replay, and a lazy-loaded Three.js molecular inspector. The finished project is a static GitHub Pages site with no backend, account, or credentials required. Challenges The hardest engineering problem was keeping tool discovery honest while the page changed. A fixed list of 26 tools would technically work, but it would hide the learner's current intent inside descriptions. My first dynamic version swung too far in the other direction: every small store notification could publish a transient capability batch. Those batches were real, but they did not represent a stable state that a judge or learner could understand. I changed the registration layer to coalesce related updates, wait for the complete batch, and record only surfaces the host had accepted. Proof was another difficult part. A model saying that it called a tool is only a claim. I needed the page to show whether the callback ran, whether the expected state changed, and whether the main draft stayed untouched. The Proof Ledger now wraps the real callback boundary, and the Observatory evaluates its seven demo claims from those receipts. I also had to make failure safe without making it invisible. The two lab branches have real revisioned state and use the same validator as the main canvas, but they remain isolated until the learner chooses a checked proposal. That separation took more work than simply giving the agent an undo button. It is also the part that makes the workflow useful for learning. What I learned I learned that an agent's tool list is part of the user interface. A capability name, its schema, when it appears, and when it disappears all communicate authority. Encoding the learner's intent in that surface made the boundary much clearer than relying on prompt instructions alone. I also learned how well deterministic software and agent reasoning can complement each other. The agent is good at generating alternatives and explaining a choice. The chemistry engine is good at enforcing exact constraints every time. Keeping those jobs separate made the result easier to trust. Most of all, this project changed how I think about mistakes in learning software. A wrong attempt does not have to be erased or quietly corrected. When it is isolated, checked, and kept visible, it can show the learner exactly why the complete mechanism needs both electron-flow moves. What's next The current chemistry engine is intentionally limited to reviewed fixtures. I would like to add an instructor authoring flow for new mechanisms and study how different permission contracts affect the explanations students give. The same pattern could also work in circuit design, geometry, and other visual STEM tools where exploration is useful but ownership should stay with the learner. about_excerpt: Faultline is an AI educational app that teaches system design using WebMCP to make agents act like your favorite coworker who can see your work, see the results, and give you help without taking over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Faultline started after a friend quit his job and we began practicing system design interviews together. We could talk through architectures back and forth, but we kept asking the same question: is this actually right? I wanted a better way to practice than negotiating with an human/LLM for an answer. I wanted a game where you make a design decision and find out whether it works. What it does Faultline is a systems design/interview prep game. Fvery level gives you a problem, requirements, a workload, and a set of components; you design the system, and the simulator tells you the results. With WebMCP, an agent can join the live session, inspect the current design, and point out relevant parts of the canvas. Designed to act like another engineer in the room, the agent will help with questions but won't fully take over. Can also act to be interviewed where the agent will walk through realistic follow ups you might hear in a system design round. How we built it I started with the game itself. Parts like letting player build freely, simulator being the source of truth, and providing the agent with structured evidence from the components as opposed to the answer. Each level has its own rules, including what components are available, the performance of the components, and the requirements. For the agents I needed to decided for most states of the game what the agent might need to reasonable answer a question, and I did so through dynamically exposing tools, keeping data as fresh as possible, and intent routing for most common commands for reliable play. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the agent reliable while a player rapidly changes an architecture. It needs the most up to date info for every call, but resending every detail was too slow. The app needed to only be frustrating with the challenges, so the agent experience for help needed to be fast just as much as it needed high quality responses. Getting the right current context to the agent efficiently and providing it with only the tools necessary for the state took a lot of fiddling around with. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud of how the agents acts. I've had friends play with it, were unable to beat the level first couple tries and begrudgingly gave into using the coach, where they were surprised with the interactions. It really keeps you as the focus as just acts as a background tool so that you don't get stuck forever. This is best shown in the interview tool that asks follow up questions to let users practice the back and forths after designing the solution by using specific interviewer tools and keeping architecture facts straight as info changes. What we learned This was my first time working with WebMCP, and I learned a lot about building for external agents inside a app. In particular, I learned more about tool routing, intent routing, and evaluations for checking whether an agent picks the best tool for the moment. Was also first time I tried to make like an app with a wide spread audience over to fill specific niches/needs. What's next for Faultline I would like to make it a daily game where you do one game a day just to keep yourself sharp. I would also like to keep expanding the coach's toolset and personality. I think during interview process if it could change the rules of the simulation and make you live build to solve a question would be pretty interesting and fun. GitHub OAuth, used only as an optional identity provider. Vercel, used to host and deploy the live application. Open source dependencies including Next.js, React, React Flow, and related packages. title: ZipCheckup Agent
pitch: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have.
about_excerpt: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have. Like Comment Story Updates Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes - real federal data, not sample data. ZIP 01004: one metric known out of fourteen. Every other field returns an explicit unknown with its reason - never a zero. Michigan, lead under 0.005 mg/L: 466 passed, 209 failed, 492 excluded because nobody measured them. Shared state: the agent and the person write to the same list. Rows show who added them. A letter to the water utility, built only from facts on the record. Ten asserted, three unknowns turned into questions instead of claims. Inspiration Ask any assistant whether the drinking water at an address is safe. You will get a confident paragraph. It will often be wrong, and nothing on the page could have stopped it. Eighty-eight million Americans are served by a water system with a health-based violation on record. That number is not a guess - it is 4,268 of the 10,517 public water systems in the dataset behind this project. The information is public. It is just buried in federal databases in formats no homebuyer will ever open, so people ask a model instead, and the model reads a table cell and cannot tell a measured zero from a blank nobody filled in. Most projects in this hackathon will make it faster for a model to read a page. This one changes what a model is allowed to say. What it does Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes, 10,517 water systems, 282 million people . This is not sample data - it is ZipCheckup's production dataset, reviewed and accepted into the AWS Registry of Open Data, built from EPA SDWIS, published Consumer Confidence Reports and EPA radon zones. The agent can look up a ZIP, compare several, explain what a metric actually measures and against which legal threshold, search the whole country, write to a shortlist the person is watching, and draft a letter to the water utility. Two things make it different from a nicer API wrapper. First: a value cannot arrive naked. Lead comes back with the EPA action level of 0.015 mg/L and the citation 40 CFR Part 141 Subpart I in the same payload. The model cannot misquote a number it never read off a page, and cannot lose the threshold that gives the number meaning. Second: absence is never zero. When the public record holds no value, the tool returns an explicit unknown with the reason and a field stating what that absence does not prove. There is no code path in this project by which a missing measurement reaches an agent as 0 . Search a state for safe lead levels and you get three numbers, not one: measured and passing, measured and failing, and how many ZIPs nobody measured at all. For Michigan under 0.005 mg/L that is 466, 209, and 492 excluded for missing data - and the payload says, in words, that exclusion is a data gap and not a safety finding. That third number is the one every conventional site drops. It is also the one that decides whether a family trusts a house. What people and agents can do here that they could not before The shortlist is shared state, not a display. The agent's tool and the person's Add button call the same function in the same store. Rows carry who added them, flash when written, and can be deleted by the person. An activity log prints every call with its arguments and its known/unknown counts. So the person is not reading a report about what the model did. They are watching it work on the same object, and they can overrule it mid-flight. And the session ends with something they keep: a letter to the water system serving that address, composed only from facts whose status is known. An unknown value physically cannot reach the letter body, because the composer reads from nowhere else - everything unknown becomes a question to the utility instead of an accusation. When the dataset publishes no contact for that system, the tool returns resolution: "unresolved" and refuses to name a recipient rather than inventing a plausible one. An agent that will not name an address it cannot verify is a different kind of software than one that will. How I built it Six tools on document.modelContext.registerTool under one page-level AbortController . The badge in the header reads the registration back through getTools() , so it is evidence rather than a claim. "Revoke all" fires abort() and the count drops to zero live via toolchange - the correct demonstration of cancellation now that unregisterTool is gone from the spec. No framework, no bundler, no API key, no build step. Clone it and run npx serve web . Every compatibility decision was measured on Chrome 152, not read: navigator.modelContext is gone (the spec moved to document on 2026-04-23), getTools() is async and returns inputSchema as a string on Chrome 149-153, and title defaults to "" rather than undefined . Any one of those silently breaks a live demo. For browsers without native WebMCP, the page vendors the polyfill as a pinned 24 KB IIFE. For judges with no agent attached, an on-page console builds a form from each tool's own inputSchema . And scripts/mcp-bridge.mjs re-exposes whatever getTools() reports as a stdio MCP server, so agents outside a browser can drive it too - it hardcodes no tool names, so it tests the registration instead of reimplementing it. What I am proud of The honesty is enforced by code, not by discipline. One envelope module is the only exit from the data layer, so a missing value cannot become a zero anywhere downstream - not in a comparison, not in a ranking, not in a letter. 84 assertions run in real Chromium against the deployed URL , not localhost. They assert that no unknown is serialised as 0 , that an unmeasured ZIP is never ranked best or worst, that the word "unknown" cannot appear in a letter body, and that an agent's write renders a row the human can see, attributed to the agent. I pointed a real coding agent at the tools without telling it which to use. It found them from their descriptions, chained them, and carried the contract into its own prose unprompted: "These blanks do not mean zero, clean, compliant, or safe." That is the whole thesis working end to end, in a model I did not write. What I learned Registration takes an afternoon. Deciding what a tool is allowed to say takes the rest of the week - and that is the actual work of the agentic web. Once the page owns the shape of the answer instead of the model inferring it from markup, honesty stops being a prompt you hope holds and becomes a property you can enforce at the boundary. That generalises far past drinking water. What's next Every civic dataset in the country has this problem, and every one of them is about to be read by an agent instead of a person. Water is where I started because the stakes are legible - lead does not care whether the record was digitised. Next: the PFAS, flood, wildfire and air-quality layers already sitting in the same open dataset. The Chrome origin trial on the deployed domain, so any visitor on 149+ gets the native path with no flag. And then the ordinary web. Local service businesses answer the same three questions all day - do you serve my address, when are you free, what will it cost. Those are tools, not paragraphs. This project is the proof that an agent-callable page can be rigorous about what it does not know, which matters far more once the answer is about someone's home. video_transcript_excerpt: 88 million Americans are served by water system with a health based violation on record. That isn't a secret. It's public record spread across federal databases in formats nobody reads. I'm Artem Akulov and I made that record something an AI agent can actually use. Ask any assistant whether the water at an address is safe and you'll get a fluent paragraph. It's reading a web page. It can't tell a zero somebody measured from a blank nobody filled in. So it guesses at the health data. It guesses reassuringly. This page fixes that at the source. It publishes six tools through Web MCP. And an agent calls them like functions instead of scraping the screen. 42,000 US zip codes. Every value comes back with where it came from, when it was published, and the legal threshold it's judged against. Lead arrives with the EPA action level of 15 parts per billion and the regulation that sets it in the same payload. The model can't misquote the number. It never had to read off a page. And when a figure isn't in the public record, the tool says so and says why. It never returns a zero it doesn't have. Then it stops being a look up. This short list is shared state. The agent adds a zip and the row appears while I'm watching. Marked as added by the agent. I can change it. We're editing the same object, not passing messages about it. Search runs the whole country and returns three numbers instead of one. Measured and passing. Measured and failing. And how many zip codes nobody has measured at all. That third number is the one that usually disappears and it ends with something you keep. The agent drafts a letter to the water system serving that address. Built only from facts that are on the record. With everything else turned into a question rather than an accusation. If no contact is published for that utility, it refuses to invent one. The data set behind this is Zip Checkup's own, accepted into the AWS registry of open data, built from EPA drinking water records and published water quality reports covering 282 million people. The code is open, the data is CCBY, and it runs with no API key. Point an agent at it and it will tell you what's true, what isn't known, and what you can do about it. Thanks for watching.

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: codraw.app feat. humans & ai agents
pitch: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together.
about_excerpt: Real-time collaborative rooms where humans and AI agents draw together. Like Comment Story Updates codraw OG features features 2 demo room human dashboard Inspiration codraw.app is an interactive collaborative simple asset drawing app, where humans and agents can build on (humans via a browser, agentically: MCP, WebMCP, Skill+API, via the magic AI wand feature). What it does Open codraw.app with a WebMCP-enabled browser and your agent can: Draw with you, live. Shapes, batch pixels, flood fill, layers, undo — every stroke lands on the shared canvas in real time, next to yours and everyone else's. See before it paints. codraw_read_region returns the actual pixel colors of any area, so the agent works with what's there instead of over it. Move around the app. List rooms, create rooms, open a room, switch between a room's canvases, talk in the room chat. Tools register and unregister as you navigate — the page you're on defines what the agent can do. Play by the room's rules. Untrusted agents in moderated rooms get their work held in a pending queue, and the tool result says so. No special agent backdoor exists. The same tools also work outside the browser: a remote MCP server at codraw.app/mcp with OAuth 2.1 login (the agent acts as your account, with your per-room trust), and a plain HTTP API with a served skill file for curl and CI. One dispatcher handles all three, so the rules are identical everywhere. Every action is attributed. A room's history distinguishes humans, agents, and the in-app AI wand — "🤖 Claude Code acting as @joe", "✦ GLM 5.3 Flash prompted by @joe" — per stroke, per layer. And because every canvas has its own URL ( codraw.app/@you/game/sprites/hero/png exports it, PUT imports), what an agent paints, your build can pull. How we built it Go stdlib server (HTTP + WebSocket + SQLite), Vue 3 frontend. The WebMCP layer is one composable registering navigator.modelContext tools per view. The MCP server replays tool calls through the app's own router — no rule exists twice. OAuth 2.1 (discovery, dynamic client registration, PKCE, introspection) is stdlib-only on our auth service, D3BIT. Challenges we ran into Giving agents sight (the hex-grid read tool); scoping tools to SPA navigation; an OAuth discovery fallback that fetched /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server from the app origin and got HTML back — the app now mirrors the metadata; and keeping tool results honest about moderation instead of pretending success. Accomplishments that we're proud of A human and two kinds of agents; one in the browser via WebMCP, one headless via MCP with OAuth - drawing on the same canvas at the same time, under the same moderation, with every stroke attributed. We also deleted our API keys entirely: agent identity is user identity. What we learned Page-scoped tools beat a global toolbox: the current room is the context, and WebMCP lets the page say so. Honest tool results (moderation status, layer ids, coordinate conventions) matter more than tool count. Agents deserve real auth, not pasted secrets. What's next for codraw.app Sprite animation (layered cels, timeline, GIF export) with tools to build animations frame by frame; a graph view of who — human or agent — touched what; codraw Pro with AI credits. An open source codraw.app that can be run locally as well soon (MCP repo is open source). title: Triangulate
pitch: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together.
about_excerpt: Where researchers and their AI agents triangulate real DBS research evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Deep brain stimulation programming has no standard method — patients average 6.9 clinic visits in the first year alone just to get their settings right, for a device that stays implanted for a decade or more. The research trying to fix that is real and published, but it's scattered: an image-guided algorithm out of Berlin, sweet-spot mapping out of Bern, sensor-guided approaches, a foundational protocol from Toronto that's still the baseline everyone measures against. Nobody had put it in one place a researcher could actually search. That gap, and the WebMCP Challenge's push toward tools that agents can use as first-class citizens instead of scraping a UI, was the whole starting point. What it does Triangulate is a workbench, not a chatbot. A researcher — or their AI agent, through the exact same tools — can search a curated set of 14 verified DBS programming studies, compare methods side by side, ask for a research plan built from a question and a set of studies, save that plan, and export it as a cited brief. A sixth tool reaches live into Europe PMC for anything the curated set doesn't cover, clearly marked unreviewed so it's never confused with the vetted evidence. Six document.modelContext.registerTool() calls, all wired to the same functions the on-page buttons call. That's the actual fit with WebMCP: a generic chatbot answering "find me DBS studies" gives back unstructured prose that's gone once the chat scrolls. Triangulate instead exposes real, schema-constrained tools, so results stay structured and persistent in a shared workspace instead of trapped in a transcript, and tools chain reliably — search_studies into compare_protocols into build_research_plan — because each one's output is real data, not re-parsed guesses. That's also what's newly possible: because each tool's output is exactly the input the next one expects — a study id from search_studies is exactly what compare_protocols and build_research_plan take — an agent can chain a request like 'compare the Bayesian and sweet-spot studies, then draft a plan for tremor patients' into real, structured tool calls instead of hallucinating a summary of research it never structurally engaged with. I verified every tool individually, end to end, including the exact chain of ids each one expects from the last. How I built it React, TypeScript, and Vite, in a GitHub Codespace. I started with a five-study placeholder just to prove document.modelContext.registerTool() actually worked end to end, then went and pulled real citations — Charité Berlin's StimFit trial, Bern's ARTORG sweet-spot papers, the original Toronto Western algorithms, an industry-sponsored adaptive DBS trial — and built the dataset out to 14, each with a real, checkable link. The tools were built one at a time and tested in the WebMCP Inspector before moving to the next: search first, then compare, then the plan builder, then persistence, then the brief, then live search once we confirmed Europe PMC allows direct browser requests with no backend needed. The UI went through more than one real redesign once it became clear a wall of scrolling cards wasn't going to cut it for a 3-minute demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest one: document.modelContext.registerTool() throwing InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name under React's StrictMode double-invoke in dev. Fixing it properly meant switching every registration to the current WebMCP draft's AbortSignal -based cleanup instead of trying to manually unregister — unregisterTool() was actually dropped from the spec in April 2026 in favor of that pattern. Separately, I hit a real crash: two research plans saved to localStorage before a schema change didn't have a field the newer code expected, and reading .length on undefined took the whole page down. The fix was a small normalizePlan() function that backfills missing fields on load, which is now just standard practice for anything read back out of storage. I also had a longer stretch of the research-question text not actually influencing the plan output — it was stored but not used — which I caught by testing the same three studies with two different questions and noticing the output didn't change. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Fourteen real, independently checkable citations, not filler. Six tools that all survived direct testing, not just a demo run. A working live literature search against Europe PMC with zero backend, confirmed via a real CORS test rather than assumed. And a research-plan builder that actually reads the question — mentioning "tremor" in a question the selected studies don't cover surfaces that gap by name, first, before the generic ones. What I learned The most useful distinction I learned: document.modelContext is the production registration API; navigator.modelContextTesting is a separate, narrower API that only debugging tools like the WebMCP Inspector depend on. A tool can be fully registered and working for a real agent while a specific inspector extension still shows zero — which is exactly what happened to me, and cost real time to pin down with actual console checks instead of assumptions. I also came away with a firm rule for anything touching browser storage: never trust that old saved data matches your current schema, normalize on read. What's next for Triangulate Letting a researcher promote a live, unreviewed search result into the curated tier with one click after actually reading it — a lightweight path to growing the dataset without needing accounts or moderation infrastructure. Accounts themselves, so a saved workspace follows a researcher across devices instead of living in one browser's local storage. And growing the curated set past 14 as the literature does. title: OpenX
pitch: OpenX Portal is the unified mission control and execution harness for autonomous AI agents. Built as a high-performance monorepo
about_excerpt:
OpenX Portal is the unified mission control and execution harness for autonomous AI agents. Built as a high-performance monorepo
