 Inspiration 

 Small and growing suppliers often miss procurement opportunities because finding relevant tenders, understanding requirements, comparing options, and preparing documents can be time-consuming and fragmented. 

 BidLens was inspired by the need to make public procurement more approachable for Zimbabwean suppliers. We wanted to explore what happens when a procurement dashboard is designed for both people and AI agents from the beginning. 

 What it does 

 BidLens helps suppliers discover and evaluate procurement opportunities through a unified intelligence workspace. 

 Users can: 

 
 Search and filter procurement opportunities 
 Review supplier fit scores and eligibility requirements 
 Identify risks and missing documents 
 Compare two or three opportunities 
 Prepare bid workspaces with checklists and notes 
 Track preparation status and bid readiness 
 Browse opportunities and records through paginated interfaces 
 

 BidLens also exposes WebMCP tools that allow an AI agent to work with the application: 

 
 find_opportunities 
 investigate_opportunity 
 compare_opportunities 
 prepare_bid_workspace 
 update_bid_workspace 
 

 Read-only tools can be used directly by an agent. Actions that change application state require explicit human confirmation. 

 How we built it 

 BidLens was built as a React and TypeScript single-page application using Vite, TanStack Router, and Tailwind CSS. The application uses realistic demonstration data modelled on Zimbabwean e-GP procurement structures. 

 The WebMCP integration is implemented through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool has a clear description, structured JSON input schema, and an execution function connected to the application state. 

 The application is deployed on Cloudflare Pages, with SPA fallback routing configured so that nested pages remain accessible when loaded directly. 

 We tested the live application using ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser and Google Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was translating a complex procurement workflow into a clear experience that would be useful to both experienced suppliers and new users. 

 We also had to connect agent tool execution to React application state while keeping the interface predictable. Browser implementations may provide tool input as either an object or a serialized JSON string, so the tool layer was designed to handle both formats. 

 Another important challenge was deciding which actions should be automatic and which should require human approval. We chose to keep discovery and analysis read-only, while requiring confirmation before creating or updating bid workspaces. 

 Finally, we converted the application into a reliable static deployment while preserving nested routes, responsive layouts, pagination, and WebMCP registration. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Built a complete procurement intelligence experience rather than a standalone technical demo 
 Implemented five functional WebMCP tools 
 Connected WebMCP tools to live application state 
 Added human confirmation for state-changing actions 
 Deployed a working public application on Cloudflare Pages 
 Verified tool discovery and read-only tool execution in ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser 
 Added responsive layouts and pagination across the application's data-heavy views 
 Published the source code with an open-source license 
 Created a practical use case focused on suppliers and public procurement in Zimbabwe 
 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP works best when applications expose meaningful, task-oriented tools instead of forcing agents to reproduce every individual user-interface interaction. 

 Structured schemas make agent interactions more reliable, while clear tool descriptions help agents understand when each capability should be used. 

 We also learned that state-changing tools need strong human-in-the-loop safeguards. Agents can help users investigate and prepare decisions, but important procurement actions should remain transparent and explicitly approved. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP allows a website to become an active workspace where humans and agents can collaborate rather than treating AI as a separate chatbot layered on top of the product. 

 What's next for BidLens 

 The next stage is to connect BidLens to authorized live procurement feeds and persistent backend storage. 

 Future improvements include: 

 
 Supplier accounts and team collaboration 
 Real-time procurement notifications 
 Document extraction and compliance checking 
 More advanced tender and supplier matching 
 Audit logs for agent activity and human approvals 
 Persistent bid workspaces

title: SkyRingAI-WebMCP
pitch: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates.
about_excerpt: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates. Like 3 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Small-business owners using an AI receptionist accumulate valuable context across call analytics, transcripts, appointments, and assistant settings. Answering a question like “Which qualified callers need follow-up?” normally means navigating several screens and then switching to another workflow to act on the answer. Conventional browser agents must guess at controls and page state, which is brittle and especially risky when changing a live voice assistant. What it does SkyRingAI-WebMCP turns the authenticated SkyRingAI customer portal into a structured, agent-operable workspace. After the existing Supabase session resolves an active customer, the portal registers seven private WebMCP tools: get_dashboard_summary search_call_history get_call_details list_upcoming_appts get_assistant_config preview_assistant_update publish_assistant_update A customer can ask ChatGPT to summarize performance, find qualified calls, inspect a bounded transcript, list upcoming appointments, read the full receptionist configuration, and propose changes. Configuration changes use an explicit preview-before-publish workflow: the preview returns field-level differences and a short-lived ID; only a separate publish request saves the reviewed change. The production demo uses a dedicated non-admin judge account with isolated fictional records, a disposable VAPI assistant, and a live inbound demo number. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP contracts, seven-tool implementation, registration lifecycle, fixture provider, tests, and runnable sanitized demo—not the private commercial SaaS. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit because the useful unit is a trusted business operation, not a page click. An agent receives bounded tools with explicit schemas, read/write annotations, and authentication-derived scope instead of guessing how to traverse a dashboard. This lets a person and agent combine analytics, call discovery, transcript review, appointment context, and controlled action in one conversation. Tool inputs cannot select a customer or tenant. Stored transcript and database text is treated as untrusted, phone output is masked, and ranges, transcript size, pagination, and configuration fields are bounded. How we built it The tool layer is organized around a provider interface. The portal resolves the authenticated Supabase user and active customer, constructs a provider bound to that trusted context, validates tool inputs, repeats customer filters on production reads, and normalizes privacy-bounded results. An abortable lifecycle removes every private tool when the authenticated session ends. Assistant updates first read the complete current configuration so list replacements can preserve stable IDs. Greeting-only changes use the existing direct assistant path. Every effective non-greeting change must complete the authenticated N8N preview workflow before a publishable ID exists. Publishing accepts only that short-lived preview ID, and the server resolves the customer again before saving and requesting the downstream VAPI update. Challenge-period enhancement SkyRingAI existed before this challenge and briefly experimented with one small public, read-only WebMCP pricing tool plus declarative form annotations. During the submission period I built a substantial new authenticated customer-portal capability with Codex: seven tools spanning dashboard analytics, call search, bounded transcripts, appointments, complete assistant configuration, and preview-before-publish updates. I added the customer-scoped production provider, validation and privacy boundaries, lifecycle cleanup, controlled N8N mutation path, automated tests, dedicated production judge tenant, and separate open-source challenge repository. This expands the early experiment into a coherent, working business operations workflow. How I used AI and Codex ChatGPT is the runtime conversational control surface. VAPI powers the voice receptionist, and N8N powers the existing non-greeting configuration generation and update workflow. Codex was the primary engineering collaborator for architecture inspection, scoping, implementation, debugging, tests, security hardening, production verification, and open-source packaging. Lovable helped provision and verify the isolated production judge tenant through its connected Supabase and existing server integrations. The feature was tested live through ChatGPT from another machine. Accomplishments Seven authenticated WebMCP tools working in production. Customer identity derived from the trusted session, never a tool argument. Bounded outputs, masked phones, safe errors, strict schemas, and untrusted-content hints. Human-reviewable, single-use preview-before-publish assistant mutations. Real N8N preview/publish integration for non-greeting changes. Verified RLS isolation and a dedicated fictional judge environment. Runnable fixture-only open-source edition with no production credentials or customer data. Passing automated tests and production build. What I learned The most important lesson was that exposing more tools is not automatically better. Agent-native product design is about creating trustworthy operational boundaries: give the agent enough structured context to be useful, keep identity outside caller-controlled input, label untrusted data, constrain outputs, and separate “show me what would change” from “make the change.” What's next After the challenge, I plan to expand customer-controlled WebMCP workflows while keeping the same authentication, tenant, privacy, and preview-before-publish model. Likely next areas include controlled follow-up actions, broader analytics questions, and additional assistant lifecycle operations. title: LUMLON
pitch: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired.
about_excerpt: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired. Like Comment Story Updates The page reads three provinces on load and plots all 77. Every card carries its observation time and source — before any agent arrives. Six site tools, declared by the page itself — no plugin, no separate server. Watches live in this browser only, never on a server. Asked about official warnings, the agent reads the expiry itself and refuses to report an expired warning as current. Nobody told it to. Inspiration Every morning I check the same thing: what is the air like today, is it safe, and can I play tennis with my son this evening? I check because my son was admitted to the hospital for it: a severe asthma attack, his airways closing, after breathing PM2.5 over a stretch of days when readings in our area were many times the level the World Health Organization calls safe. That is why "is the air safe today?" is not a curiosity in my house. It is a decision, every morning, before anything else gets decided. So I started building LUMLON: a Thai app that reads air, weather, and hazard conditions in real time. It exists, and you can open it — https://lumlon-web-dev.vercel.app is our development build, mid-redesign and not launched yet. I would rather you looked than took my word for it. What it is for is simple — to tell a person, day by day, at a time they choose or the moment they ask, whether it is safe to be outside. Not so they can study a chart, but so a father and son can plan an ordinary evening without gambling on it. Air you can plan around is also cheaper than a hospital admission, and in my family, that is not a figure of speech. The data already exists. Checking it does not scale. Today that means jumping between several apps, government agencies, and websites — each with its own shape, its own gaps, and its own idea of what "no data" means. It takes time, and on a morning you are in a hurry, you skip it. Would it not be better to simply ask — or to be told at the moments that matter — without opening anything at all? That is the kind of problem WebMCP is actually for. The person asking does not want a dashboard; they want an answer, in their own words, about their own province, right now. And people have already moved. They reach for an AI tool first now, which makes an agent a practical way to get this kind of information to someone — not a novelty. LUMLON was always meant to reach people through whatever channel they already use, not only inside one app. What WebMCP adds is that the answer can come from us: specific readings, each carrying its source and the time it was taken, instead of whatever an agent can assemble on its own. An agent also does something a website cannot do for everyone at once — it turns a reading into an answer in the language and the words of whoever is asking. That is why one of these six tools does not return a number at all. It returns a judgment about a specific activity, together with the readings it used and the reason it reached that answer. A number tells you what the air is like. A person still has to decide whether to go outside. So we did not build a chatbot on top of a website. We made the website itself something an agent can read, and kept the human looking at the same screen the whole time. What it does LUMLON exposes six tools to any WebMCP-capable agent, for all 77 provinces of Thailand. Tool What it does Kind search_locations Turns a place name into a province code. Thai or English, loose spelling. read get_environment_snapshot Air quality, short forecast, and official hazard alerts — each alert carries its own expiry, because they come from a dated snapshot. read get_safety_briefing Decides whether an activity is advisable and explains why , quoting the readings. read create_watch Saves a rule that warns when a reading crosses a threshold. write list_watches Lists the rules saved in this browser. read delete_watch Removes one rule. destructive It is a working page before an agent arrives. Open it with no agent at all and it reads three provinces on load — live PM2.5 and AQI, plus the official hazard alerts from a dated snapshot, which every card says on its face — and plots them on a map of all 77 provinces drawn from our own registry. You can search a province in Thai or English and read it yourself, with one click, through the same data path a tool call takes. This matters for a reason beyond looks: an agent-ready site can only be judged on what the agent adds , and that needs a "before" to compare against. A blank page waiting for a tool call is not a product an agent improves — it is a log viewer. What people and agents do together, concretely. You ask "is the air safe for a morning run in Chiang Mai tomorrow?" The agent calls two tools and answers in a sentence. At the same moment, the page in front of you updates — the same reading, the same timestamp, the same source. The map moves to Chiang Mai on its own; the card that appears is labelled read by the agent , next to cards labelled read by this page , so you can always tell which of the two of you did what. You did not lose the screen by talking to an agent; you gained a second way to drive it. Then you say "watch this and warn me if it goes above 75," and a rule appears as a card you can see — and that you remove the same way you made it, by asking. The panel lists your watches; it does not hide them, and it does not let anything but a tool call change them. The map moves without a seventh tool. We deliberately did not add a set_map_view tool to let the agent pan the screen. The view follows the tools it already has: search a place, the camera frames it; read a place, the pin lights up. Tool descriptions are charged against the agent's context on every single turn, so a tool is a cost, not an achievement — and this one would have bought nothing that the existing events did not already carry. Three decisions that make this usable rather than merely present: Every block of data carries when it was observed and where it came from. A number without a timestamp is a number nobody can check — and the person hearing an agent read it aloud cannot see the screen to judge for themselves. Missing data is reported, never hidden. If a source cannot be read, the answer says so, in a gaps field the agent reads out. "Could not read" and "there are no alerts" are different facts, and collapsing them is the single most dangerous thing a safety tool can do. For the same reason, a briefing never says good while something it needed was unavailable: missing data can lower our confidence, but it never lowers a warning. Read tools and write tools fail in opposite directions, on purpose. A read tool with one number missing still answers the question that was actually asked, and names what it could not read. A write tool with anything unvalidated refuses the whole command. Both write tools are annotated as writes, and delete_watch is additionally marked destructive. In the session we recorded — with approvals set to allow everything — the agent still stopped and asked before it deleted a rule. How we built it The tools do not know where their data comes from. They only ever talk to a provider interface, and that interface is in this repository: src/webmcp/providers/types.ts . The implementation behind it here is the bundled one, which calls only public sources. Be precise about what you can and cannot check in this export. The second implementation — the one that reads the backend of the product we are building — is not in this repository. The export is generated by following what the shipped entry actually imports, and since this entry runs on the bundled provider, the other implementation is never reached and never copied. So what you can verify here is the seam, not both sides of it: one interface, one implementation, and six tool files that name neither. That seam is the reason this entry can be frozen for judging while the product keeps moving, and it is also the reason we are telling you the second half is missing instead of letting the sentence imply it is here. To be exact about what that does and does not mean: this WebMCP layer was built for this challenge, and the product ships with it switched off. The shared interface is what makes it portable — not a claim that agents are driving our production app today. The module is invisible when it is off. WebMCP registration lives behind a build flag and a dynamic import. With the flag off, a scan of our own build output finds no trace of the module — 2,838 files swept, zero hits, on the tree we build from. We check this rather than asserting it, because we found the opposite of what we assumed the first time we measured: an unset environment variable is not a constant, so the bundler could not prove the branch was dead, and it emitted the chunk anyway. The upstream sources are switchable without a cod

title: OpenBento
pitch: A living intelligence dashboard where humans and AI agents organize the web together.
about_excerpt: A living intelligence dashboard where humans and AI agents organize the web together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web is still mostly designed around humans opening tabs, searching pages, and manually organizing what they find. AI agents can answer questions about the web, but they usually operate in a separate chat experience rather than inside the same persistent workspace as the user. OpenBento explores a different model: what if humans and agents could work on the same web-native intelligence dashboard? What it does OpenBento is a persistent dashboard for following topics as they evolve. Each Canvas contains one live Dashboard where users can combine persistent WatchBots, web/news Cards, X posts with rich media and engagement data, playable YouTube Cards, notes, structured Columns, financial Cards, and AI assistance. A WatchBot owns a dedicated Column. New discoveries appear at the top of that stream instead of endlessly expanding the workspace. When something matters, the user can drag that Card out of the live feed and place it directly onto the Dashboard, preserving it while the WatchBot continues monitoring. The result is somewhere between a live research desk, TweetDeck, an intelligence dashboard, and an AI workspace. Why WebMCP is a strong fit OpenBento is fundamentally about shared state between humans and agents . Without WebMCP, an AI assistant can describe what the user should do, but it cannot naturally operate the same web application the user is already working in. With WebMCP, OpenBento exposes meaningful application actions directly to compatible agents. An agent can work with the same persistent Canvases, Cards, WatchBots, and Dashboard state that the human user sees. The agent is not controlling the application through screenshots or brittle coordinate-based browser automation. It interacts through explicit tools published by the website itself. That makes agent actions more reliable, understandable, and aligned with the application's own permission and domain model. What humans and agents can do together A person can ask an agent to create or modify parts of the workspace while continuing to interact with the same Dashboard manually. For example: A user asks an agent to create a WatchBot for Apple news. OpenBento creates a persistent WatchBot and its dedicated live Column. The WatchBot begins collecting relevant web, X, and YouTube developments. The user pulls an important Card out of that stream and pins it elsewhere on the Dashboard. A WebMCP-capable agent can later create Cards, move content, update the Canvas, or manage the WatchBot. Both the human and the agent continue working against the same persistent state. This turns the agent from an external chatbot into a participant in the user's workspace. How WebMCP is implemented OpenBento registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The WebMCP layer maps a safe set of snake_case tools onto the same authoritative domain action system used by the application's own UI. Current tools cover retrieving Canvas state, creating and switching Canvases, creating/updating/moving/resizing Cards, managing viewport state, fullscreen Dashboard presentation, creating and managing WatchBots, and reading WatchBot status. OpenBento currently exposes 15 WebMCP tools . The WebMCP implementation does not maintain a separate privileged mutation layer. Authentication, ownership checks, validation, and persistence pass through the same shared domain executor used by the human UI. Architecture OpenBento uses Next.js 16, React, TypeScript, Supabase PostgreSQL/Auth, Railway, XYFlow, OpenAI, X API, YouTube Data API, Sentry, and Resend. The application runs as a web service plus dedicated background workers for different monitoring providers. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was making background AI activity coexist with a persistent spatial interface. An early version placed every newly discovered Card directly onto an infinite Canvas. That quickly became unusable. We redesigned OpenBento around a finite Dashboard with dedicated streaming Columns. WatchBots continuously update their Columns while users can pull important information out into the persistent Dashboard. We also had to make WebMCP a genuine part of the application's architecture instead of a demo-only wrapper. WebMCP actions use the same domain action catalog, authentication, validation, and persistence layer as the human UI. What we learned The most interesting lesson was that agent-friendly websites benefit from exposing intent-level operations , not reproducing mouse and keyboard interaction. A tool like create_watchbot or move_card communicates much more useful application semantics than asking an agent to infer coordinates and manipulate the UI visually. WebMCP makes that model native to the website. What's next OpenBento can expand into a broader personal intelligence environment with richer market Cards, more social/news providers, AI-generated layouts, configurable Dashboard templates, team collaboration, and additional WebMCP actions. AI organizes the story. Sources remain the story. title: Trinity Gate
pitch: Trinity Gate lets AI agents act through WebMCP while proving capability, authority, execution, and outcome before anything is called done.
about_excerpt: Trinity Gate lets AI agents act through WebMCP while proving capability, authority, execution, and outcome before anything is called done. Like Comment Story Updates Locked request at deterministic reset with Capability → Authority → Execution → Verification visible. Acme Corp change is capability-valid but blocked pending explicit human approval. Account update VERIFIED_COMPLETE, email CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE, overall request PARTIALLY_COMPLETE. No AI action is done until Trinity Gate can prove it. Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of taking real actions across the web, but capability alone does not make an action complete. An agent can have the wrong permissions, require human approval, encounter an execution failure, or simply lack the capability needed to perform part of a request. Yet users can still be left with a conversational response that sounds like the work was done. Trinity Gate explores a stricter model: An AI agent should never claim an external action is complete unless it had the capability and authority to perform it, execution actually occurred, and authoritative evidence proves the intended result. What it does Trinity Gate evaluates agent actions through four gates: CAPABILITY → AUTHORITY → EXECUTION → VERIFICATION Only VERIFIED_COMPLETE means done. The demo uses one combined request: “Upgrade Acme Corp to Priority support and email them the updated agreement.” The two requested actions deliberately produce different outcomes. Account update The account-change capability exists, but changing the customer's support tier is consequential. Trinity Gate returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human sees the exact target and proposed change and must explicitly approve it in the application. No WebMCP tool can grant that approval on the human's behalf. After approval, the agent can execute the change: Acme Corp: Standard → Priority But successful execution is still not enough. Trinity Gate rereads authoritative application state and compares the observed result with the exact action that was executed. Only after that evidence matches does the account action become: VERIFIED_COMPLETE Email action The same user request also asks the agent to email the updated agreement. Trinity Gate intentionally exposes no email capability. Instead of implying the message was sent, it reports: CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE Action not performed. Because the account change is verified while the email action never occurred, Trinity Gate reports the overall request as: PARTIALLY_COMPLETE One successful action cannot hide another action that never happened. Why WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product rather than an added integration. Trinity Gate's web application exposes structured capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. The agent can discover what the application actually allows it to do, inspect authoritative state, prepare actions, evaluate them, execute eligible actions, and request verification. At the same time, the application retains control of consequential authority and proof. This creates a cleaner human-agent relationship: the agent discovers and uses structured web capabilities; the human retains consequential approval authority; the application determines what actually happened and what evidence supports the final claim. Without that separation, tool invocation and successful completion can easily be treated as if they mean the same thing. Trinity Gate makes them explicitly different. How we built it Trinity Gate is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed on Vercel. The hackathon demo deliberately uses deterministic browser-side application state instead of a CRM, email provider, database, or external SaaS backend. This keeps the WebMCP behavior reproducible for judges while still exercising real browser-native WebMCP tools. The deployed application registers eight tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) They are: trinity_gate_diagnostic list_customers get_customer prepare_action evaluate_action execute_action verify_action locked_demo_request Each tool exposes an explicit name, description, and input schema. Human approval is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The same governed domain logic is shared by the visible application and the WebMCP handlers, covering capability, authority, approvals, execution records, authoritative rereads, evidence, verification, request aggregation, stale-state protection, and deterministic reset behavior. Verification and testing We wanted the project's own development process to follow the same principle as the product: proof before claims. The finished project was verified with: 24/24 unit tests passing Playwright browser testing across desktop, tablet, mobile, and reduced-motion configurations native WebMCP discovery and safe-call testing in compatible headed Chrome production lifecycle verification against the deployed application deterministic Reset Demo verification Gitleaks secret scanning Semgrep OSS security analysis clean TypeScript build and lint checks Native testing confirmed all eight deployed WebMCP tools were discoverable and that no agent-callable approval or rejection tool exists. Challenges The hardest part was not registering a WebMCP tool. It was deciding what a trustworthy completion claim actually means. That required separating several concepts that are often collapsed together: capability from authority approval from execution execution from verification individual action success from overall request success We also had to ensure that approval was bound to the exact action, target, intended state, and relevant state version so stale or mismatched approval could not authorize a different action. Another challenge was making partial completion explicit. If one action succeeds and another cannot even be attempted, the overall request must not be summarized as success. Accomplishments we're proud of The part we are most proud of is that Trinity Gate does not merely demonstrate an approval screen. It demonstrates an end-to-end trust model: discover → inspect → prepare → evaluate → approve → execute → reread → verify The agent cannot approve itself. Execution alone cannot produce VERIFIED_COMPLETE . A missing capability cannot produce fake success. And a partially completed multi-action request remains visibly partial. What we learned WebMCP makes it possible for web applications to expose structured capabilities to agents without forcing those agents to infer actions from visual interfaces. But exposing a capability creates a second problem: deciding how much authority the agent should have and what evidence is required before a human should trust its completion claim. We learned that these are separate questions: Can it do this? May it do this? Did it do this? Can we prove the intended result occurred? Trinity Gate exists to keep those questions separate. What's next Trinity Gate is the standalone WebMCP proof built for this challenge, but the trust model behind it is designed for a much larger system I am building called Trinity Syntara . Trinity Syntara is an AI operating system for coordinating agents, persistent context and memory, permissions, human decision boundaries, and verified action across real workflows and external systems. The goal is not simply to give AI more tools. It is to give AI the correct amount of authority and make sure it can prove what actually happened before reporting work as complete. Trinity Gate isolates and proves one critical part of that larger problem for the open web: CAPABILITY → AUTHORITY → EXECUTION → VERIFICATION In Syntara, this same principle is intended to operate continuously across broader agent workflows. An agent may be able to interact with development tools, communications platforms, business applications, or other connected systems, but capability alone will never be treated as proof of completion. The same rules demonstrated in Trinity Gate remain important: an agent cannot claim authority it was never granted; consequential actions can require explicit human approval; successful execution is not the same as verified completion; unavailable capabilities must be reported honestly; partial completion must remain visible; authoritative evidence determines the strongest completion claim the system is allowed to make. Future directions for Trinity Gate itself include richer approval policies, persistent or signed evidence, broader connectors, and multi-system authoritative verification. Syntara is not part of the hackathon submission, and none of its private implementation is included here. Trinity Gate is the standalone public WebMCP proof of this trust model. Links Live application: https://trinity-gate.vercel.app Source code: https://github.com/gstephens-cyber/trinity-gate Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=meDUsAOvj3A Built With chrome gitleaks playwright puppeteer react semgrep typescript vercel vite vitest Try it out trinity-gate.vercel.app github.com Submi

title: Tree Radar
pitch: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore.
about_excerpt: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore. Like Comment Story Updates Explore 118,403 official street-tree records across Taichung on an interactive map. Search by species and inspect matching trees with their official record details and locations. Inspiration Cities publish valuable information about their trees, but that data is often difficult for ordinary people to explore. Tree Radar began as a way to turn official municipal tree datasets into a searchable, visual map that makes urban trees easier to discover. The WebMCP Challenge raised a different question: what if an AI agent could work with the same interface instead of requiring a separate API or agent-only application? The goal became to let people explore trees visually while allowing an agent to understand the available city data, search it through structured tools, and bring useful results back onto the same map. What it does Tree Radar is an interactive city tree map built from public municipal data. For the WebMCP Challenge, it exposes three browser-native tools: get_city_coverage — lets an agent understand which city datasets are available find_trees — searches the tree dataset using structured criteria show_trees_on_map — turns selected search results into visible state on the map The current WebMCP demo includes more than 118,000 Taichung street-tree records. Together, the tools create a human-agent loop: a person can ask about trees in natural language, the agent can discover and call the appropriate tools, and matching trees can then be shown on the same interactive map for the person to explore. How we built it Tree Radar is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, and MapLibre GL JS. The WebMCP implementation registers three explicit tools through the browser's model context. Each tool has a bounded responsibility and structured inputs and outputs. The workflow is deliberately separated into three steps: discover available city coverage search for matching trees explicitly choose which results to display on the map This keeps information retrieval separate from state-changing behavior: searching does not unexpectedly change the map. The production build was tested in a WebMCP-capable browser to verify tool discovery, structured calls, tree search, and the final map transition. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was deciding what should become an agent capability and what should remain normal application behavior. Exposing too much would make the integration harder to understand and less predictable. The three-tool design came from keeping the agent surface small and making state-changing behavior explicit. Municipal tree data also contains variations in species naming. Search behavior was refined to support useful partial species matching while keeping results bounded and predictable. Accomplishments that we're proud of The result is not a separate AI demo layered beside Tree Radar. The agent and the existing web interface participate in the same task: the agent handles structured discovery and search, while the map remains the shared visual surface where people can inspect the result. The WebMCP flow has been validated end to end in production with all three tools discoverable and callable. Tree Radar existed before this challenge as a city-tree exploration product. The WebMCP integration is a new extension built specifically for the WebMCP Challenge. The challenge work includes the browser-native WebMCP tool layer, the three-tool discovery/search/map workflow, WebMCP-specific acceptance testing, and a dedicated challenge repository whose commit history documents this work separately from the pre-existing product. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is useful for more than retrieving information from a website. It can create a bridge between agent reasoning and an existing visual interface. In Tree Radar, the agent does not replace the map. It helps a person reach meaningful results, then hands those results back to the interface where spatial context becomes visible. Designing a small, explicit tool surface also made the interaction easier to reason about than exposing every possible application action. What's next for Tree Radar Tree Radar is expanding toward broader city coverage while keeping the same principle: official public data should be easier for people to explore and understand. The WebMCP experiment also points toward a larger possibility for Tree Radar: as more city datasets become available, agents could help people navigate increasingly large collections of urban tree data without replacing the visual and geographic context that makes that data meaningful. title: Ninth Tool
pitch: Runs your page's WebMCP tools in a real browser and shows which promises it silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Twenty behaviours, twenty reproductions.
about_excerpt: Runs your page's WebMCP tools in a real browser and shows which promises it silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Twenty behaviours, twenty reproductions. Like Comment Story Updates The Silent Drop Problem: Demonstrating how browser engines silently drop destructiveHint, error envelopes and signals. Live 20-Behaviour Catalogue: all six groups, from the six rows a page author can act on to the fourteen that are facts about the host. Defect Inspection & Remediation: Exact reproduction command and standard gap analysis per behaviour row. Live In-Browser Audit: Running all 20 probes in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, scoring 13 broken, 5 kept, 1 by design, 1 unsettled. Dynamic Tool Mutation: The nt_get_findings tool appears only when findings exist and is withdrawn when cleared. Headless DevTools CLI Runner: Running the same twenty behaviour probes from a terminal, with zero dependencies. Architecture and behaviour matrix: two transports, twenty rows in six groups, and the tools the page publishes to an agent. Ninth Tool: A Reproducible Behaviour Probe for WebMCP Ninth Tool executes your page's WebMCP tools in the browser and shows which promises the browser silently drops, with the command that reproduces each one. Live, no account: https://upgradedev.github.io/ninthtool/ Code (MIT): https://github.com/upgradedev/ninthtool Compatibility: Chrome or Edge with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Inspiration I was adding WebMCP to a page, writing the shape I knew from building MCP servers. I marked a tool destructiveHint . I returned { isError: true } when it refused. I passed a signal on the descriptor so it would withdraw. All three were accepted without complaint and none of them did anything. Nothing threw, nothing reached the console, and the tool list carried no warning. Existing checkers read the declarations a page publishes and told me the page was fine, because by the only thing they look at, it was. The gap is not in what a page declares. It is in what the browser does with the declaration, and reading cannot see that. What it does It runs twenty behaviours against a live WebMCP tool surface and reports each one with the exact command that reproduces it. Six rows read the tools the page publishes, snapshotted before the probe registers anything of its own. Fourteen rows are facts about the host: 3 where the browser diverges from the W3C draft, 5 the draft cannot express, 3 silent traps, 1 by design, 2 that hold. On its own page, in Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled, the reading is 13 broken, 5 kept, 1 by design, 1 unsettled, 20 tested . It labels that run PARTIAL rather than rounding the unsettled row up. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The subject being tested is WebMCP itself. Whether a host honours destructiveHint , whether a refusal survives the boundary, whether a tool registered with a signal actually withdraws: none of it is visible from outside a browser, and none of it can be read off a declaration. This is not a page that uses WebMCP to deliver something else. WebMCP is the thing under test, so the only place the work can happen is inside a page that speaks it. How it creates a better user experience A page author gets what their browser actually did, next to the one command that reproduces it, instead of a linter's reading of their source. No account, no install, and nothing about their page is uploaded anywhere. The audit runs in the tab they already have open, against a subject document in a same-origin frame. Every row that could not be run says so, with the reason, rather than counting as a pass. A run with one unobserved row reports PARTIAL . That is the difference between a result you can act on and a green tick you have to trust. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before This page publishes its own WebMCP tools, so an agent can run the audit, list the twenty behaviours, explain one row in full and read the findings without touching the screen, while a person watches the same rows fill in beside it. The nt_get_findings tool does not exist until a run has produced findings, and it is withdrawn when they are cleared. An agent that asks for findings which are not there is answered by the tool surface itself rather than left to guess. That is the behaviour this suite is named for, demonstrated on itself rather than described. The auditor is a WebMCP page, so it is also a subject. How WebMCP was implemented document.modelContext.registerTool publishes three tools from this page at rest and a fourth while findings exist. Three carry readOnlyHint . The one that runs the audit deliberately does not, because it drives forms. The subject page it drives is a separate document in a same-origin frame that promotes two ordinary forms to tools through the declarative HTML attributes, so both halves of the standard sit on one surface. The probe registers its own throwaway tools with a signal in the options bag and withdraws them when it is finished, which is how the withdrawal row gets measured at all. How I built it Gathering is not deciding. The probe runs inside a document and records what happened, with no opinion about what a pass is. The judge is pure, runs deterministically, and cannot reach a browser. 533 unit tests and 97.95% line coverage across 57 files at commit 231c45f , counting each file once against an 85% floor for lines, branches and functions. Eleven below-floor metrics occur across six files, and the gate names every file instead of averaging it away. Reproduce it with node --experimental-test-coverage --test tests/unit | tee coverage.txt then node tests/unit/coverage_gate.mjs coverage.txt --per-file --threshold=85 . Dual transports. The in-browser runner, plus a zero-dependency headless Chrome DevTools Protocol client. No bundler, no test framework, no lock file, no runtime dependencies. Run it against any page from a terminal: npx --yes https://github.com/upgradedev/ninthtool/tarball/main https://your-page.example The package is not published to npm, so the tarball URL is the whole install. Safety By default it calls no tool of yours and submits no form. Calling your read-only tools needs an explicit flag you pass yourself. Submitting a form runs only against the fixture this tool serves itself. It is not invisible, and that is stated rather than hidden: registering a probe tool is a document-level event that your page can see. Honest limits A preregistered study on thirteen independently authored WebMCP pages has run, and its hypothesis failed . Five of twenty rows told those pages apart, and every one of them was already readable from the tool list. Taking it apart afterwards showed why: at most two rows could ever have told one of those pages from another, against a threshold of three fixed before anyone looked, and both were switched off by the run's own read-only default. The bar could not be cleared by any result. That is a defect in the protocol, not a measurement of what this tool reaches. Two findings it did report about strangers' pages were checked against their own source and retracted as defects in this tool , with the handler lines cited. One page had rejected the missing argument at its first line. On the other, this tool's own control call was as malformed as the one it meant to break. That is the thing worth reading. Any suite that runs against pages it does not own will produce false findings. The useful question is whether it catches them and publishes the retraction beside the claim, in the same generated file. It did. One of the two study-specific oracle weaknesses behind those retractions is now closed. The other stays open on purpose: the obvious fix was built, measured against a copy of the tree, and it turned this suite's own flagship true positive into an abstention. That measurement is published rather than the fix. The protocol was written and committed before any page ran, the failure is published in evidence/impact/results.md , and the primary metric was not changed afterwards to make it read better. Five rows have known fail-open paths, and P2 is only partially closed. They were found by external review and reproduced before publishing: P4 treats unreadable provenance as local because it filters only fromThisDocument === false . P3 walks only top-level schema.properties , so an undescribed nested parameter passes. D1 accepts any toolchange event without proving that the target tool caused it. P5 removes only required[0] , always uses the same good/bad/bad/good order, and later resolves the snapshotted tool by name. Later required keys, position-dependent behaviour, or a same-name replacement can produce a false pass or misbound call. P6 also resolves by name, stringifies answers, is order-sensitive, and counts every resolved value, including an error envelope, as an answer. A replacement writer can be called, distinct structured states can collapse to the same text, and a resolved refusal can satisfy the

title: go.lmm.best
pitch: An Online Go Game Where Humans Play by Click and AI Plays Through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An Online Go Game Where Humans Play by Click and AI Plays Through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Human vs. AI Go, Powered by WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Go has extremely simple rules, yet every move can change the direction of the entire game. That contrast made it an ideal environment for exploring a larger question: 

 
 What happens when an AI does not merely generate an answer, but directly participates in an interactive application? 
 

 Most AI board-game demos hide the interaction behind a traditional backend API. The AI receives a board state, returns a coordinate, and the application handles everything else. I wanted to make the interaction more explicit. The human player should place stones naturally by clicking the board, while the AI should observe the game and make its own moves through WebMCP tools. 

 The project became an experiment in building a shared digital environment where a human and an AI interact with the same game state through different interfaces. 

 What the Project Does 

 The project is an online Go game in which: 

 
 The human player places stones by clicking intersections on the board. 
 The game engine validates moves, captures stones, and updates the position. 
 The AI reads the current game state through WebMCP. 
 The AI chooses a move and calls a structured WebMCP tool to place its stone. 
 Both players see the updated board immediately. 
 

 The AI does not directly manipulate the page or bypass the game rules. It must submit a move through the same controlled game interface used by the rest of the application. 

 Conceptually, the game follows a state transition model: 

 S t + 1 = T ( S t , a t ) 

 where: 

 
 (S_t) is the current board state, 
 (a_t) is the move selected by the human or AI, 
 (T) is the rule engine that validates and applies the move. 
 

 A move is accepted only when: 

 a t ∈ A ( S t ) 

 where (A(S_t)) represents all legal actions available in the current position. 

 How I Built It 

 I separated the project into three main layers: the interface, the game engine, and the AI interaction layer. 

 Interactive Go Board 

 The frontend renders the Go board and converts mouse clicks into board coordinates. When the human clicks an intersection, the interface sends the selected coordinate to the rule engine. 

 The board component is responsible for displaying: 

 
 Empty intersections 
 Black and white stones 
 The latest move 
 Captured stones 
 The current player 
 Invalid-move feedback 
 

 Keeping the visual board separate from the underlying game state made the interface easier to update and debug. 

 Go Rule Engine 

 The rule engine is the source of truth for the match. It determines whether a move is legal before modifying the board. 

 Its responsibilities include: 

 
 Enforcing turn order 
 Detecting occupied intersections 
 Calculating connected stone groups 
 Counting liberties 
 Removing captured stones 
 Preventing illegal self-capture 
 Handling repetition rules 
 Supporting pass actions 
 

 Neither the human interface nor the AI can directly modify the board. Every attempted move must pass through this engine. 

 WebMCP Integration 

 I exposed a small set of structured tools that allow the AI to interact with the game. The core tools provide functionality similar to: 
 get_board_state()
play_move(x, y)
pass_turn()
get_game_status()
 
 The AI first retrieves the current position, reasons about possible moves, and then calls play_move with a board coordinate. 

 The tool layer validates the request before forwarding it to the rule engine. This prevents the AI from playing outside the board, moving twice, placing a stone on an occupied point, or acting on an outdated game state. 

 The complete interaction loop is: 
 Human clicks the board
 ↓
Rule engine validates the move
 ↓
Board state is updated
 ↓
AI reads the state through WebMCP
 ↓
AI selects and submits a move
 ↓
Rule engine validates the AI move
 ↓
The interface renders the new position
 
 Challenges I Faced 

 Keeping the AI and Interface Synchronized 

 The most difficult problem was maintaining one authoritative game state. 

 The human interface, rule engine, and AI operate asynchronously. Without careful coordination, the AI could read an older position and attempt a move after the board had already changed. 

 I addressed this by treating every move as a transaction. Each action is checked against the latest board state and current turn before it is accepted. 

 Implementing Go Rules Correctly 

 Go looks simple until captures, liberties, suicide rules, and repeated positions are introduced. A single move can affect several neighboring groups, so validating a move requires more than checking whether an intersection is empty. 

 I learned to model the board as a graph. Each stone is a node connected to adjacent stones, and group traversal can be used to calculate liberties and determine whether a group should be captured. 

 Designing Tools for an AI 

 Giving an AI unrestricted access to application state would have been easy, but unreliable. The harder and more useful approach was designing a small tool interface with clear inputs, outputs, and validation rules. 

 For example, the AI should not need to understand the internal structure of the frontend. It only needs a stable representation of the board and a safe way to submit an action. 

 This taught me that effective AI tools should be narrow, predictable, and difficult to misuse. 

 Coordinate Conversion 

 Go coordinates can be represented in several ways: array indexes, screen positions, human-readable coordinates, or protocol-specific notation. Mixing these formats caused incorrect moves during early development. 

 I solved this by defining one internal coordinate system and performing conversions only at the boundaries of the application. 

 Handling Failed AI Actions 

 An AI can occasionally submit malformed parameters, select an illegal move, or act on stale information. The application needed to recover without freezing the game. 

 Instead of silently ignoring errors, the WebMCP layer returns structured feedback explaining why the move failed. The AI can then request the latest board state and try again. 

 What I Learned 

 This project changed how I think about AI integration. 

 I learned that an AI becomes much more useful when it can interact with a structured environment instead of only exchanging text. WebMCP allowed the browser application to expose meaningful capabilities while keeping the game engine in control. 

 I also learned that tool design matters as much as model intelligence. A powerful model connected to vague or unsafe tools can still behave poorly. A smaller set of well-defined tools often produces more reliable results. 

 From the game-engine side, I gained a deeper understanding of state machines, graph traversal, asynchronous synchronization, and defensive validation. 

 Most importantly, I learned to treat AI actions as untrusted external input. Every AI move must be checked exactly as carefully as a human-generated request. 

 What I Am Proud Of 

 I am proud that the project creates a direct and understandable interaction between a human, an AI, and a live application. 

 The human simply clicks the board. The AI observes the same match, reasons about the position, and responds through WebMCP. Both participants operate inside the same rule-controlled environment. 

 The result is more than a Go game. It is a small demonstration of how AI agents can safely participate in interactive web applications. 

 What Is Next 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 Adjustable AI difficulty 
 Multiple board sizes 
 Move history and SGF export 
 Game replay 
 Position analysis 
 Suggested moves for beginners 
 Timed matches 
 Spectator mode 
 Support for different AI models 
 Human-versus-human and AI-versus-AI modes 
 

 I would also like to expose richer analysis tools, allowing the AI to explain candidate moves, identify weak groups, and teach Go while playing. 

 The long-term goal is to turn the project into both a playable online game and a practical example of human–AI interaction through WebMCP.

title: Sushi Daw
pitch: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace.
about_excerpt: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Sushi: A DAW Built in Code, Controlled Through WebMCP Inspiration Sushi began with a compatibility problem disguised as a music problem. My collaborator Avery and I both love making music, and we share a lot of the same taste, but we approach the process from almost opposite directions. Avery is comfortable in traditional DAWs. He uses Logic Pro, has experience with FL Studio and BandLab, and understands music through tracks, effects, timelines, and familiar production controls. I have used those tools, but they have never been the way I naturally want to make music. I am much more interested in Strudel and TidalCycles: writing patterns as code, changing them live, and treating a composition as something programmable. That left us without a good place to meet. When Avery sent me a Logic project, I could not simply open it on Linux. Even if we were using DAWs on the same platform, proprietary project formats and different software would still make collaboration awkward. In the other direction, I could send him a Strudel composition as a few lines of text, but unless he learned the syntax, there was not much he could do with it. We wanted a workspace where neither of us had to abandon the way we preferred to work. Avery should be able to interact with music through a visual interface. I should be able to work directly in Strudel. An agent should be able to participate without pretending to be a person clicking through a DAW. That shared workspace became Sushi. What it does Sushi is a browser-based, code-native DAW powered by Strudel and its TidalCycles-inspired pattern language. Underneath the interface, the composition is still code. That makes a Sushi project lightweight, inspectable, programmable, and easy to share. On top of that code, Sushi provides a more familiar music-production interface for arranging tracks, selecting sounds, adjusting effects, and shaping a composition without requiring the user to understand Strudel syntax. The important part is that these are not two separate modes. When someone changes a supported property in the interface, the Strudel source changes with it. When someone edits the source, Sushi reflects that change back into the interface. A traditional producer, a live coder, and an agent can therefore manipulate the same underlying composition instead of passing increasingly lossy translations between different tools. WebMCP adds the third side of that collaboration. An agent can inspect the composition and its current playback state directly in the page, modify or write music, validate the result, and observe the updated source and interface without requiring the user to copy code back and forth between a chat window and the editor. When an edit fails Strudel validation, the agent receives diagnostics from the running environment and can correct its work. This feedback loop makes a major difference. The agent is not writing music blindly and returning a plausible-looking block of code. It is working inside the actual instrument. Because the composition itself is programmable, the musical program becomes a high-leverage control surface for both humans and agents. The DAW is built in code, and WebMCP gives the agent access to that code in its real context. How we built it Sushi started as a relatively simple Astro application written in TypeScript. Astro was a pragmatic choice because it is the framework I already enjoy using, but it also gives the project room to grow without splitting everything into separate repositories or deployments. The application, documentation, and other supporting pages can coexist in the same project while the interactive workspace remains focused and lightweight. Inside that scaffold, we integrated Strudel as the musical runtime and built Sushi’s interface around its source representation. We deliberately avoided treating the interface as a separate DAW model that merely exports Strudel later. Instead, every feature has to respect the same contract: Anything that happens in the interface must be represented in the code, and anything represented in the supported code must remain visible and editable through the interface. That constraint shaped nearly every architectural decision in the project. A track cannot exist only as hidden application state. An effect cannot be added through a UI-only shortcut that the source does not understand. The interface must work with the musical program rather than bypassing it. We then connected the workspace to WebMCP so an agent could participate through that same underlying model. Rather than automating coordinates or simulating mouse clicks, the agent can work with the composition structurally and receive feedback from the running application. Sushi registers a typed WebMCP surface against the browser’s native model context. Agents can inspect a structured snapshot of the project, read or patch the canonical Strudel source, validate candidate source against the running Strudel engine, control playback, edit tracks and timeline state, and load or inspect composition templates. Mutating operations carry a base revision and transaction ID, so stale or duplicated actions are rejected instead of silently overwriting human changes. Successful source edits pass through the same validation and source-to-interface synchronization path as human edits, returning structured state, diffs, and diagnostics to the agent. The result is a shared artifact with three possible collaborators: one person working visually, another working in code, and an agent working through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into Performance became a challenge almost immediately. Strudel is already a mature and highly interactive environment, so Sushi could not merely produce the same output eventually. Editing and playback had to feel responsive enough to function as an instrument. As we introduced interface state and synchronization, we repeatedly found places where our application was doing substantially more work than Strudel itself. We had to become much more careful about when the composition was evaluated, what caused components to update, and how changes moved through the application. Music software makes performance problems unusually obvious: latency and interruption are not just technical metrics. They directly affect whether the creative process feels usable. The larger challenge was maintaining synchronization between code and interface. Almost every feature sounds straightforward until it has to work in both directions. Adding an effect button is easy if it only changes hidden state. It becomes much harder when that action must create valid Strudel, preserve the rest of the user’s source, remain editable as text, and still be understood by the interface after the code changes again. It was tempting at several points to introduce shortcuts: parallel state, special internal representations, or UI features that only resembled Strudel behavior. Those approaches might have made an individual feature easier to ship, but they would have broken the central promise of the project. WebMCP introduced another form of synchronization problem: an agent may act on a project while a human is still editing it. We addressed that by requiring mutating operations to carry a base revision and transaction ID. Stale or duplicated actions return a structured conflict instead of silently overwriting newer work. Over time, we established more reliable patterns for preserving these contracts. Once those patterns became part of the architecture, development became noticeably smoother. I could describe a feature to my coding agent and expect it to extend the existing model rather than inventing another path around Strudel. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The accomplishment we care about most is that Sushi stopped being merely a hackathon idea and became something we actually wanted to use. A large part of building it was the impatient feeling that we needed to finish the next feature so we could stop developing for a moment and start making music with it. Avery and I have already been able to play with the workspace from our different perspectives, which is the original problem Sushi was meant to solve. We are also proud that the visual editor and code editor are not competing sources of truth. They are two views into the same instrument. That gives Sushi the accessibility of a DAW without giving up the expressive power and portability of Strudel. The WebMCP integration demonstrates something we find especially exciting: an agent interface does not always need to be a giant catalog of tiny actions mirroring every control in an application. title: Pending: Human
pitch: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates The deterministic T+60 result compares the approved response with the do-nothing baseline. Choose one of three deterministic crisis missions and invite a WebMCP-enabled AI teammate. A live flash-flood response with graph-based vehicle movement, named roads, and human-impact forecasting. The AI reads structured city state while the human controls dispatch, routes, priorities, and approval. Full game view: live roads, facilities, incidents, city metrics, and synchronized AI activity. Inspiration Browser agents are usually asked to operate interfaces designed only for human eyes. That becomes fragile when an application contains a live model with more meaning than its visible controls can express. A crisis dashboard may show a blocked road, a failed power station, and an overloaded hospital, but the causal chain connecting them is difficult to reconstruct from pixels or DOM labels. We wanted to explore a different relationship: not an agent that simply clicks faster than a person, but a human and an agent operating the same complex system through complementary interfaces. What it does Pending: Human turns a sixty-minute urban crisis into a shared decision exercise. The deterministic simulation creates cascading infrastructure failures and tracks exposed residents, injuries, untreated critical cases, fatalities, hospital load, road travel time, emergency vehicles, and incident resolution. The AI teammate uses WebMCP to investigate structured city state, trace root causes, forecast the cost of doing nothing, compare three compound response plans, and stage one candidate for review. The player chooses the mission doctrine, dispatches vehicles and routes, can build an independent counterproposal, and makes the final decision. Simulating is never executing. A proposal remains pending until the human presses the visible approval control. There is deliberately no WebMCP approval tool. Why WebMCP Pending: Human is built around state that is richer than its visible dashboard. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic contract over the same facts used by the simulation engine: named roads and facilities, passability, power dependencies, hospital pressure, response routes, at-risk populations, and deterministic future outcomes. This avoids guessing from color, screen position, animation, or fragile markup. It also creates a stronger safety boundary. The agent receives deep investigative and counterfactual capabilities without receiving final authority to act. The tool surface changes with the stage. It begins with one entry capability, then exposes only what is useful at the current checkpoint. One integrated assessment call reads the evidence and issues three exact revision-bound previews; a second call lets the agent exercise judgment by selecting one. Short guidance tools explain and highlight the next human control without clicking it, and an event-wait tool keeps the shared session synchronized. A better human + agent experience The simulation, agent, and human have distinct powers: The simulation owns the facts. Every live and forecasted consequence comes from deterministic TypeScript rules. The agent compares possible futures. It connects evidence across infrastructure systems and explains trade-offs. The human owns the decision. The player sets values, accepts social costs, and authorizes consequential action. City time freezes while the agent analyzes and while a proposal awaits approval, so model latency cannot cause extra simulated deaths. Findings are mirrored into the page transcript, and the approval card shows benefits and costs before the player decides. The human can disagree by building a separate plan without erasing the AI proposal. Together, people and agents can identify a cross-system root cause, establish a shared no-action baseline, compare policy futures under human-selected values, and verify the result against the same rules. Doing this reliably through a human-only interface was previously slow and brittle. How we built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application. The road graph, casualty model, scenarios, incident clearance, vehicle travel, forecasts, and scoring all live in one deterministic simulation engine. A shared store manages the live clock, event queue, plan previews, human approval boundary, and teammate transcript. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the page and routed by the current simulation phase. The live workflow uses enter_pending_human_stage, analyze_crisis, propose_emergency_plan, post_next_guidance, focus_next_control, wait_for_city_event, and analyze_turning_point. Granular district, road, facility, hospital, power, routing, forecast, and simulation tools remain available for semantic diagnostics. There is no external AI API inside the application. The WebMCP-enabled browser supplies the agent. There is also no database, login, map API, or hidden backend simulation. Challenges The hardest design problem was keeping a continuous co-op experience responsive when an agent model could take tens of seconds to reason. We introduced time freezing, phase-aware tools, event waiting, and a two-call decision path that batches structured investigation while still requiring the agent to choose among candidates. Another challenge was visual causality. Response vehicles originally felt decorative. We rebuilt movement around the same road graph exposed to WebMCP, made congestion and closures change travel speed, anchored arrivals to visible nodes, and let on-scene units progressively resolve incident markers. Accomplishments Live play and forecasts share one source of truth. Simulating a plan never mutates the live city. Stale previews cannot execute after the city revision changes. AI and human plans remain visible together. High-impact actions cannot bypass human approval. Three difficulty-scaled missions are deterministic and replayable. Forty-two automated tests cover the engine, routing, approval boundary, and agent flow. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it exposes meaning that cannot be reliably recovered from the human interface. It is also useful for defining what an agent cannot do. A good agent experience is not the largest possible toolbox; it is a clear sequence of meaningful capabilities, shared state, and explicit authority boundaries. What's next Future work could add a scenario authoring system, richer field observations, and deeper doctrine negotiation while preserving deterministic evaluation and human approval. The current version intentionally prioritizes one complete collaboration loop over an open-ended city model. Pending: Human is a fictional training and interaction-design prototype. All people, casualties, incidents, and outcomes are simulated.
