title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . pitch: Talk or type — Inquisitive's agent plans over 9 WebMCP tools to sketch architecture diagrams live on Excalidraw, while any WebMCP agent can inspect, edit, and extend the same canvas.
about_excerpt: Talk or type — Inquisitive's agent plans over 9 WebMCP tools to sketch architecture diagrams live on Excalidraw, while any WebMCP agent can inspect, edit, and extend the same canvas. Like Comment Story Updates darkmode session to pdf light mode inquisitiveD arch 2 inquisitiveD arch 1 Inspiration Describing complex architecture in text is simple, but visually mapping several projects over a period of time, it remains a major bottleneck. While typical AI agents struggle to parse complex web UIs, WebMCP changes the paradigm by enabling web apps to expose explicit, structured tools directly to models. title: MemoryBook
pitch: A collaborative digital memory book that lets AI understand contributions and use WebMCP to organize, create, and edit the book directly.
about_excerpt:
A collaborative digital memory book that lets AI understand contributions and use WebMCP to organize, create, and edit the book directly.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Memory books are built from many small pieces: photos, stories, memories, events, and messages submitted by different people. Collecting those contributions is relatively easy. Turning them into a coherent and meaningful book is much harder. 

 MemoryBook explores a different approach. Instead of using AI only to generate text or answer questions, the application exposes meaningful book operations through WebMCP. This allows an AI agent to understand the contents of the book and actively help organize and build it. 

 The goal is to make AI a useful collaborator inside a real web application while keeping the user in control. 

 What it does 

 MemoryBook is a collaborative digital memory book application where people can submit memories and photos and an organizer can turn them into a finished book. 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can interact with the application using structured tools. 

 The current integration allows the AI to: 

 
 retrieve the current MemoryBook status and context 
 list submitted contributions 
 analyze which important school-year events are missing 
 propose a thematic spread based on the submitted memories 
 build that thematic spread directly in the MemoryBook 
 reorder pages in the book 
 

 This creates an end-to-end workflow in which the AI can first understand the collected material, reason about it, propose an editorial decision, and then make an actual change to the book when requested. 

 How we built it 

 MemoryBook is a full-stack web application built with React, TypeScript and Vite on the frontend, with a Node.js/Express backend and PostgreSQL for persistent data. 

 The visual editor supports editable text, drawing, images, layers, undo/redo, page navigation, saving and page previews. 

 For the WebMCP integration, I designed tools around meaningful user intentions instead of low-level interface controls. 

 These include tools for retrieving book context and status, listing contributions, checking event coverage, building a thematic spread, and reordering pages. 

 The AI therefore does not need to simulate mouse clicks or manipulate individual interface elements. It can discover structured capabilities exposed by the website and use them to work with the same MemoryBook data as the normal user interface. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was connecting AI actions to a real, persistent editor rather than creating a scripted demonstration. 

 WebMCP operations had to work with the same pages, contribution data, saved state and previews used by the normal application. 

 Another challenge was choosing the right level of abstraction for the tools. Low-level controls would make the AI responsible for operating the UI. Higher-level WebMCP tools allow it to work with concepts that actually matter to the user: contributions, missing events, thematic spreads and page order. 

 Reliable saving and synchronization were also important because an AI-created page must behave like any page created or edited manually. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The most important accomplishment is a working end-to-end WebMCP workflow. 

 The AI can inspect real submitted memories, analyze their coverage, propose a thematic spread, and then build that spread directly in the MemoryBook. 

 The resulting content is not just an AI response in a chat window. It becomes part of the actual editable book. 

 The project also demonstrates that WebMCP can support both read-only analytical operations and actions that modify application state, while allowing the user to decide when an operation should be executed. 

 What we learned 

 Building MemoryBook changed how I think about AI integration in web applications. 

 An embedded chatbot can answer questions about an application. WebMCP enables something different: the website can expose what it is capable of doing, and an AI agent can use those capabilities as tools. 

 The most useful model is not necessarily AI replacing the interface. 

 A person may prefer a visual editor for creative decisions. An AI agent may be better at reviewing many contributions, identifying missing themes and organizing information. Both can work with the same underlying application and book. 

 What's next for MemoryBook 

 MemoryBook is currently a working prototype focused on demonstrating the WebMCP workflow. 

 The larger direction is a complete collaborative memory-book platform where groups can collect memories and photos, organize them with AI assistance, visually edit the result, and produce a finished digital or printable book. 

 Future development can expand the collaboration workflow, improve AI-assisted layout and organization, and add production-ready publishing and export capabilities. 

 WebMCP can make this process substantially easier by allowing AI agents to handle organizational and repetitive editorial work while keeping people in control of the final book.

pitch: A local-first WebMCP workspace where AI agents discover, match, and monitor student opportunities using 11 deterministic browser tools—with strict schemas and human-in-the-loop write approval.\n

A local-first WebMCP workspace where AI agents discover, match, and monitor student opportunities using 11 deterministic browser tools—with strict schemas and human-in-the-loop write approval.

 💡 Inspiration 

 Every year, millions of students, researchers, and early-career developers miss out on career-defining fellowships, high-impact internships, and competitive hackathons simply because opportunity tracking is broken. Opportunities are scattered across fragmented job boards, company portals, and academic lists with shifting deadlines and convoluted eligibility criteria. 

 With the advent of autonomous AI agents, we wondered: Why are agents still forced to browse the web like clumsy humans—scraping messy DOM trees, hallucinating CSS selectors, and breaking brittle form buttons? 

 When Google and the W3C introduced WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) , we saw the future: a web where applications expose their capabilities directly to in-browser AI models as structured, strongly-typed tools. 

 We built OpportunityOS to pioneer this new paradigm: an agent-native, local-first workspace that connects students with opportunities through 11 deterministic WebMCP tools, while keeping humans firmly in control of consequential writes. 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 OpportunityOS is a browser-native opportunity management engine designed for both human operators and autonomous AI agents: 

 
 Autonomous Opportunity Discovery & Matching: Agents discover 11 registered WebMCP tools directly through document.modelContext . They can search by domain, evaluate candidate eligibility, run multi-factor weighted rankings, and generate comparative matrices—with zero hallucination. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Write Governance: While read operations ( search , filter , rank , compare ) execute autonomously, consequential write operations ( save_opportunity , create_action_plan , update_application_status ) are intercepted by a security gate that requires explicit human approval before mutating state. 
 Live Surveillance & Application Tracking: Provides a unified command center featuring days-remaining countdowns, interactive 4-step milestone checklists ( Resume Tailored , LOR Requested , Statement Drafted , Portal Submitted ), and rapid deadline reminder chips ( ⚡ 48h Warning , 🚨 24h Crunch ). 
 Real-Time Surveillance Telemetry Feed: An immutable audit log records every agent interaction with millisecond timestamps, execution latencies, tool call signatures, and payload inspections. 
 Cinematic 3D Centerpiece & Bespoke Dual Themes: Features a real-time WebGL 3D cyber-butterfly sculpture with aerodynamic multi-phase wing kinematics, styled with Google's modern Unbounded typography and a tailored dual-theme system (Obsidian Cyber-Cyan Dark Mode and Royal Cobalt Sapphire & Porcelain Pearl Light Mode). 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 OpportunityOS is built with a strictly client-side, local-first architecture without external proxy dependencies or API credential leakage: 

 
 WebMCP Integration ( src/webmcp.js ): Implemented a production-grade WebMCP engine that registers 11 tools into document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool features strict JSON Schema boundaries, parameter type limits, and untrustedContentHint: true tagging on external data to prevent prompt injection. 
 Frontend Architecture ( src/main.js ): Built with Vanilla JavaScript and Vite for lightning-fast performance, zero bundle bloat, and instantaneous reactive UI state updates. 
 3D Procedural Engine (Three.js WebGL): Crafted a custom 3D cyber-organic butterfly sculpture featuring dual-layer aerodynamic wing geometries, interactive mouse parallax banking, pulsating reactor crystal lighting, and dynamic theme-adaptive shaders. 
 Design System ( src/styles.css ): Engineered with Google's geometric Unbounded typography and an adaptive CSS token system that transitions between deep obsidian neon and a vibrant royal cobalt sapphire palette. 
 

 

 🔒 Security & Safety Invariants 

 We designed OpportunityOS under the principle: "Built for agents. Not built to trust them blindly." 

 
 Strict Schemas & Bounded Inputs: Every tool argument is strongly typed with bounded string lengths and integer ranges to eliminate runaway buffer allocations. 
 Untrusted Content Demarcation: All catalog-derived data is explicitly labeled with untrustedContentHint: true , instructing agents to treat external text as untrusted data. 
 Fixed ID Addressing: Tools operate strictly on catalog-validated entity IDs, preventing arbitrary SQL or prompt injections. 
 Zero Secret Leakage: Operates local-first in the browser runtime without requiring backend API keys or credential proxies. 
 Deterministic Services: Local scoring algorithms provide reproducible and explainable candidate evaluations. 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Bridging WebMCP with Visual Feedback: Standard agent tools run invisibly in background execution contexts. We had to build a custom interceptor that visualizes agent reasoning in real-time, pauses execution when write permissions are requested, and renders a native confirmation modal. 
 Light Theme Luminosity & Contrast: Ensuring that rich, high-contrast aesthetics translated gracefully between dark and light modes without washed-out grays required developing a bespoke Royal Cobalt Sapphire & Porcelain Pearl palette with high-specificity CSS inversion rules. 
 Aerodynamic 3D Kinematics: Getting the Three.js butterfly to flap with realistic organic flight physics required decoupling the upper and lower wing matrices and applying phase-lagged sine wave oscillations with subtle wingtip aero-tremor. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 Fully Compliant WebMCP Implementation: Built all 11 tools adhering strictly to the W3C WebMCP draft specification with complete schema validation. 
 Zero-Latency Local-First Runtime: The entire app runs offline-ready, respecting user privacy and keeping all application milestones on-device. 
 Stunning Visual Identity: Created a design that breaks away from generic AI templates, combining sculptural 3D motion, spacious modern cards, and the bold Unbounded typeface. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 
 How WebMCP transforms web apps from passive user interfaces into structured, actionable APIs for AI models. 
 Techniques for prompt-injection defense when agents process untrusted catalog content. 
 Crafting human-in-the-loop security patterns where agents move fast while humans stay in total control. 
 

 

 🔮 What's Next for OpportunityOS 

 
 Chrome Extension Companion: Injecting OpportunityOS's WebMCP context into third-party portals like LinkedIn, Handshake, and university research directories. 
 Local LLM Integration (Gemini Nano / WebLLM): Running an on-device SLM directly inside the browser tab to execute missions with zero server costs. 
 Agent-Assisted Portfolio Assembly: Using WebMCP tools to automatically assemble tailored portfolios and statement drafts for verified deadlines.

title: CrisisDesk — Agent-Native Incident Response
pitch: Give the agent a problem, not a prompt. CrisisDesk lets an AI agent investigate real incidents via real WebMCP tools, propose a fix, and act only after a human approves.
about_excerpt: Give the agent a problem, not a prompt. CrisisDesk lets an AI agent investigate real incidents via real WebMCP tools, propose a fix, and act only after a human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most "AI + app" projects bolt a chatbot onto an existing UI and hardcode what it's allowed to say. I wanted to build the opposite: an app designed from day one so that a real AI agent — not a scripted demo — could discover its capabilities and use them the way a human would, through a genuine protocol rather than screen-scraping or prompt engineering tricks. Incident response felt like the perfect domain to prove it. On-call engineers already live the exact loop an agent is good at: gather evidence from five different dashboards, correlate it under time pressure, form a hypothesis, and — critically — never act alone on something risky. That last part is the whole point of CrisisDesk: the agent investigates freely, but a human always has the final say before anything changes. What it does CrisisDesk is a simulated SRE platform. Four incident scenarios ship with it — a payment API regression from a bad deploy, a database connection pool exhausting itself, a search-indexing backlog, and a memory leak — each with real, correlated, time-series metrics, logs, and deployment history. Click "Investigate with Agent" on any incident and the agent: Gathers evidence (incident details, service status, deployments, logs, metrics, dependencies) through real WebMCP tools. Correlates the evidence and proposes a root-cause hypothesis with a confidence score. Drafts a remediation plan. Proposes executing it — and then stops . A real approval dialog appears, and nothing happens to the simulated environment until a human clicks Approve. Every one of those steps is a real, independently-discoverable tool registered via document.modelContext.registerTool , not a scripted animation. You can inspect the exact input/output JSON of every call in the live "Agent Activity" feed. How I built it The stack is Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) + TypeScript + Tailwind + shadcn/ui on the frontend, Recharts for the metrics, and Google's Gemini API for the agent's reasoning. The simulation itself (incidents, services, logs, metrics, deployments) is a deterministic, resettable, entirely client-side data layer — WebMCP tools execute in the browser by definition, so that's where their data lives too. The architecture keeps one hard rule: Gemini never touches the app directly. It only ever picks a tool name and arguments; the actual call always goes through document.modelContext.executeTool(...) — the exact path a fully independent WebMCP agent (Chrome's origin trial, ChatGPT Desktop) would use if it discovered CrisisDesk on its own with zero app-specific code. If a real WebMCP-capable browser is present, the badge in the top bar says so; if not, a same-shaped local polyfill takes over and says so just as honestly. The one high-impact tool, execute_remediation , enforces human approval inside its own execute() function — it's a real await on a Promise that only resolves when a person clicks a button, not a UI convention layered on top of an agent that could technically act without it. Challenges I ran into The Gemini free tier is stricter than it looks. My first working version asked Gemini to decide every single tool call one at a time — a natural, ReAct-style loop. It worked, but burned ~10 API requests per investigation. Testing quickly revealed the free tier caps gemini-3.6-flash at 5 requests/minute and 20 requests/day. At that rate, two full investigations exhausted an entire day's quota. I redesigned the loop: the app now gathers all the read-only evidence itself (still real WebMCP calls, just sequenced deterministically instead of decided one-by-one by the model) and asks Gemini to do its actual reasoning — correlate, hypothesize, plan, summarize — in a single batched call. Same real tool calls, one-tenth the API usage. Windows and Netlify's Next.js plugin don't get along. netlify deploy --build reliably failed at "Failed publishing static content" — traced it down to the local Windows account lacking SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege (Developer Mode off), which the plugin's static-asset publishing step seems to need. Rather than force a system-level Windows setting change, I shipped on Vercel instead, which the hackathon rules explicitly allow. Making the demo resilient, not just working. A live third-party API call is a single point of failure for a judged demo. So beyond retry-with-backoff on transient rate limits, I wrote a deterministic, evidence-grounded fallback analysis for each of the four incident scenarios. If the live Gemini call fails for any reason — quota, outage, missing key — the exact same real tool calls execute with that content instead, and the experience doesn't visibly change. Nothing about WebMCP is faked either way; only the source of the analysis text differs. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A WebMCP implementation that's genuinely spec-compliant (researched the actual spec and hackathon-provided code sample before writing a line of tool code) and honest about native-vs-polyfill support, never misrepresenting one as the other. Human-in-the-loop that's enforced in the tool's own code path, not just the UI. A full Vitest suite — including feeding the fallback content through the real tool executors, human-approval flow included — that caught two real bugs before they shipped (a missing isError flag on failed read-tool results, and log data that didn't actually support one incident's stated root cause). The full loop — investigate, hypothesize, plan, approve, execute, resolve — verified end to end against the live production deployment with the real Gemini API, not just locally. What I learned How much of "agentic" design is really about where you draw the line between what the model decides and what the app decides deterministically — and that pulling that line in the right place is also just good cost engineering. And that a demo's reliability is a feature you have to design for explicitly, not something you get for free from a third-party API. What's next for CrisisDesk A real datastore behind the existing repository abstraction (Postgres/Supabase — the app is already structured so this is a swap, not a rewrite), a couple more analysis tools ( assign_incident , verify_recovery ), and validating the same tool layer against a real native WebMCP agent as browser support matures past the current origin trial. title: Blackout: Escape Together
pitch: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out.
about_excerpt: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out. Like Comment Story Updates The game hero banner Light mirror puzzle AI companion robot with torch light on Inspiration My wife is a learning support teacher. She supports children with different learning needs, including children on the autism spectrum. Her work makes one thing clear: each child needs different support. The language, pace, instructions, and activities that work for one learner may not work for another. We began asking how AI could help create more flexible opportunities to practice communication. Could a child give a short instruction to a companion and see something happen? Could “Turn on the light” become a useful request inside a game? Could a teacher adapt the challenge to the child’s interests, needs, and abilities? Paper-and-pencil activities have their place. We wanted to explore another option: practice through play, where communication has a visible purpose. Blackout: Escape Together is our 1st technical exploration of that idea. We started with an escape room to test how a human and an AI companion could communicate, coordinate, and act in the same world. What it does Blackout is a first-person 3D escape room for one human and one AI companion. In a compatible host with WebMCP enabled, the player can say “Start game.” The AI chooses a name and receives its character role, current room state, and available abilities. The player can make requests such as: “Turn on the light.” “Come here, follow me” “Hold this button.” “Draw a blue circle.” These requests produce visible actions. The companion moves through the room, aims its torch, operates controls, and draws with crayons. The partners solve connected puzzles involving mirrors, light, codes, and two door locks. They can exchange roles, but the human remains responsible for movement and several physical actions. For learning, the opportunity is to connect words, intentions, and outcomes. A request matters because it helps something happen. The current build is a game prototype. It does not yet include a teacher challenge editor, individual learning plans, or validated educational outcomes. How we built it We settle on with Escape Room concept early on and my wife designed the initial code relay puzzle where AI will need to hold a button and read the code out while the player is on the other side of the room, typing in the code. We then layer it with a few more puzzles to create a chain where one solution leads to another. The game is built using Three.js with help from Codex. The game engine controls movement, collision, puzzle state, inventory, and action checks. The rendering layer turns that state into characters, light beams, controls, and animations. WebMCP connects the AI to the room through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has defined inputs and follows the game’s rules. The player do not need to know the available tools as the game should provide all the tools the player need to solve the puzzle. This lets the AI perform specific actions without guessing where to click: Shared pointing supplies live coordinates for requests such as “Come here.” Discovering equipment adds the related ability to the tool registry. One request can start a continued movement order or button hold. Drawing uses a bounded batch of crayon marks. Companion tools cannot move the human or bypass required human actions. The model interprets requests and selects actions. Local code handles continuous movement, animation, and sound. The game uses Web Audio and is hosted through ChatGPT Sites. Conversation and speech come from the player’s compatible host. We did not add a separate AI or voice backend. Challenges we ran into Haha we didn't know about the challenge until the last few days. So we spent most of our time brainstorming and 3D game is something that we are not familiar. The 2nd challenge was connecting language to reliable action. If the companion accepts a request to hold a button, it still needs time to reach it. The game must distinguish between “I am moving” and “I am holding it.” Voice delay also affected the design. A code observed during the current round remains valid, so a delayed spoken reply does not erase progress. Also AI kept taking screenshots and taking actions outside of the game. The educational direction introduces another important challenge: flexibility. A dark room, moving enemies, or keyboard controls may create barriers for some learners. A learning version would need adjustable demands and different ways to participate. It cannot assume that every child wants to speak, enjoys the same sensory experience, or learns at the same pace. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete room in which human and AI actions affect the same visible world. The companion can provide useful help while leaving meaningful decisions and actions to the player. Shared pointing and discovered abilities make WebMCP part of the experience, rather than an extra chat interface. Automated tests cover movement, puzzle rules, input validation, discovery, cancellation, and replay. Native WebMCP checks exercise companion tools alongside keyboard and mouse actions through the room. Most importantly, we now have a working prototype for exploring how a request can become a meaningful shared action. What we learned Communication practice needs a purpose. A short request can become part of reaching a goal, making a choice, or creating something. That is the opportunity we want to explore through play. We also learned that the learner must retain control. The companion should support participation, allow time, and leave room for the human to try. Speech would be one way to participate, not a requirement for every learner. Future activities should support different communication methods. Finally, a working game does not prove that learning has occurred. We need to test whether learners understand the actions, use the language meaningfully, and apply what they practice beyond one familiar challenge. What's next for Blackout: Escape Together We want to develop a teacher-guided learning mode with challenges that can be adjusted to each learner. Planned options include: Checklists - Understanding multi-steps instructions Choosing a small set of words, requests, or concepts to practice. Adjusting the number of steps and the level of prompting. Giving more response time, with no speed requirement. Using calm, well-lit scenes without enemies or sudden effects. Adjusting sound, movement, text, and visual complexity. Supporting spoken requests, typed input, and simple phrase or symbol choices. Exploring compatibility with augmentative and alternative communication tools. A first activity could involve asking the companion to turn on a light. A later activity could combine two requests or require the partners to exchange roles. These are proposed learning activities, not features of the current build. Before use with children, we need age-appropriate access, adult supervision, privacy protections, and suitable content controls. We want to develop and test these activities with educators, families, and relevant specialists. Success should be measured against each learner’s goals, not only whether they finish a room. Our aim is to give teachers another flexible way to support practice—and give learners a meaningful reason to communicate, explore, and create. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. Built With chrome css3 express.js gemini html5 javascript node.js redis server-sent-events upstash vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jason Ofua Like Share this project: Updates Jason Ofua started this project — Aug 27, 2026 03:41 AM EDT

title: zeroedit
pitch: ChatGPT images that you can edit
about_excerpt: ChatGPT images that you can edit Like Comment Story Updates Editor page with advertisement poster Home page with all the listing of generative documents specific skill poster chinese poster api virew Inspiration ZeroEdit began with a problem I had while working on another SaaS product. I needed quotation documents that could be edited manually, updated through an API, reused for different clients, and exported reliably. I had tried building something similar before, but every solved problem exposed several new ones. But now things are different so I decided to give it a try . What it does It basically gives ChatGPT images an editable and controllable canvas. Many people use ChatGPT to create moodboards, posters, social graphics etc. even if the image generated looks really good with skills. It is still very hard to manipulate it further according to your need exactly . let alone reuse it for some other purposes. If you ask the model to regenerate one detail , it can change everything else because of nondeterministic nature. Our version zero edit should not be this final, it should be something you start with . Through WebMCP, an agent can: Inspect the active document and editor capabilities. Create a document from editable text, images, shapes, groups, and styles. Upload generated or licensed image assets safely. Render and inspect a candidate before presenting it. Repair a visible issue without replacing the whole design. Show every proposed operation in Review. Wait for the user to approve or reject the changes. After approval, the result remains a normal editable document. The user can move layers, change text, replace images, adjust typography, undo changes, and export PNG or PDF. A document can also be published as a reusable API template. New data can produce new outputs without asking an image model to recreate the design. ZeroEdit also has a Figma handoff for continuing the work in an established design tool. ZeroEdit is not intended to replace Figma or canva. It focuses on the stage before that, the exploration phase. How we built it Taking apart old repos of mine and referencing new repos like openpencil etc for some stuffs Challenges we ran into Compositing layers with each other hard, in first try I noticed it has basically no way of telling what is good composition from bad . so we (codex mostly) added a inspect and repair loop basically, so that agent can inspect . Fonts caused another serious issue during rendering , it still has not been fixed properly. Image transfer was also difficult from chatgpt images to application. codex creates a short-lived upload reservation so an agent can upload the original image bytes directly and receive an approved workspace asset. and lot more I don't even remember half. Accomplishments that we're proud of Saving time for users and money for AI companies . What we learned Skills.md files are to be taken seriously for the end result of the agent . pitch: Human players and AI agents collaborate to solve 5 interconnected puzzles across surveillance feeds, security terminals, auxiliary power grids, and archived exit protocols.
about_excerpt:
Human players and AI agents collaborate to solve 5 interconnected puzzles across surveillance feeds, security terminals, auxiliary power grids, and archived exit protocols.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Here are the submission section details for THE LAST TERMINAL : 

 

 Inspiration 

 Traditional browser AI agents interact with web applications through brute force: taking high-resolution screenshots, parsing complex DOM trees, predicting CSS selectors, and firing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fragile, slow, and burns tens of thousands of tokens per action. 

 When WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) emerged as a proposed browser standard ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), we realized web applications no longer had to be passive visual interfaces. Websites could directly expose machine-readable capabilities to AI agents. 

 We wanted to showcase this paradigm shift in a way that was instantly understandable and fun. An escape room was the ultimate sandbox—demanding puzzle reasoning, state prerequisites, data extraction, and tool sequence execution! 

 

 What it does 

 THE LAST TERMINAL is an interactive, browser-based cyberpunk escape room where human players and AI agents collaborate to escape an abandoned digital research facility before the emergency countdown reaches zero. 

 
 5 Interconnected Subsystems : Surveillance Matrix, Security Terminal, Auxiliary Power Control, Archive Database, and Emergency Exit Override. 
 10 WebMCP Capabilities : Exposes structured capabilities ranging from inspect_surveillance("CAM-07") and read_log("LOG-2049") to restore_power(["C","A","D","B"]) and unlock_exit("7319") . 
 Dual Execution Engine : Human UI interactions and AI WebMCP tool calls invoke the exact same underlying JavaScript game engine logic. 
 Real-Time Agent Feed & Trace : A live terminal logs tool calls in real time, accompanied by a full JSON execution trace inspector for hackathon judges. 
 Demo Agent Simulator : Includes a 90-second automated execution mode so anyone can watch an AI agent solve the room step-by-step without needing external API keys. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 Core Tech Stack : Next.js 14 (App Router), React 18, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 
 WebMCP Integration ( src/lib/webmcp/ ) : Registered 10 structured tools with strict JSON Schemas using navigator.modelContext.registerTool imperative API, wrapped in a hydration guard to prevent re-registration during React re-renders. 
 Unified Game Engine ( src/lib/game/ ) : Built a central state machine ( gameEngine.ts ) powering both human clicks and agent tool calls. 
 Web Audio API Synthesizer ( src/lib/audio/sound.ts ) : Built a zero-external-asset audio generator for terminal typing clicks, success chimes, failure buzzers, and power-up sweeps. 
 Developer Debug Bar ( ?debug=true ) : Added a secret query parameter mode for instant puzzle completion and state inspection during testing. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Enforcing Prerequisites Without Crashing : Ensuring that tools like open_archive() correctly check state prerequisites ( power === 'online' ) and return structured error payloads ( PREREQUISITE_NOT_MET ) rather than throwing unhandled exceptions. 
 Graceful Fallback & Polyfilling : WebMCP is an emerging browser feature. We needed to support native navigator.modelContext while building an in-memory tool polyfill and automated simulator for standard browsers. 
 Zero-Dependency Architecture : Ensuring the entire application ran client-side with zero backend infrastructure, zero paid APIs, and zero external databases while keeping the build Vercel-ready. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 >90% Token Reduction : Demonstrated how structured WebMCP tool calls eliminate the heavy token overhead of DOM parsing and visual screenshot analysis. 
 Zero Paid Dependencies : Built the entire experience to run 100% locally in the browser with zero external infrastructure. 
 100% Test & Build Validation : Achieved a clean Next.js static build and 100% pass rate on our standalone engine test suite ( npm run test:engine ). 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP transforms web applications from passive UIs into agentic APIs . 
 Human + Agent co-op design patterns—where humans supply visual intuition and agents perform rapid tool inspection—create a powerful collaboration model. 
 

 

 What's next for The Last Terminal 

 
 Multi-Agent Co-Op : Expanding to multi-agent escape rooms where specialized WebMCP agents (e.g. Security Agent, Power Agent) solve puzzles in parallel with human teams. 
 useWebMCPTool React Hook : Packaging our WebMCP registration layer into an open-source React hook library for Next.js developers. 
 Community Puzzle Creator : Allowing developers to construct their own WebMCP escape rooms using custom JSON schemas!

title: Exposed
pitch: Your AI agent finds your HIPAA exposure in three minutes — and can't take the one decision that matters.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent finds your HIPAA exposure in three minutes — and can't take the one decision that matters. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The sister site, lab.hipaa.technology, teaches doctors how to adopt AI safely — and its only way to raise a hand is a mailto: link in the footer. Meanwhile the practices most at risk aren't deciding whether to use AI. They already are: an ambient scribe on live patient audio, ChatGPT on a consumer tier, no BAA, no consent workflow, no risk analysis that mentions AI. They don't need another article. They need to know what they're exposed to, in the time between patients. WebMCP made it possible to let their agent do the asking. What it does Ten questions about how a practice already uses AI. A readiness score and the three sharpest exposures, free, each with the statute underneath. A personalised remediation roadmap, built from a thirty-control library, gated behind an email the human types themselves. Nine WebMCP tools: Tool Role check_ai_vendor_baa , check_state_ai_rules Hook tools — work with no assessment started start_readiness_check , answer_check_question , get_readiness_score , explain_risk The check email_remediation_roadmap , open_21_day_mission , book_compliance_review Conversion — each hands a decision back to the human How we built it React + TypeScript, imperative registration in the top-level document: document.modelContext with navigator.modelContext fallback, feature-detected, Strict-Mode safe, silent when the API is absent. Every input schema is additionalProperties: false with bounded enums. No free-text input anywhere in the assessment, so patient information cannot enter it. Every tool returns { display, spoken, next_step, disclaimer } . spoken is written to be read aloud, because in an agent flow the human may never see the page. The legal disclaimer travels inside the return value, not just the footer. The gate: email_remediation_roadmap takes no email argument and rejects one if supplied. It pauses execution and opens a real dialog on the page. The human types. The agent can't. Answers stay in the browser. The server keeps email, score, state, clinician count, specialty and three risk-category IDs — never the itemised gaps. Built entirely inside the challenge window. /webmcp on the site documents tools, schemas and the AI MAY / HUMAN MUST boundary. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext both exist in the wild; we register against whichever is present. ChatGPT's browser supports a subset — no declarative forms, no iframes. Everything is imperative, top-level. Language is a legal surface. No "audit", "certified" or "compliant" anywhere — copy, tool names, descriptions or return values. The site says what is missing ; it never says a practice is or isn't compliant. Cutting thirty controls to ten questions. Completion collapses past seven. Ten is the ceiling; the thirty stay in the codebase to power the roadmap. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent can run the whole check in one prompt, and ChatGPT's browser lists all nine tools first try. A gate the agent cannot pass on its own — designed as a feature, not a limitation. A data model chosen for the client's legal position: a written record of a named practice's admitted gaps is a discoverable document, so we never hold one. Shipped, on a real domain, with a live activity rail showing every tool call and every human decision. What we learned The best tool surface is the smallest one. Copy belongs in tool return values. And the most important tool is the one that refuses to act — the gate is the product. What's next for Exposed Roadmap email delivery, state-law overlays beyond recording consent, booking straight into a calendar, and the hand-off into the 21-day adoption mission at lab.hipaa.technology. title: Lattice Perps
pitch: A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
about_excerpt:
A safety-first WebMCP trading cockpit for Hyperliquid: agents propose bounded paper trades, humans control authority, and every action is policy-checked with transparent receipts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Web agents can operate a web page, but actions that change state still need to be understandable, inspectable, and safe. 

 We wanted to explore what an agent-native trading interface could feel like without asking anyone to connect a wallet, approve a signer, or risk real funds. Lattice Perps is our answer: a browser-local paper-trading experience where a human and a browser agent can use the same interface, the same account, and the same visible evidence. 

 The project is inspired by Hyperliquid perpetual markets, but this public showcase intentionally stops at deterministic local simulation. 

 What it does 

 Lattice Perps is a paper trading flight recorder for WebMCP. 

 The app starts with one browser-local paper account containing $100,000 of simulated USD and four fixed markets: 

 
 BTC 
 ETH 
 SOL 
 HYPE 
 

 A human can place market or limit orders from the visible interface. Market orders fill at the displayed simulated mark price. Limit orders rest locally and can be cancelled by their local order ID. 

 A browser agent can perform the same paper-trading actions through six WebMCP tools: 

 
 paper_get_markets 
 paper_get_portfolio 
 paper_get_open_orders 
 paper_get_activity 
 paper_place_order 
 paper_cancel_order 
 

 Every human action, system event, and WebMCP call is written to the visible Agent Tape . The portfolio panel updates from the same underlying account state, showing equity, available balance, margin used, realised PnL, unrealised PnL, positions, open orders, and fills. 

 The key idea is simple: 

 
 One local account. One shared state. Two ways to interact. 
 

 You can trade from the page or ask your browser agent: 

 
 Buy 0.05 BTC at market, then show my paper portfolio. 
 

 The result is visible in the Agent Tape and reflected in the portfolio immediately. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. 

 The human interface and WebMCP tools share one LocalTradingStore . This prevents the UI and agent surface from developing separate balances, positions, orders, or activity histories. 

 The store provides: 

 
 deterministic simulated markets and mark prices 
 market and limit order handling 
 position netting and PnL calculations 
 simulated fees and margin checks 
 local order cancellation 
 browser persistence through localStorage when available 
 an in-memory fallback when browser storage is unavailable 
 a visible activity history for human and WebMCP actions 
 

 WebMCP registration is feature-detected through the browser's document.modelContext surface. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human trading interface still works. Tool inputs use explicit schemas and reject unexpected fields so the agent surface remains narrow and predictable. 

 The project also includes automated tests for the local trading store, WebMCP tool definitions, and the rendered paper-trading interface. 

 Safety by design 

 This showcase deliberately has: 

 
 no wallet connection 
 no exchange connection 
 no network order submission 
 no real funds 
 no private keys 
 no deposits or withdrawals 
 no production trading capability 
 

 WebMCP is treated as an invocation layer, not an authentication or authorization mechanism. The public demo is designed to make the interaction model visible without pretending that a browser tool registration is equivalent to trading authority. 

 Challenges 

 The hardest part was making the human and agent paths genuinely share state. A separate “agent balance” or fake tool response would have made the demo look convincing while hiding the real interaction model. Instead, both paths call the same store and produce the same portfolio projections and activity records. 

 Another challenge was making the demo useful even when the browser does not support WebMCP. The interface therefore remains complete on its own, while WebMCP enhances it when the browser exposes the API. 

 Finally, we had to make the boundaries clear. A trading demo can easily imply that a real exchange, wallet, or signer is involved. The local simulation, explicit labels, and Agent Tape are designed to keep the demo honest. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agent-native interfaces benefit from visible evidence, not just successful tool calls. A tool invocation is much easier to understand when the user can see its source, timestamp, status, and effect on the shared account. 

 We also learned that deterministic simulation is valuable for WebMCP development. It makes the experience reproducible, easy to reset, and safe to demonstrate while the browser API and authority model are still evolving. 

 What's next 

 A future version could connect this interaction model to a separately approved testnet account behind explicit human authority, policy checks, and post-action reconciliation. 

 For this submission, we intentionally keep the public experience local, deterministic, and risk-free.

title: Falsify
pitch: A browser-native research workspace where humans and WebMCP agents test ideas against frozen contracts, shared evidence, and approval-gated decisions.
about_excerpt: A browser-native research workspace where humans and WebMCP agents test ideas against frozen contracts, shared evidence, and approval-gated decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Falsify started from my work on Kaggle hackathons and machine learning competitions. I wanted a system that could analyze a target model, explore several research branches in one session, and keep each branch grounded in its own evidence. The practical goal was to reduce context contamination and hallucination as a long research session accumulated hypotheses, failed attempts, and partial results. A frontier GPT model using Ultra reasoning and subagents can already explore several branches in parallel. That helped with throughput, but it did not solve visibility. When multiple paths were active, I still could not answer simple questions at a glance: Which configuration produced the best result? Which branch failed for a technical reason? Which idea had already been tested? What should run next? Conversation logs were too linear for this job. I added an experiment graph so that model lineage and outcomes would be visible, then introduced tickets as an active reservation queue for research ideas. A person can record a hypothesis before stepping away, while a main orchestrator or a Codex agent connected through WebMCP can read the current progress and understand what the ticket is asking for. The longer-term goal is an overnight research loop in which the agent uses the accumulated evidence to refine or rewrite the next ticket when its assumptions are no longer valid, then continues with the correct experiment instead of blindly following stale instructions. The current browser MVP establishes the state, provenance, and approval rules needed for that workflow. What changed for this submission The earlier project focused on coordinating multi-branch research inside a single session. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built a browser-based research control plane that turns that progress into shared, inspectable state. I added the ticket queue, experiment lineage graph, frozen research contract, deterministic browser runner, evidence comparison views, human approval center, and 12 task-specific WebMCP tools. Human actions and agent actions now operate on the same workspace instead of producing separate conversation histories. What it does Falsify is a browser-based research workspace operated by a human and a WebMCP agent through the same shared state. Every project begins with a research contract that defines: the objective and primary metric the evaluation protocol the experiment budget the minimum effect required to count as an improvement the configuration keys an experiment may change Once the baseline produces valid evidence, the contract freezes. Ideas enter the workspace as tickets. A claimed ticket becomes exactly one experiment node under a frozen parent. Running the node produces evidence, and a decision can then promote it, discard it, or create follow-up tickets. This structure prevents a result from being reinterpreted after the fact. It also preserves the path from an idea to its configuration, run, evidence, and final decision. Technical failure and scientific failure are handled differently. If a run crashes or diverges before producing a valid measurement, the node becomes repairable. It is not labeled as a regression because the hypothesis was never properly tested. A valid but worse measurement, on the other hand, remains part of the scientific record. How I built it This submission is a browser-only MVP. It has no backend, user account, remote runner, or arbitrary code execution. The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. Project state is stored in IndexedDB. Experiment training runs in a Web Worker so that the interface remains responsive. The demonstration uses a deterministic two-moons classification problem and a small multilayer perceptron implemented from scratch. A fixed seed and frozen evaluation contract make the results repeatable during judging. The application registers 12 focused WebMCP tools on document.modelContext. They cover the complete research loop: inspect the project list and create tickets claim a ticket materialize an experiment start or cancel a run inspect evidence compare nodes commit a decision The tools call the same application service used by the React interface. Agent actions therefore appear in the human workspace without maintaining a separate copy of the project. Falsify deliberately exposes no generic shell, file, or delete tool. Mutations are checked against the frozen research contract, project revision, and idempotency key before execution. In Copilot mode, starting a run and committing a decision return an approval request instead of executing immediately. The proposal appears in the Approval Center, where a person can inspect and approve it. Manual mode applies approval gating to every agent mutation. Challenges The first challenge was preserving one consistent state machine across the human interface and WebMCP tools. A command had to obey the same rules regardless of whether it came from a button or an agent call. The second challenge was handling retries and concurrent actions safely. Each mutation includes an idempotency key and expected project revision. Retrying the same request replays its original result, while stale commands are rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. The third challenge was separating technical failure from scientific evidence. A diverged run must remain repairable, while a valid negative result must remain immutable. Treating both outcomes as a simple failed status would undermine the research record. The final challenge was making the demonstration deterministic without hiding the real workflow. The benchmark is intentionally small, but it still performs actual training in a Web Worker and produces metrics, curves, configuration differences, logs, and a decision boundary. What I learned I learned that an agent tool catalog is more than an API surface. Its names, descriptions, schemas, approval behavior, and output annotations collectively define what the agent believes it is allowed to do. I also learned that sharing storage is the easy part of human-agent collaboration. The harder part is sharing meaning: which contract governed a run, why a node exists, whether a measurement is valid, and who approved the next step. Explicit state transitions, frozen inputs, provenance links, and narrow tools made those boundaries easier for both the human and the agent to understand. What is next The next version will connect the same research model to local repositories and real experiment runners. Planned work includes a local daemon, SQLite and artifact storage, one Git worktree per experiment node, coding-agent adapters, and remote execution. The current browser profile remains intentionally narrow. It demonstrates the complete measure, compare, and decide loop without granting an agent generic access to the user’s machine. title: ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone
pitch: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look.
about_excerpt: A detective game where your agent reads every byte of the evidence and sees none of it. 25 WebMCP tools, no screenshot tool, and a case that only closes when the human and the agent both look. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Verification Panel Inspiration Co-op games need a second person. That is why I never play them. Every agent demo I have seen has done the same thing: the agent screenshots the page, clicks the button, and the human watches. The human is a spectator to their own software. I wanted the reverse. An agent that is genuinely powerful and genuinely incomplete, where I am the half it cannot replace. So I asked myself a question: what if the agent could read everything on the page, and see nothing? What it does Orpheus is a co-op detective game you play alone, because your agent is player two. A physicist is dead. His workstation was seized intact. Files, mail, messages, photos, a browser, a terminal, a system log. Every application on that desk is also a tool your agent can call. Twenty-five of them. Your agent can search every file, read every email, and filter fifty-one log entries down to the six that matter. What it cannot do is see. I gave it no screenshot tool, no vision tool, and no pixel access anywhere in the registry. It gets the filename, the camera, the timestamps, and not one pixel. So when the case turns on what is visible in a photograph, it opens the image on your screen and asks you what is in it. You describe. It searches what you described. The case will not unlock until a correlation has run through a tool and you have done your own looking. How I built it I built it using Next.js and React, fully client side. No backend, no database and no sign-up. I set one rule and it carried the whole build: if the human can do it and the agent can do it, the logic exists once. My register.ts declares 25 tools and implements none of them. Each delegates to the same service functions the UI calls, so the agent can never reach state a human could not. I added a static check that fails the build if the tool layer ever imports a data module directly. On top of that, 4 declarative HTML forms using the WebMCP declarative API. Then I added some guardrails: a 1500 character output budget, untrustedContentHint on every tool returning prose the agent did not author, and a nine verb terminal allowlist that refuses rm , chaining, and injection. Challenges I ran into The agent solved the whole case in one turn. It made forty tool calls, then handed me a finished report. I have to say it was correct, but completely against the point. Asking a model to slow down is like asking it not to delete a file. It might comply. It might delete the file anyway. So I put it in the tool layer: after five reads with no human action, read tools stop answering and tell the agent to hand back. I left actuation ungated, because putting a document on my screen is the behaviour I want. My hints made a blind agent sound sighted. They described photo contents to help the player along, so the agent just told the player everything right away. I rewrote every hint to give a location and a question. "The window glass, lower half. Tell me what is there." A tool result silently ate my rules. The output budget trims by halving the longest array, which was the protocol array in the briefing. A model asking for the rules of play was getting one rule of seven, with no sign the rest existed. I found it by measuring the payload instead of trusting it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The blindness is a mechanic, not a disclaimer. A prompt asking a model not to look is only advice, and it will look anyway if it decides it needs to. Withholding the capability from the registry is a rule. The page audits itself. If you want to test it yourself, open the LINK console and press QUICK VERIFY. 15 checks run against the tool registry in front of you, in your own browser. And it generalises, which I proved instead of claiming. I built a second instance at /apollo13 running the same 25 tools over the real Apollo 13 accident record: the Review Board report, the Mission Report, five voice loop threads, nine NASA photographs with real byte sizes and SHA-256 prefixes you can check yourself. I invented nothing. Where the primary sources contradict each other, I left the contradictions in. A corpus that resolves its own conflicts cannot teach you to find one. Same engine, same tool layer, one data file and a route. All of it is public domain. What I learned Withholding a capability is a design tool, and an underused one. The interesting question is not what else I can let an agent do. It is what it should have to ask me for. And a prompt is not a mechanic. Anything I wanted to actually be true had to live in the tool layer. What's next for ORPHEUS: A Case You and Your Agent Can't Crack Alone My corpus is a single interface, so any archive fits: a leaked document dump, a codebase post-mortem, a medical file, a legal discovery set. The version I want to build next is not fiction. It is the archive where letting an agent click freely is exactly what you cannot allow, and where the person reviewing it needs a partner that can hold fifty thousand files and no judgment at all.
