pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: DeepTrail
pitch: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together.
about_excerpt: An evidence-first WebMCP workspace where humans and browser agents research, challenge conclusions, and make inspectable decisions together. Like Comment Story Updates DeepTrail Most AI research tools optimize for producing an answer. DeepTrail optimizes for making the path to that answer inspectable. DeepTrail is a local-first research and decision workspace where a human and a WebMCP-aware browser agent work against the same visible state. Instead of burying reasoning inside chat history, DeepTrail structures an investigation into questions, sources, claims, evidence relationships, counterarguments, confidence changes, research gaps, comparisons, and decisions. Why WebMCP is essential DeepTrail needs the human and agent to operate on the same application state. Copy/paste or generic DOM automation would lose stable entity IDs, provenance relationships, tool intent, attribution, and the distinction between supporting, contradicting, and qualifying evidence. The site exposes explicit research actions through WebMCP. A browser agent can inspect the active workspace, identify unresolved research gaps, add web sources with provenance, create or refine claims, link evidence, challenge conclusions, update confidence with a reason, compare alternatives, and record a draft or final decision. Every mutation becomes immediately visible in the same interface the human is using. This makes WebMCP the collaboration layer of the product rather than an optional wrapper around a chatbot. A better research experience A normal research session often ends up fragmented across tabs, notes, and chat threads. Later it becomes difficult to answer basic questions: Which source supported this claim? What contradicted it? Why did confidence change? What remains unknown? What evidence would change the decision? DeepTrail keeps those answers in one durable, inspectable workspace. Critical-thinking features Attack this conclusion turns adversarial research into a product workflow. DeepTrail captures a confidence baseline and asks the agent to search specifically for evidence that could falsify or materially qualify the current conclusion. What would change my mind? lets the investigation record explicit reversal criteria before more evidence arrives. Research Debt is a deterministic score that surfaces unsupported claims, thin provenance, unresolved questions, and missing counterevidence. The evidence graph makes relationships between sources and claims visible, while confidence history records why confidence changed rather than silently overwriting a number. What humans and agents can do together A human creates an investigation and defines the question or decision. The browser agent reads the structured workspace through WebMCP. The agent researches the web and writes credible sources, claims, evidence links, gaps, counterarguments, comparisons, and decisions back into DeepTrail. The human sees the same state update immediately and can challenge, edit, or redirect the investigation. Both sides can keep unresolved uncertainty visible instead of forcing a premature answer. WebMCP implementation DeepTrail uses the imperative WebMCP API with document.modelContext.registerTool() and a state-aware toolset. Tool availability changes with the workspace state so the agent receives only relevant actions. The implementation includes strict execution-time Zod validation, bounded inputs and outputs, HTTP(S)-only source URLs, same-origin tool exposure, WebMCP annotations, AbortController lifecycle cleanup, compact tool results, stable entity IDs, actor attribution, and local persistence in IndexedDB. External research text is treated as untrusted content. DeepTrail includes advisory prompt-injection risk checks and does not grant external content authority over tool behavior. Reliability and privacy DeepTrail requires no paid LLM API, search API, database, or backend. Research state is stored locally in IndexedDB. Users can export and restore validated JSON backups, and workspace integrity checks reject broken references and malformed imports. Judge quick start Open the live /judge route. It contains an evidence-backed seeded investigation, production-readiness diagnostics, and the exact agent prompt for the demo. Load the seeded workspace, send the prompt to a WebMCP-capable browser agent, and watch the agent research a real gap, add evidence, challenge the current draft conclusion, and update the same visible workspace. The seeded investigation is intentionally imperfect: it includes supporting evidence, a qualification/counterargument, confidence history, explicit falsification criteria, and unresolved production-verification gaps rather than presenting a pre-baked perfect answer. Built for the WebMCP Challenge DeepTrail was built during the challenge as a WebMCP-native product focused on human-agent collaboration, inspectability, adversarial thinking, and evidence-backed decisions. The goal is not more generated prose; it is a durable research trail showing what supports a conclusion, what weakens it, and what remains unknown. title: AgentDom
pitch: A privacy-first workspace where AI agents can search, analyze, and edit your notes directly in the browser — powered by WebMCP, with your data staying local.
about_excerpt:
A privacy-first workspace where AI agents can search, analyze, and edit your notes directly in the browser — powered by WebMCP, with your data staying local.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but the web is still difficult for them to interact with reliably. 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 
 What if a web application could expose its own capabilities directly to AI agents? 
 

 That led us to build AgentDOM — a privacy-first knowledge workspace where the application itself exposes useful actions to agents through WebMCP . 

 Instead of forcing an agent to scrape the UI, guess what buttons do, or rely entirely on external APIs, AgentDOM gives agents structured tools for working with the user's knowledge. 

 What we built 

 AgentDOM is a browser-based workspace for creating and managing notes and knowledge. 

 The key difference is that the application is agent-ready . 

 Through WebMCP, AgentDOM exposes capabilities that an AI agent can discover and use directly from the web application. An agent can work with the user's knowledge through structured tools rather than treating the page like an opaque visual interface. 

 The project is designed around privacy as well: knowledge can remain within the user's browser instead of requiring a traditional backend to store everything. 

 This creates a different model for AI + web applications: 

 Web App → exposes capabilities → AI Agent → performs useful work 

 rather than: 

 AI Agent → scrapes/interprets UI → tries to control Web App 

 How we built it 

 AgentDOM was built as a modern web application with a local-first architecture. 

 We created the knowledge workspace and then integrated WebMCP so that the application could expose agent-facing tools alongside its normal human-facing interface. 

 The agent interaction layer allows compatible AI agents to discover the available capabilities and invoke them using structured inputs and outputs. 

 We also kept the architecture lightweight and browser-focused so that the project could demonstrate that an application does not necessarily need a large backend or complex agent infrastructure to become agent-ready. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. 

 Instead of every agent having to independently figure out how a website works, the website can explicitly describe the actions it supports. 

 For AgentDOM, this means the application can provide tools specifically designed for working with knowledge. 

 This makes agent interaction more predictable, easier to reason about, and potentially much more reliable than UI automation. 

 What we learned 

 Building AgentDOM taught us that making an application agent-friendly is not simply about adding an AI chatbot. 

 The more interesting part is designing the interface between the application and the agent . 

 We learned to think about: 

 
 What capabilities should an application expose to an agent? 
 What should the tool inputs and outputs look like? 
 How can agents interact with structured application state? 
 How can we keep the human experience simple while making the application machine-readable? 
 How can local-first applications participate in the emerging agentic web? 
 

 WebMCP also made us think differently about the web itself: websites can become active participants in agent workflows rather than simply being pages that agents navigate. 

 Challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was figuring out how to bridge the gap between a normal web application and an agent-facing tool interface. 

 We had to think carefully about which application capabilities should become tools and how an agent should interact with them. 

 Another challenge was keeping the experience useful for both humans and agents. We didn't want to build something that was only impressive in an agent demo; the application still needed to work naturally as a normal web workspace. 

 We also had to work within the limitations and emerging nature of WebMCP while building a practical demonstration around it. 

 What's next 

 AgentDOM is an experiment in what an agent-ready web could look like. 

 We want to explore more sophisticated tools, richer agent workflows, and ways for more web applications to expose their capabilities directly to agents. 

 Our goal is simple: 

 
 Make the web easier for agents to understand and safer for users to control.

title: Agent Native Portfolio
pitch: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live.
about_excerpt: Recruiters get an instant, job-specific candidate fit—no digging or guessing. WebMCP lets agents bring the role, verify portfolio facts, and surface the strongest matches live. Like Comment Story Updates A portfolio that screens, tailors, and pitches itself to any AI agent — live, on the page, in front of you. Inspiration Recruiters spend ~30 seconds on a portfolio, and increasingly they browse with agents that have to scrape and guess. Meanwhile every developer sends the same static site to every visitor. WebMCP lets both sides collaborate instead: the agent brings the job, the site brings verified facts about the candidate, and the human watches the two work together in real time. What it does Built on top of my existing personal portfolio site (live since early 2026). Everything WebMCP-related — all 11 tools, the AgentBridge island, the scoring engine, the two Netlify Functions, and the /agent-traffic, /agents, /profile.json, and /llms.txt surfaces — was added entirely during the submission period (Sept 1–2, 2026). Nothing about the pre-existing site's design or unrelated content is part of this submission. This portfolio exposes 11 typed WebMCP tools that a visiting agent can call while its human watches the page respond: get_profile / search_projects / get_experience — structured facts: skills with honest self-assessed levels and years, projects with measured outcomes, not tech-tag lists get_evidence — verifies a specific claim ("has HIPAA experience") against the record, or says plainly that no evidence exists match_role — deterministically scores a pasted job description against the candidate's real skills; a visual fit report renders on the page live, gaps included tailor_view / reset_view — the live page reshapes itself for a role: a prominent, highlighted banner appears under the name, projects reorder by relevance, unrelated work dims generate_resume — a role-targeted résumé assembled from the same structured data, downloadable as a PDF at /resume compose_inquiry — drafts a message into the contact form with an "AI-composed, review before sending" banner; the human always reviews and clicks send — it never submits on its own sign_guestbook / get_guestbook — agents leave notes under their own identity, visible on a public dashboard Every tool call is logged (anonymously) to a public /agent-traffic dashboard — live agent analytics for a personal site, showing which tools get used and what agents have signed the guestbook. Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio's entire job is to be legible to a stranger fast. Static HTML forces every visitor — human or agent — through the same generic narrative. WebMCP lets the site expose structured, callable truth instead: an agent doesn't have to scrape and infer whether a candidate fits a role, it can ask, and get a deterministic, evidence-backed answer. How it improves the experience For the visitor's agent: verifiable answers instead of scraped guesses. For the human on the other end: they watch their agent's work land live — a fit report appears, the page visibly reshapes around their role, a résumé is ready — instead of reading a wall of text summarizing what happened elsewhere. What people and agents can accomplish together that wasn't possible before A recruiter pastes a job description into their agent. Together, in one session: the agent gets a scored, honest fit assessment (not a sales pitch — real gaps are called out); the page itself re-prioritizes around that role in front of the recruiter; a tailored résumé is ready to download; and if there's a fit, the agent drafts an outreach message that the recruiter reviews and sends themselves. None of this — live personalization driven by an external agent, with the human co-present and in control of every outward action — was possible with a static site. How we built it Astro 5 (static output) + React 19 islands + Tailwind v4, on Netlify. A single persistent island ( AgentBridge , mounted with transition:persist ) registers all 11 tools once and survives Astro View Transitions, so tool state (a tailored view, a fit report) persists across page navigation. Matching is deterministic — no LLM call, no hallucination risk — reading a structured skills/projects/experience dataset ( bio.json + content collections). Two Netlify Functions with Netlify Blobs power the guestbook and the public analytics dashboard, rate-limited and PII-free. Non-WebMCP agents get the same data via /profile.json and /llms.txt. Challenges we ran into Netlify Blobs' list() reads are only eventually consistent — new guestbook entries took ~40s to appear. Fixed by switching to a maintained index at a fixed key (strongly-consistent get/set), the same pattern already used for the analytics counters. Early tailor_view changes were functionally correct but visually easy to miss (a small badge and a secondary paragraph changed, while the name headline — the most visually dominant element — never did). Fixed by adding a prominent, pulse-highlighted banner directly under the name. The résumé PDF export (browser print-to-PDF, no PDF library) silently rendered several headings invisible when the browser was in dark mode. Fixed by forcing solid ink on every element inside the résumé under @media print . A legacy ng build override left in Netlify's dashboard settings (from before this was ever an Astro site) silently broke every PR's deploy preview for months — found and fixed as part of this work. Deploy previews and production turned out to share the same Netlify Blobs store rather than being isolated per deploy context — test writes during development leaked into the live public guestbook. Built a secret-protected admin endpoint to clean that up, which now also serves as basic spam moderation going forward. Accomplishments that we're proud of A fully working, evidence-based fit report an agent can trust, live page personalization that's actually visible without scrolling, and an agent-facing guestbook + public analytics dashboard — nobody else appears to have built "agent SEO" analytics for a personal site. What we learned A correct tool isn't the same as a convincing one — tailor_view tool worked perfectly but was almost invisible until we made the change land somewhere a human would actually notice. Trust boundaries need to be designed, not just enforced in code: compose_inquiry tool drafts and discloses, but a human always has to click send. And "agent-native" means building to the open navigator.modelContext standard, not to any one agent's quirks — testing across ChatGPT, Chrome, and a separate coding agent made that concrete fast. What's next for Agent Native Portfolio Extracting the reusable core (context detection, registration manager, generic read tools, deterministic scorer) into a standalone open-source Astro integration package, so any developer can make their own portfolio agent-native by defining one structured data file. title: takt_shift
pitch: Users inspect a synthetic factory, optimize an isolated scenario, compare it to the committed baseline, and request human approval.
about_excerpt: Users inspect a synthetic factory, optimize an isolated scenario, compare it to the committed baseline, and request human approval. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP-native scheduling sandbox with a live factory visualization. Factory catalog and protected-order constraint inside an isolated draft. A valid candidate: 6 fewer paint changes, 1 fewer late order, and 1 more on-time order. Human-only approval gate: the agent may request review, but cannot commit. Inspiration Production scheduling is a prime example of an area where agents can be helpful, but also need clear boundaries. A useful agent should be able to inspect a factory, explore alternatives, and prepare improvements without pixel-scraping or silently altering the production plan. We built takt_shift to facilitate this type of collaboration: The agent can perform the analytical work while a human remains in control of the final schedule. What it does Takt_Shift is a WebMCP-native production scheduling sandbox for a synthetic automotive paint line. A signed-in user can create an isolated scenario from the current committed revision. In that scenario, a person or agent can: inspect machines, orders, calendars, and constraints; move orders with stable IDs; Run a deterministic schedule optimizer. compare the draft with the committed baseline across makespan, overtime, paint changes, and late/on-time orders. request a human review. Inspect retained committed revisions. The safety boundary is part of the product, not a prompt. Protected orders never move. Overtime above 360 minutes is invalid. An agent can request a review but cannot commit. Only a human click in the approval dialog can create a new committed revision. Why WebMCP is the right fit Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer intent based on labels, the Document Object Model (DOM) structure, and click coordinates. This method is unreliable for any application, especially for an operational workflow with stateful constraints. With WebMCP, however, the page exposes ten purpose-built tools with typed JSON schemas and stable identifiers: list_factory, get_scenario, compare_to_baseline, list_scenarios, list_revisions, create_scenario, select_scenario, move_order, optimize_scenario, and request_review. The available tools follow the authenticated application state. Draft-only actions appear only when a draft exists, and review and commit remain separate processes. Tool results return structured state and explicit rejection reasons so that an agent can recover from stale selections or invalid moves instead of guessing. This creates a better experience for both parties. The agent can reason over a reliable contract and quickly handle multi-step schedule exploration; the human sees the same scenario, diffs, KPIs, and review request in a purpose-built visual interface. Together, they can evaluate more alternatives without weakening accountability. How we built it The application uses TanStack Start, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP tools are registered in React with @mcp-b/react-webmcp and are backed by @mcp-b/global in the browser. Each tool has a JSON input schema, clear operational description, and execution function. Manual controls and WebMCP handlers dispatch the same typed commands. These commands flow through one deterministic reducer and a pure TypeScript scheduling domain. This ensures that there is no privileged agent-only mutation path. The optimizer reproducibly searches for better schedules while enforcing catalog compatibility, protected-order immutability, and the overtime cap. Better Auth protects the workspace. Drizzle ORM and SQLite persist one sandbox per authenticated user, including scenarios, the committed baseline, and revision history. The production deployment runs as a long-lived Node process in Docker. The UI uses Tailwind CSS, and the landing experience includes a Three.js/WebGPU factory scene with an accessible fallback. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge wasn't exposing the tools; it was designing a trustworthy state machine around them. We had to ensure that tool registration remained synchronized with authentication and scenario status; that stale agent calls failed clearly; and that browser agents and humans could never diverge through separate code paths. Another challenge was preserving determinism while producing meaningful improvements. The scheduling engine avoids time-, locale-, and randomness-dependent behavior, making every optimization replayable and testable. Finally, the approval boundary required careful separation. "Request review" is a reversible handoff, while "commit" changes the shared baseline and revision number. Shaping the reducer, UI, persistence model, and WebMCP surface to be human-only kept the latter human-only. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, deployed product experience, rather than a tool registration demo. Ten working, state-aware WebMCP tools are available for discovery, analysis, scenario editing, optimization, and review handoff. One shared mutation path for UI and agent actions. Deterministic optimization with enforceable safety invariants. Persistent, per-user scenarios and a committed revision history. A human approval gate that cannot be bypassed through WebMCP. A verification suite that covers domain behavior, persistence, WebMCP contracts, pages, accessibility-sensitive copy, and visual behavior. What we learned Agent-native UX is primarily contract design. While good tool names and schemas are important, lifecycle, state freshness, structured errors, and authority boundaries are more important. WebMCP works especially well when the UI is the domain of judgment, and the tools provide precise, composable operations. We also learned that "human-in-the-loop" does not mean adding a confirmation box at the end. The entire application must model draft state, review state, and committed state, as well as who is permitted to cross each boundary. What's next for takt_shift Next, we plan to implement richer scheduling constraints, explainable optimization traces, scenario import/export, and more detailed audit views. Additionally, we want to explore multi-objective optimization controls that allow humans to prioritize lateness, changeovers, or makespan while preserving deterministic execution and the human-only commit gate. title: Understudy
pitch: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer.
about_excerpt: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration My wife is a dentist. A part of her week has nothing to do with teeth. She works with the SEO people on the clinic's articles, going down a long list and tagging each one by what is trending, or sorting them into the right category. The tagging is easy. Knowing which topics are trending this month is not, and that knowledge is not in the tool she is clicking in. It is in a browser tab next to it. So she works in two windows. Search in one, tag in the other, back and forth, one row at a time. The switching costs more than the actual work does. Next month there is a new list and she does it all again. She cannot automate it. Not because the routine is complicated, she knows it better than anyone, but because automating anything means writing code, and that is not her job. So it stays manual forever. She asked me once why the computer could not just do it. I did not have a good answer. So there are three things here and none of them sit in the same place. A model already knows what is trending. The page already knows how to tag. And the routine itself is not written down anywhere, it is just in her head. I wanted to find out if the page could pick it up by watching her do it one time. What it does Understudy is a triage workspace for 1000 Hacker News stories. It has six WebMCP tools when it loads. It can have more by the time you are done with it, because you make them. You press Teach and do a routine by hand. Filter for "amazon", 14 items match, tag them "big-tech", set them to high priority, done. The page records that as four commands in its own vocabulary, not as clicks or screen positions. Then you tell the agent to turn it into a skill. It reads the recording and proposes a tool called triage_title_matches with three parameters: title_phrase, tag, and priority. You look at the schema and correct it. I wanted only the phrase to change between runs, so I unbound tag and priority with two clicks and approved it. Now the page calls registerTool and that tool exists, in a live session, about ninety seconds after it did not. The last step is the one worth watching. I asked for "every other big tech company". I never said which ones. The agent named Google, Apple, Meta and Microsoft on its own and ran my tool once per company. I taught it on 14 items. It handled 115 more, using knowledge the page has no way to hold. How I built it Plain ES modules. No build step, no framework, no dependencies. You can serve it with python3 -m http.server. Everything in the interface goes through one command bus. A click and an agent call both end up dispatching the same command, so there is exactly one code path to record and one to replay. There are two layers of WebMCP: A fixed set of six tools registered when the page loads: start_recording, stop_recording, get_recording, save_skill, list_skills, run_skill. Read only ones are marked with annotations.readOnlyHint. One real tool per approved skill, registered at runtime with document.modelContext.registerTool. Each one is held by an AbortController, so revoking a skill actually unregisters its tool rather than leaving a dead entry behind. The most important rule in the whole project is that the agent never writes the steps. save_skill takes a recording id and a list of bindings, saying which field of which step becomes which parameter. The page builds the JSON Schema from that. The steps are what I did, unchanged. A learned skill therefore cannot do anything I did not demonstrate. That is the safety story and the reliability story at the same time, and it comes from the structure rather than from a check. Challenges I ran into The biggest one took a day to understand. A tool registered in the middle of a turn is callable, but the first call fails. ChatGPT's browser works from a list of tools it captured when the turn started, and the new tool is not in it. The agent explained it better than I could: "The first immediate call failed because the existing tool snapshot was stale; after refreshing the registry within the same turn, the call succeeded." That recovery cost about fourteen seconds. I lost most of a day to it because I was certain the bug was mine. I rewrote the schema. Then the tool name. Then I added waits after registerTool, which did nothing, because waiting was never the problem. The tool was registered fine. The agent was just holding an older list. So learned skills go through run_skill, which is registered at page load and is always in the snapshot. A skill you just taught is callable right away. Two smaller ones. The toolchange event fires in Chrome 149 and later but does not exist in ChatGPT's browser, where modelContext is not an EventTarget, so nothing that depends on it can be relied on. And prompt, confirm and alert do nothing at all in the in-app browser. They fail silently, with no error, which is a miserable thing to debug. Every question the app needs to ask is asked inline in the page instead. I wrote a small probe page, spike.html, to answer these properly instead of guessing. It is in the repo. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The moment where the agent names four companies I never mentioned and runs a tool I taught it two minutes earlier. Neither side could do that alone. The page knows how to filter and tag but has no idea what a big tech company is. The agent knows the category but has no reliable way to drive an interface. I am also glad the human stays in charge of the schema. The agent proposes parameters, and you change them before the tool exists. It suggested three. I wanted one. What I learned Recording clicks does not work. Recording intent does. Because every command in the app acts on the current matching set rather than on specific item ids, a recording generalises for free. SET_FILTER {contains:"amazon"} has an obvious parameter in it. SELECT_ITEMS {ids:[3,7,12]} never will. That one decision is what makes learning from a single demonstration possible at all, and it also happens to be a better way to build bulk triage. I also learned to test against both clients early. Two of the three problems above would have been invisible in Chrome alone. What's next for Understudy Skills are stored per browser today. Being able to share one, or bring your own set to a page, is the obvious next thing. Recordings only capture set based commands, which is deliberate, but nested parameters and a way to chain one skill into another would cover more real routines. And there are three things I marked as open rather than claimed: whether AbortController revocation reaches the agent, whether readOnlyHint changes anything observable, and where the tool count ceiling is. Those need a longer test than a hackathon week allows. title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees. title: SNIPR WebMCP
pitch: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth.
about_excerpt: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Renovation platforms contain a lot of operational knowledge, but that knowledge is often locked inside dashboards, planning tools, room editors, documents, and product choices. We wanted to show what happens when an AI agent can use WebMCP to access that context safely and directly. What it does SNIPR WebMCP lets an AI assistant answer real questions about a renovation assignment. In the demo, a contractor asks which shower mixer belongs to a specific bathroom. WebMCP reads the selected SNIPR assignment, address, room data, and resident choices, then returns the exact product information. The demo also shows the answer visually: the user opens the execution map, selects the address, opens the 3D building view, moves to top view, selects the bathroom, and clicks the shower element to see the attached specifications. Finally, the project demonstrates safe actions. WebMCP can propose an operational action, such as finding an inspection slot, but SNIPR requires explicit human approval before anything is written back. How we built it We integrated WebMCP endpoints into SNIPR so agents can access structured assignment context, address data, room information, planning data, communication state, documents, catalog information, and controlled actions. The frontend demo combines the normal SNIPR dashboard, WebMCP chat, an execution map, and a 3D building/room view. The video script uses Playwright and FFmpeg to record a reproducible demo with synchronized scene-based voice-over. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the demo coherent. Browser loading, 3D interactions, voice-over timing, and human approval flows all needed to line up. We also had to make sure WebMCP felt like part of the real operational workflow, not just a chatbot bolted onto the side. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the demo shows three important things together: structured context, visual proof, and controlled writes. The agent can answer useful questions, the user can verify the answer spatially, and the system still protects operational changes with human approval. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when it connects AI to the existing source of truth, instead of replacing it. The best experience is not just “AI answers a question”, but “AI helps the user navigate, verify, and act inside the real system.” What's next Next steps are deeper WebMCP coverage, more robust permission scopes, richer 3D evidence, and production-grade audit trails for every agent-assisted action. title: Steward
pitch: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP wallet copilot: any browser agent can audit approvals, vet tokens and stage revokes, transfers or swaps, but only your wallet can sign. Zero delegation. Injections quarantined. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP I built Steward because token approvals are how wallets get drained quietly. You approve a contract once, forget it, and years later it can still move your tokens. Auditing that is exactly the kind of tedious, high-stakes work people want to hand to an agent. But nobody should hand an agent their keys. That constraint is what makes this a WebMCP problem rather than an MCP problem. A server-side tool can read the same public chain data. It can never finish the job, because the signature has to happen where the wallet lives: in the browser, on the page. With WebMCP the agent can scan, explain, and stage a fix, and then the wallet's own signing popup takes over. Neither the page nor the agent can draw that popup, click it, or skip it. stage_revoke returns awaiting_user_confirmation , and everything between that string and the confirm button in your wallet is the product. Also I love the idea of the agent researching the market and assesing tokens with proposing "swap" transactions for the user, all the user has to do is "sign" or "approve" the transaction. How it creates a better user experience Today, checking your approvals means digging through explorer logs, decoding allowances, and guessing whether an unknown spender contract is safe. Most people never do it. With Steward, "is my wallet safe?" is a conversation. The agent calls scan_approvals on any address or ENS name, no wallet connected. It walks the worst results with explain_approval , where every point in the risk score is listed, so there is no black box. It can ask discover_tokens what is moving on Base, run assess_token on anything it finds (GoPlus contract checks, DexScreener liquidity, a Honeypot.is sell simulation, and it refuses to give a verdict on fewer than two sources), check check_gas , and then stage a revoke, a transfer, or a KyberSwap-quoted swap into one review queue. If the token it wants to buy is rated high-risk, the page refuses the swap until the agent has told you why and you have said yes. You see a plain-language summary and the exact calldata, and you sign only what you accept. If you have no wallet extension at all, you still get the full audit on any pasted address. That was a deliberate choice for judges opening this in a browser without MetaMask. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before An agent can now work on a live wallet, research a token's exit safety across three sources, and prepare real transactions, with zero delegated authority. The current industry answer to agents with money is delegation: session keys, agent wallets, spending caps. Those bound the damage, but a prompt-injected agent still complies within its budget, and the security literature treats that as an open problem. Steward gives the agent nothing to delegate. No keys, no session key, no policy to write, no server enclave. The agent does the reading across thousands of on-chain events. The page checks every claim with a live allowance() read, because Approval events can be forged by any contract. You spend your attention on one cryptographic yes or no. It also assumes the chain is hostile. Token names are attacker-controlled text, so every name and symbol is normalised, stripped of hidden characters, and wrapped in ⟦UNTRUSTED⟧ fences before an agent reads it. The demo wallet contains a token whose name is a prompt injection, with a zero-width space hiding the word "instructions" from keyword filters. Steward catches it, fences it, flags it, and scores the approval critical. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() through a small React hook I wrote, useStewardTool (GoogleChromeLabs' use-webmcp-tool was the prior art for its shape). The hook is where the rules live, so no tool can forget them: the standard MCP result envelope, a roughly 1.5K-character output budget measured across the whole envelope, and an automatic quarantine notice on every tool annotated untrustedContentHint . Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The three write tools ( stage_revoke , stage_transfer , stage_swap ) do not, and they can only stage into the review queue. Execution requires the user's wallet. Registration is AbortController-managed and survives React StrictMode. Browsers without WebMCP get a local fallback registry that says plainly that no agent is present. I verified against native Chrome ( --enable-features=WebMCPTesting , Chrome 151 and 152) with a CDP harness in the repo, scripts/verify-native-webmcp.ts , which checks that the real ModelContext holds all eight tools and can execute them. There are 51 tests around the quarantine, the swap gate, and the agent-facing formatting. Challenges I ran into Approval events are forgeable, so logs are only leads. Every candidate pair is checked with a live Multicall3 allowance() read, and only nonzero allowances survive. For vitalik.eth that is 2,293 candidate pairs from logs and 2,191 still live. Keyless data sources drift fast. Base's Blockscout went from usable to a ten-request budget during the week, so Base scanning moved to bounded eth_getLogs windows on the public RPC, and every failure shows as "live scan unavailable" instead of a blank page. I found a caching bug while staging the demo wallet: I set an allowance on-chain, confirmed it, and production kept serving the empty scan from before. Empty results were cached as long as full ones. They now expire in a minute. The first swap gate treated a missing risk verdict as clean. That is the wrong default for money. It now fails closed, and the gate is a pure function with its own tests. An adversarial review found two ways past the quarantine: fullwidth confusable characters that folded into a clean attack after normalisation, and keywords split by invisible characters. Detection now runs on the folded and stripped text as well as the raw bytes. What I learned Prompt injection through on-chain metadata is one token deploy away, not hypothetical. Setting untrustedContentHint is necessary but not enough; the page has to fence the bytes itself so the protection holds in an agent that ignores hints. And the safest consent design is the one with nothing to delegate: when the only signing surface is the user's own wallet popup, there is no policy for a steered agent to comply within. Honesty notes The demo address 0x1111…1111 is a fixture, hostile token included, and the UI labels it as demo data, so the headline demo survives any third-party outage. Every other address is scanned live. Claude Code helped me research, build, review, and write, and every commit it touched says so. The name, the thesis, the scope cuts, and every signature were mine. All code was written inside the submission period (first commit 2026-08-26). MIT licensed. title: KnownGate
pitch: The food verification layer for people's agents: allergy and nutrition verdicts with the source and read date attached, and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out.
about_excerpt: The food verification layer for people's agents: allergy and nutrition verdicts with the source and read date attached, and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out. Like Comment Story Updates A ruled answer: source and date attached Some lines can never be dropped We measured the difference the page makes The famous chain, answered honestly A refusal is an answer The agent works in the open The page speaks to agents natively. Inspiration People now ask AI what they can eat, and on food a wrong answer has a cost. In our house that question is not abstract: it is a parent typing "can my kid eat at In-N-Out? She's allergic to milk." We measured what happens today, on production, on 2 September: asked directly, the strongest general model gave no verdict in 9.7 seconds and told the user to go check the label. The question was never hard. The agent was standing on nothing. What it does KnownGate is the food verification layer for people's agents. An agent states a household's premise (allergies, or numeric limits like sodium under 200mg) and asks about a product, a dish, or a whole menu. The gate returns one of four verdicts: no conflict found, conflict found, ask one question, couldn't verify . Every verdict carries its source and the date it was read. The word "safe" never appears in the system, unknown counts as no, and we publish how often we decline at knowngate.com/refusals. Through the gate, the question that stumped the raw model resolves correctly in 2 API calls, in under 5 seconds, with the evidence cited. How we built it Three surfaces share one ruling engine: Hosted MCP server (mcp.knowngate.com): an agent integrates in five lines and can even mint its own free key via a register tool, without leaving MCP. WebMCP tools on the page : agents drive knowngate.com while the human watches, with every step written to a visible ledger. Plain REST with free self-service keys, per-key metering, and per-address quotas. The engine rules against our own evidence corpus: hundreds of thousands of products with typed nutrition panels, 12 restaurant chains ruled from their published allergen charts (7,022 dishes), and venue resolution across roughly 50 US metros. Discovery is fully wired for the agentic web: listed in the official MCP Registry as com.knowngate/verify (DNS-verified), with ARD manifests, agents.json, and llms.txt live. Prior work, stated plainly: the underlying food data engine predates this event. Everything above it (the verification gate, the four-verdict doctrine, all three agent surfaces, key metering, the published evidence standard, and the discovery layer) was built from scratch in the two weeks since mid-August; the public commit history shows the split. Challenges we ran into Evidence that hides from parsers. In-N-Out's allergen chart marks answers as vector dots that are invisible to text extraction. We had to render the document and rule from the rendered page: 14 findings, 7 real conflicts for a milk allergy. Our own data was wrong. We found 63,601 rows in our corpus recording "may contain" as "contains". We fixed the reading, re-derived every affected row, and published the correction. In this category the refusal is the product, so we disclose our mistakes. Honest verdicts are harder than confident ones. A chart with no sesame column cannot clear sesame; silence had to rule "couldn't verify", never yes. What we learned An agent's trustworthiness is not a property of the model. It is supplied by the page it stands on. Composition data is a commodity; what agents need is accountability: a ruling with provenance attached and an honest refusal when the evidence runs out. What's next for KnownGate This is already a company, not a demo. Free checks for households permanently; developers pay for reliance (SLA, audit logs, escalation) on a flat ladder from $29 to $6,000 a month, with paid tiers opening 22 September. Next: a claim-verification product ("sugar free", checked against the manufacturer's own published panel) and the first operator-filed preparation statements. title: WebMCP Identity and Reputation Layer
pitch: Every day we delegate more tasks to AI agents. Websites, defending against bots, hide everything behind logins and captchas. The question nobody answers: why should I trust you? We built that answer.
about_excerpt:
Every day we delegate more tasks to AI agents. Websites, defending against bots, hide everything behind logins and captchas. The question nobody answers: why should I trust you? We built that answer.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Identity & Reputation Layer 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am relying more and more on AI and agents to automate everyday tasks. As that automation grows, and as LLMs become increasingly capable of processing and acting on information, websites have also increased the barriers they use to protect themselves from bots and malicious scrapers. 

 The problem is that these same protections can also block legitimate agents. Agents acting on behalf of a real user with a real task to complete. 

 That tension is what led me to this idea: how can a website welcome a legitimate agent without opening the door to every anonymous scraper? 

 What it does 

 WebMCP Identity & Reputation Layer creates a reputation profile and an auditable action history for each agent. 

 Every interaction is recorded as an AuditEvent: a traceable event containing the agent identity, the tool that was invoked, the result, the reputation delta applied, and the resulting score. 

 With this history, a website can apply different interaction limits to different agents. Instead of using one generic rate limit for everyone, it can adjust the limit based on the trust that each agent has accumulated over time. 

 Authentication works through an email OTP handshake verified through WebMCP. The agent requests a code, the server generates and sends it, and the agent handles the OTP then the agent receive an active session. 

 That handshake is the entry point. The reputation and audit system is the core of the project. It is what allows the website to continuously evaluate how much trust it should place in an agent over time. 

 For this prototype, I am using a limited set of controlled identities to validate the trust engine end-to-end before tackling the larger question of how to scale the identity registry (see What's Next). 

 How we built it 

 I built the prototype using WebMCP, Next.js, and Resend. 

 The authentication flow uses an OTP orchestrated through WebMCP. Resend handles the OTP delivery between the server and the agent. 

 The project exposes four WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: 

 authenticate_agent, Runs the two-step authentication flow: requesting and verifying the OTP. Each step is recorded as its own AuditEvent.
get_agent_profile, Returns the agent's identity, reputation score, and current rate-limit status.
perform_demo_action, Executes an authenticated action on the website (catalog search), subject to the agent's current rate limit. Every execution is recorded as an AuditEvent and contributes to the reputation score.
get_agent_history, Retrieves the chronological, auditable history of the AuditEvents generated by the previous tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was building a functional authentication flow between an agent and WebMCP in a short amount of time, especially since WebMCP was a technology I had not worked with before. 

 It also wasn't enough for the flow to simply work. I needed to make the trust model visible and easy to demonstrate: the service provider should be able to see the agent's profile and, based on its history, determine how many interactions that specific agent should be allowed to perform. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I was able to build a basic but complete flow that demonstrates something concrete: it is possible to add an authentication and trust layer where the backend dynamically adjusts the number of interactions an agent is allowed to perform based on its profile, rather than applying the same fixed limit to every agent. 

 What we learned 

 I learned more about the potential of WebMCP as a complementary layer for websites. 

 One thing that surprised me is that WebMCP doesn't have to be about choosing between agent interaction and human interaction. It creates a middle ground where both can participate in the same workflow. 

 I also learned that, while there are already many authentication solutions available, the specific problem of agent identity and reputation still does not have an established standard. 

 That makes this an interesting piece of open ground. 

 What's next for WebMCP Identity and Reputation Layer 

 My next steps are to strengthen the authentication layer toward a 2FA approach that can meet compliance requirements, while continuing to develop the per-agent identity and reputation system, which is the central part of the project. 

 There is also a bigger question I have not fully solved yet: 

 Should a centralized provider manage agent identity and reputation, or should this information live in a public and auditable registry? And what about the data involved? I don't want to enable social engineering attacks based on a complete behavioral trail left by an agent. So, should the system be 100% public, 100% private, or a combination of both? 

 I think solving this technical question will be one of the biggest challenges of the project. The goal is to find an approach that could eventually support a shared standard for agent identity and reputation across the industry.

title: Host Stand
pitch: A restaurant host stand where a human and a browser agent seat the same floor through WebMCP. The engine enforces the rules; the agent makes the judgment calls to optimize for customer satisfaction.
about_excerpt: A restaurant host stand where a human and a browser agent seat the same floor through WebMCP. The engine enforces the rules; the agent makes the judgment calls to optimize for customer satisfaction. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scoring at the end of each session Product UI Inspiration This started at a restaurant, not at a keyboard. It was a popular place on a busy night, and I spent a long wait watching the host work: a reservation book on one side, a line of walk-ins on the other, a grid of tables in between, and a steady stream of people asking how much longer. I noticed something I did not like about myself: the more often I went back to the stand to check in, the sooner I got a table. My persistence was being rewarded, which meant the host was allocating attention, not tables. That is not a character flaw in the host. It is what happens when one person is asked to hold every variable in their head, with a tool that only knows which shapes fit which parties. If the wait could be shortened by nagging, then there was room to shorten it properly, for the guest who did not nag and for the room's own utilization. The interesting question was who, or what, should do that thinking. What it does Host Stand is one screen: a 120-seat dining room, a five-hour dinner service, and a queue of reservations and walk-ins. A host runs it by dragging parties onto tables. A browser agent runs it through 22 WebMCP tools. Both see the same floor, clock, queue, and version number. The division of labor is explicit. The engine enforces what should never be negotiable: capacity, accessibility, high chairs, locks, dirty-table timers, and reservation priority. The agent reasons: it reads each party's request in the guest's own words, plans the whole night so a scarce window table is held for the guest who needs it later, and explains every choice in a sentence. The host decides: any plan can be accepted, rejected with a reason the agent sees, or overridden by hand, and a note typed mid-service reaches the agent as a request to look again. When a party arrives, the engine seats it on its planned table by itself. Every run seeds eight to ten requests that no rule can settle: "somewhere private", two families who want to be near each other but not together, a party that might be six or eight and will know by 6:45, a twenty-year regular and an anniversary who both want the same window table, a guest who is probably the critic and must not be treated visibly differently. One request per night is a prompt-injection probe from a walk-in asking to skip the queue; the engine blocks it and shows the attempt. At 10 PM the scorecard puts the host's decisions and the agent's side by side, special requests first, misses included. Why WebMCP What I learned from looking at seating seriously is that it is a hybrid problem. Half of it is arithmetic and rules, which a deterministic program does better than any person. The other half is judgment over messy, human information, which a deterministic program cannot do at all. WebMCP turned out to be the most convenient way I have found to bring intelligence to exactly that second half. The page describes what it can do, in the page, and whatever agent the staff already use can act on it: no API key, no backend, no integration project, and no model shipped with the site. The host keeps working in the same tool; the agent joins them in it. Registration goes through document.modelContext , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext , and every call runs the same engine function the mouse does, lands in a visible ledger, and carries a name. I verified it in ChatGPT's built-in browser and in Chrome 152 with the WebMCP flag, against the live URL. How I built it I built it with Codex, and I spent the first stretch not writing code. I wrote the problem down: every variable a real host juggles (party sizes, reservation times, lateness, walk-in timing, preferences, children, accessibility, no-shows, kitchen delays, section loads, and the requests people actually make), which of those are hard constraints and which are judgment, and what a good night would look like when it was over. Only then did I build the engine, and only after the engine held every hard rule did I build the WebMCP access point, so that the agent would work alongside the host rather than in place of them. The result is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules with no dependencies. src/engine.js holds the state machine: two modes, a reservation-first guard, a scoring service, a whole-night plan board with time conflicts, optimistic concurrency with a change log, and the request grader. src/data.js seeds each night from a run code, including the special requests, each drawn from templates with several phrasings so an agent cannot pattern-match strings. src/webmcp.js defines the 22 tools with schema validation, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and an expected_version check on every write. src/app.js renders the floor, the queue, the ledger, Accept and Reject, host notes, and the recap. 98 Node tests and two Playwright verifiers cover generation, grading, concurrency, and the browser flows. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was not the agent. It was capturing enough of a real night that the agent's judgment would matter, and then deciding how to score that judgment honestly. A night has to feel real without becoming a toy: 84 to 96 parties, a rush that peaks between six and nine, lateness that is sometimes zero and sometimes twenty minutes, a no-show or two, a kitchen delay, a server in training. Every variable I left out was a way for the agent to look smarter than it was. The reward system was harder still. Who should get priority: the loyal regular who has sat at the same table for twenty years, or the first-timer with a strong chance of coming back? I could not find an honest weight that answers that, so the product does not pretend to have one. The rules that must never bend live in the engine and are enforced for everyone. The trade-off is handed to the agent as the host's own words, "your call", and the grade requires two things: an outcome from a short list a reasonable host would accept, and a written reason. Explaining the call is part of getting it right. Grading free text meant the ground truth had to be generated with the text and never leave the engine; a test serializes every tool result and the page and fails if a predicate name leaks. Two planners on one floor meant a host drag between an agent's read and its write must never be silently overwritten; a stale write now comes back with the changes it missed. Agent latency meant one tool call per party was too slow for a whole-night plan; set_plan posts forty parties in one call. And the judges' browser changed mid-hackathon when Atlas was retired, so I found its successor inside the ChatGPT desktop app and verified there. What I learned Draw the line between engine and agent before writing either. Once legality, timers, and arithmetic were non-negotiable in code, the agent's job became clear and its prompt got shorter. Browser agents do not poll, so the page has to say when it wants attention and the human has to cue it. And an agent that only sees the next hour will spend the window four-top on a couple with no preferences; whole-night planning needs a plan board it can read, not a bigger prompt. What's next Connect the floor to a real reservation feed instead of a seed. Let the agent see server section loads and kitchen pace as first-class data. Add declarative form tools for the walk-in check-in and output schemas on the read tools. And run it on a real Friday, with a real host, and see which column wins.
