title: Infinite Awareness Agent Lab
pitch: A human-led WebMCP experiment where AI prepares awareness protocols, structures reflections, protects blinded scoring, and compares privacy-conscious personal and collective signals.
about_excerpt: A human-led WebMCP experiment where AI prepares awareness protocols, structures reflections, protects blinded scoring, and compares privacy-conscious personal and collective signals. Like Comment Story Updates A fictional participant records a direct observation before the agent structures it for review. Blinded scoring protects the hidden condition while the person reviews usefulness, novelty and testability. The agent separates observation, interpretation and uncertainty; saving requires visible human confirmation. Read-only personal and cohort signals show aggregate patterns without exposing raw reflections or claiming efficacy. The prepared three-minute session updates the same visible page state shared by participant and agent. The initial session: a fixed three-minute protocol ready for WebMCP preparation, with later stages still locked. Judge Sandbox overview: eight registered WebMCP tools, fictional data and a protected hidden condition. The main Infinite Awareness experience—the human-facing 33-day programme that inspired the isolated Agent Lab. Inspiration: Infinite Awareness began with a simple problem: people can collect ideas about meditation, consciousness and self-awareness for years without turning those ideas into a repeatable practice they can examine for themselves. The existing Infinite Awareness application addresses that gap through a structured 33-day programme combining progressive awareness sessions, journaling, forecasting, blinded outcome scoring and personal analysis. The programme is designed as structured educational self-observation rather than treatment or proof of efficacy. The WebMCP Challenge presented a new question: 'What should an AI agent be allowed to do inside this experience—and what must remain human?' An agent cannot meditate, experience awareness or decide what an observation means for somebody. It can, however, organise the experiment, retrieve the correct protocol, structure an observation, protect the scoring method and analyse privacy-conscious trends. That division of responsibility became the foundation of the Infinite Awareness Agent Lab. What it does: The Agent Lab is an isolated, fiction-only WebMCP demonstration. A participant can open the live page in a compatible browser and ask an agent to help run an awareness experiment using natural language. The page exposes eight structured WebMCP tools: Read-only tools: 1 get_today_protocol retrieves the fictional participant’s current day, purpose, instructions and safety guidance. 2 analyse_personal_signal returns aggregated fictional personal trends without exposing raw reflections. 3 compare_collective_signal compares the participant’s aggregates with a fictional cohort after checking a fixed minimum sample threshold. 4 explain_safety_boundary explains the educational scope, consent rules, privacy boundary and stop guidance. Guarded tools: 5 prepare_session prepares the correct shortened demonstration session but cannot complete the human practice. 6 draft_observation turns a fictional participant’s words into a structured draft without saving it. 7 save_confirmed_observation saves the reviewed draft only after a visible human confirmation. 8 score_blinded_outcome records usefulness, novelty and testability scores without revealing whether the session was an intention or control condition. Every tool call creates a visible, structured update on the page so the participant can verify what the agent did. Why WebMCP?: A normal chatbot would need the participant to paste information into a conversation or depend on fragile screen interpretation. WebMCP allows the website to expose narrow, typed actions directly from the live page. The agent can discover the available tools, understand their input schemas and work with the same visible application state as the participant. No separate plugin or remote MCP server is required for the demonstration. This makes the experience both easier and safer. The agent receives only the information needed for the current task, while the website continues enforcing progression, validation, privacy and consent. Human and agent collaboration: The agent provides structure, consistency and analysis. The person retains experience, consent and interpretation. The agent can: Retrieve and explain the protocol. Prepare the correct session. Structure an observation for review. Preserve the blinded scoring sequence. Calculate and compare fictional aggregate signals. The person must: Decide whether to practise. Have the actual experience. Review the agent’s proposed draft. Explicitly confirm anything being saved. Review and confirm outcome scores. Decide what the resulting information means. The central principle is: 'An agent can organise the experiment. Only a person can have the experience.' Existing project and new challenge work: Infinite Awareness existed before the challenge as a 33-day commercial awareness-training application built over a month and a half with AI and human collaboration. The work added during the challenge is the WebMCP-powered Agent Lab, including: Eight registered WebMCP tools. An isolated /agent-lab experience. Fictional participant and cohort data. Structured tool results displayed in the interface. One-time visible human confirmations. Privacy-conscious personal and collective analysis. Blinded scoring protections. Safety and educational-scope boundaries. WebMCP discovery, execution and confirmation tests. Judge instructions, submission documentation and demonstration materials. The challenge extension is intentionally isolated from the existing production application. It does not connect to production customers, journals, payments, course records or private data. How we built it: The tools are registered from the top-level page using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool has a narrow JSON input schema, a clear description and an explicit read-only or guarded behaviour. The execution handlers reuse one shared page state so tool results and human interactions remain synchronised. The confirmation bridge was especially important. Saving and scoring initially required a confirmation identifier in the public tool input. Testing in ChatGPT’s browser showed that this identifier was held inside the page and was not available to the agent. We redesigned the bridge so the public tools accept only their genuine task inputs. Their execution closures independently validate the current page-held confirmation. Each confirmation is consumed after one successful use and cannot be replayed. Challenges: The largest challenge was making the agent useful without allowing it to overstep. We needed to ensure that: An agent could not save an unreviewed reflection. A confirmation could not be reused. Scoring could not happen before the observation was saved. The intention or control condition remained blinded. No raw reflections appeared in personal or cohort analysis. The demonstration made no medical, psychological or efficacy claims. The pre-existing application remained clearly separated from the new challenge work. Accomplishments: The public challenge repository passes all eight bundled tests, TypeScript validation, the production build and GitHub CI. The live sandbox was also verified for clean non-WebMCP fallback behaviour and native WebMCP discovery in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ChatGPT successfully discovered all eight tools. Direct save and scoring calls failed before confirmation, succeeded exactly once after visible confirmation and failed when confirmation reuse was attempted. The blinded condition remained hidden throughout. What we learned: WebMCP tool design is not simply about exposing functions. Tool descriptions, input schemas, visible page state, confirmation handling and verifiable results are all part of the user experience. We also learned that human control works best when it is enforced by the application rather than left to an instruction in a prompt. The agent can request an action, but the page itself determines whether the required human review has happened. Human-led, AI-assisted creation: Like the experience it enables, this project was built through human-agent collaboration. I defined the purpose, methodology, safety boundaries and final decisions, while AI tools helped implement, test and refine the WebMCP extension. That process reinforced the principle at the heart of the project: AI should expand human capability without quietly taking away human agency. What’s next: The Agent Lab now has a stable public home, a reviewed MIT-licensed repository and a compliant 2:55 demonstration video. After the challenge, I want to make the Agent Lab freely available so more people can explore structured awareness, reflection and self-observation without surrendering their privacy, judgement or control to an algorithm. AI may become one of the most consequential changes in human history. As it increasingly shapes how we work, communicate and understand ourselves, we nee

title: Sourcing Scenario Room
pitch: A shared procurement decision workspace where buyers and AI agents operate on the same sourcing state through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A shared procurement decision workspace where buyers and AI agents operate on the same sourcing state through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As a procurement director working with complex supplier decisions, I regularly see how difficult it is to combine structured sourcing data, judgment, negotiation constraints, and human accountability in one workflow. 

 AI can already help buyers analyze supplier offers, but it usually sits outside the sourcing application. That creates friction: users copy data into chat, interpret the answer, and then manually reconcile it back into their working system. 

 Sourcing Scenario Room came from the idea that this interaction should be different: the buyer and the AI agent should operate on the same visible sourcing state through WebMCP, while the human keeps decision authority. 

 What it does 

 The application starts from a fictional sourcing case with three supplier offers evaluated across five dimensions: price, delivery lead time, capacity, quality, and supply risk. 

 The buyer can express sourcing intent in natural language. Through WebMCP, the agent reads the current application state and updates the shared workspace directly. 

 A typical flow is: 

 
 The agent reads the current sourcing case. 
 The buyer makes delivery within 12 weeks mandatory, prioritizes supply continuity, and asks to keep two suppliers alive. 
 The agent updates the workspace and creates an AGENT PROPOSAL. 
 The agent generates a negotiation plan for the live shortlist. 
 The buyer revises the proposal directly in the application, for example by keeping Boreal in the shortlist while limiting the acceptable price premium to 3%. 
 The workspace becomes HUMAN-REVISED. 
 The agent reads that revision and adapts the negotiation plan accordingly. 
 

 The agent can propose and adapt, but it cannot award a supplier. Decision authority remains with the human buyer. 

 How we built it 

 Sourcing Scenario Room is a client-side React/Vite application using native WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 It exposes three WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_sourcing_case 
 update_sourcing_scenario 
 draft_negotiation_plan 
 

 The human interface and the WebMCP tools operate on the same canonical React sourcing state through shared application actions. 

 There is no backend, database, authentication layer, OpenAI API integration, or external API dependency. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was designing a demo that made the human-agent interaction clear without hiding it behind unnecessary complexity. 

 I deliberately limited the case to five sourcing dimensions, three suppliers, and three WebMCP tools. 

 Another challenge was preserving human decision authority. The application therefore makes the state transitions explicit: 

 BASE CASE → AGENT PROPOSAL → HUMAN-REVISED 

 This makes it visible when the agent has proposed something, when the human has changed it, and when the agent is responding to the latest human decision. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The most important result is that the agent is not simply generating advice beside the application. 

 The buyer and agent work through the same sourcing workspace. The agent can read the current state, modify the scenario, generate a negotiation artifact, observe a later human revision, and adapt to it. 

 That creates a genuine human-agent loop while keeping supplier selection authority with the buyer. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest insight was that WebMCP changes the interaction model. 

 The valuable part is not simply allowing an AI to call functions. It is enabling the human and the agent to collaborate through the same visible application state. 

 Human revisions become first-class inputs to the next agent action instead of context that must be manually reconstructed in chat. 

 What's next for Sourcing Scenario Room 

 The same pattern could extend to richer procurement workflows such as tender preparation, supplier risk, negotiation tracking, sourcing approvals, and contract review. 

 More broadly, the approach could apply to enterprise workflows where humans and agents need to collaborate on structured decisions while preserving explicit human authority.

title: AI-Native Responsible Travel via WebMCP
pitch: Connecting AI-first travelers with community-driven tourism, eco-travel, and support community impact using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Connecting AI-first travelers with community-driven tourism, eco-travel, and support community impact using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Today, travelers ask AI first before making decisions—asking conversational agents to plan itineraries, find ethical stays, and compare transport. But for a "people-first" grassroots organization like OpenmindProjects , spending money on expensive online ads or SEO agencies to show up in those searches is impossible. Every dollar goes directly to local community education, teacher training, and IT camps in Southeast Asia. Commercial online travel agencies (OTAs) spend millions capturing visibility. We rely strictly on organic discovery and being recommended by AIs. We asked: If travelers are asking AI first, how can a zero-budget NGO ensure AI agents accurately discover our work and connect travelers to our community projects? That is why WebMCP is a complete game-changer for Openmind.Travel . By exposing our platform directly to browser-native AI agents via registerTool() , we make our community catalog instantly discoverable, transparent, and actionable—leveling the playing field without spending a dime on ad budget. What It Does Openmind.Travel exposes clean client-side tools directly inside the browser runtime. Without handling payments or managing direct travel inventory, our WebMCP integration lets an AI agent: Discover Ethical Travel: Search community-led tours, local guides, destinations, and authentic itineraries. Compare Transport & Logistics: Retrieve partner flight and ground transport options (in USD by default, with multi-currency support). Explore Real Impact: View UN SDG-aligned causes, track real fundraising progress, read traveler stories, and discover "impact treasures" (geocaches at project sites). Reviewable Affiliate Hand-off: Generate direct, reviewable partner checkout URLs where standard affiliate commissions automatically fund local Openmind Projects initiatives. Why WebMCP is Game-Changing for Us 1. Built for the "Ask AI First" Era When users ask their browser AI agent to find ethical travel in Southeast Asia, WebMCP allows the agent to execute structured queries ( searchTours , getImpactMetrics ) directly on Openmind.Travel instead of guessing or scraping stale HTML. 2. Zero-Budget Organic Visibility Grassroots NGOs cannot outspend multi-billion-dollar OTAs on search ads. WebMCP turns Openmind.Travel into an AI-native API layer inside the browser, securing organic recommendations through structured data quality rather than marketing spend. 3. Built-In Trust & Seamless User Experience Action happens directly in the user's active browser tab. The AI presents clear options with reviewable affiliate links, ensuring full transparency: travelers pay normal prices on partner sites, while affiliate commissions automatically fund local learning camps. Key Comparison Feature / Aspect Traditional Travel Affiliate Sites Openmind.Travel via WebMCP Visibility Strategy Multi-million dollar paid ads & aggressive SEO. Organic AI discovery via structured registerTool() APIs. Discovery Method Manual search across dozens of browser tabs. Conversational AI discovery ("Ask AI first") with structured tool calls. Community Impact Profits kept by corporate intermediaries. Partner affiliate commissions fund local education projects automatically. Integration Model Fragile DOM scraping or static links. Native browser tool execution via navigator.modelContext . Tech Stack Protocol Standard: WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext / registerTool() ) Frontend Layer: React / JavaScript client runtime Data Sources: Partner travel APIs (flights, transport) & Openmind Projects Community Impact Database Tool catalog Tools are grouped by domain and map to existing OpenmindTravel JSON endpoints. Destinations — search_destinations , list_categories , list_countries , get_popular_destinations , autocomplete_airport Tours — search_tours , get_tour_facets , get_tour , list_volunteer_projects , get_partner , search_suggestions Guides — list_country_guides , get_country_guide , search_youtube_videos , list_airline_guides , get_airline_guide Trips — plan_trip , list_trip_ideas , get_trip_idea , save_trip_idea , get_itinerary , save_itinerary Flights — search_flights , get_flight_calendar Transport — search_transport Community — get_globie_pet , list_community_posts , search_community_posts , get_community_post Give / Impact — get_impact_overview , list_impact_causes , get_impact_cause , get_impact_travel_options , list_impact_treasures , get_impact_treasure , get_impact_stories , start_donation Result envelope Every tool returns a consistent, agent-friendly envelope so agents parse outcomes reliably: // Success { success: true, data: { /* ... */ }, markdown?: string, url?: string } // Failure { success: false, error: { code: string, message: string } } url hands a navigation side-effect to the agent (a prefilled search or a booking step), while markdown carries a human/agent-readable summary. How we built it Openmind.Travel (the responsible-travel platform) already existed before the submission period. The WebMCP layer described here is the new work we built for \ this hackathon, so the platform can be used by AI agents directly in the browser. We wrote a lightweight, dependency-free TypeScript layer that feature-detects document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext , then registers 8 tool groups against our existing Express + PostgreSQL backend. A shared http.ts helper ( apiGet / apiPost ) keeps requests and error envelopes consistent. The "Give" tools reuse one source-of-truth impact data module so the rendered page and the tools never disagree on figures. Donations default to USD and produce a ready_for_user hand-off with a PayPal checkout URL. Architecture File Purpose types.ts Minimal type declarations for the WebMCP browser API ( ModelContext , annotations). http.ts Shared request helpers ( apiGet , apiPost ) and the ok / fail result envelope. registerTools.ts Entry point that feature-detects WebMCP and registers every tool group. tools/ One module per domain, each exporting a register*Tools(modelContext) function. WebMCP flow sequenceDiagram autonumber actor User participant Agent as Agent (ChatGPT / Chrome) participant Page as OpenmindTravel page participant MCP as document.modelContext participant Tool as WebMCP tools (tools/*.ts) participant API as Backend API User->>Page: Opens the app in a WebMCP-enabled browser Page->>MCP: registerWebMCPTools() MCP-->>Page: feature-detect (modelContext available?) Page->>MCP: registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) MCP-->>Agent: exposes the tool catalog Agent->>MCP: invoke tool with input MCP->>Tool: execute(input) Tool->>API: apiGet / apiPost (JSON) API-->>Tool: JSON response Tool-->>MCP: ok(data, markdown, url) / fail(error) MCP-->>Agent: tool result envelope Agent-->>User: summary + optional navigation (url) Registration (once, on load). The page feature-detects WebMCP and registers every tool group. The agent discovers the resulting catalog. Invocation (per request). The agent calls a tool with a typed input. The tool's execute function talks to the backend, then wraps the result in the standard ok / fail envelope. Acting on the result. The agent reads data (and optional markdown ), and can use url to trigger navigation (e.g. a prefilled search or a booking step). Security model We treated security as a requirement from day one: nothing is exposed to other origins by default, the backend uses a CORS allow-list, destructive actions require consent, and all tool descriptions/inputs are bounded. Every tool declares its behavior through annotation hints so the agent and browser can apply the right guardrails: Hint Meaning Where used readOnlyHint No mutation All read/discovery tools destructiveHint Irreversible write create_booking (persists a booking) idempotentHint Safe to retry save_trip_idea , save_itinerary untrustedContentHint Returns user-generated/external data Community posts, impact stories, YouTube results openWorldHint May access the network Tools that call the backend / external APIs Additional constraints: Character budgets — tool names ≤ 30 chars, descriptions ≤ 500 chars, parameter descriptions ≤ 150 chars, and output capped at 1.5K chars via a truncate() helper so results stay fast and predictable. Input validation — schemas use additionalProperties: false , Nostr public keys/event ids match a 64-char hex pattern, airport codes match [A-Z]{3} , dates are YYYY-MM-DD , and collection limits are clamped to a safe maximum. Consent — destructive tools state "Confirm with the user before calling", and hand-off tools return a ready_for_user payload for explicit review. The whole thing is progressive enhancement : if WebMCP isn't available, it is a silent no-op and the site works exactly as before. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT & Codex outage. title: DOGAGA
pitch: Teach a browser video editor by example, let the agent generalize, then approve the result.
about_excerpt: Teach a browser video editor by example, let the agent generalize, then approve the result. Like Comment Story Updates DOGAGA's live editor with WebMCP connected: Teach by Example, an applied agent suggestion, actual Preview, and the shared timeline. Inspiration Video editing is visual, but editing intent is semantic. Meaning lives in operations such as track order, clip timing, fades, opacity, still-image duration, canvas settings, and transitions—not only in pixels or DOM controls. AI-assisted creative tools often place an agent beside the editor rather than inside the editor's structured state. The agent may generate instructions, click the interface indirectly, or operate through a separate backend. After either side edits, the other side may no longer know the real project state or the human's intent. DOGAGA explores a page-native alternative: the open web application exposes its live semantic editing state and actions through WebMCP while the person keeps the normal visual editor and final approval. What it does DOGAGA is a compact, local-first browser video editor where the human UI and a WebMCP agent operate on the same live timeline. Its collaboration loop is: Human teaches by performing a normal edit in the visual editor. DOGAGA captures semantic meaning from the supported before/after change. The agent generalizes that treatment to analogous current assets through a reviewable Edit Plan. The human approves or rejects the proposal before the timeline changes. For example, a person can load three still images, click Teach agent , add the first image to V2, set it to three seconds with a 0.5-second fade, and stop teaching. DOGAGA exposes the completed semantic demonstration through get_project_state . When the person asks, “Do the same to the other still images,” the agent can propose the corresponding operations. The app shows that plan without mutating anything; only the person's Apply action commits it. The same live project then powers actual Preview and browser-native Export. There is no fixed hackathon scene, agent-only timeline, remote editing backend, hidden replay, or fake preview. Why WebMCP is a strong fit WebMCP lets the page define an explicit contract for agent-readable state and semantic actions. The agent does not have to infer a timeline from screenshots or guess which DOM element represents a trim, fade, track, or still-image duration. This creates a better user experience because people can communicate intent through editing itself instead of translating every creative choice into a prompt. The agent receives safe, structured meaning; it can reason over current assets and propose a generalization; the person retains visible control and final approval. This human-agent workflow was difficult with conventional UI automation. Mouse-coordinate or DOM macro replay captures mechanics, not meaning. A separate MCP server can also create a second copy of the project that drifts from the open editor. DOGAGA keeps the visual UI, agent state, Preview, and Export synchronized in one page-owned project. How we built it DOGAGA uses React, TypeScript, and Vite and is deployed on Cloudflare Pages. A single EditorController and command executor power both human editing and all WebMCP mutations. The page registers typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() through use-webmcp-tool . The canonical editor state contains safe asset descriptors, video/audio tracks, clips, canvas settings, transitions, and playhead state. Collaboration metadata includes a small Project Brief, the completed humanDemonstration , and a reviewable editPlan . Local File objects and object URLs are kept separately in a session-only runtime media map. They are deliberately excluded from agent-visible state. WebMCP sees only safe asset IDs and descriptors—never absolute paths, file handles, object URLs, media pixels, or private Teach by Example snapshots. DOGAGA exposes 23 WebMCP tools : 21 core/collaboration tools plus add_image_clip and set_still_duration . Direct mutation tools share the UI executor. propose_edit_plan validates a complete multi-step proposal without mutating the timeline. Human Apply revalidates and commits atomically; Reject leaves the project unchanged. Preview uses browser-native video/audio elements and canvas composition. Export uses Canvas, Web Audio, and MediaRecorder, prefers MP4 when supported, and falls back to WebM. Normal editing and export do not upload source media to a DOGAGA server. Product capabilities The submitted public app supports: local video, PNG/JPEG/WebP still-image, and audio loading multiple video and audio tracks still-image display duration and transparent PNG overlays split, trim, reorder, delete, and cross-track clip movement playback speed, visual fades, and cross dissolves track opacity/visibility, audio mute, and clip volume actual multi-layer Preview with play, pause, and seek 16:9, 9:16, 1:1, and 4:5 canvases with contain/cover fitting browser-native composited video/audio Export and download Project Brief, Teach by Example, and reviewable agent Edit Plans Challenges we ran into The hardest architectural constraint was preserving one real source of truth. WebMCP could not become a second editor state, and human actions could not bypass the same validation used by agents. Local-first privacy added another constraint: the agent needs enough structured context to edit intelligently, but local file handles, paths, object URLs, and media contents must remain private. Browser-native media also required careful synchronization. Preview and Export must reflect the same clip timing, track ordering, fades, image duration, audio mixing, and canvas settings. Still images introduced separate semantics from videos while still needing to participate in the same layered timeline and export path. Finally, Teach by Example had to capture meaning rather than input events. DOGAGA compares supported semantic before/after state, exposes only the completed safe result, and routes any generalization through the existing reviewable Edit Plan path. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real public editor rather than a challenge-only demo One shared state and executor for the human UI and 23 WebMCP tools Semantic Teach by Example with explicit human approval Actual multi-layer Preview and browser-native Export Local-first media boundaries that keep source files out of agent state Non-mutating proposal validation and atomic Apply Transparent PNG and still-image support across editing, Preview, Export, and WebMCP A reproducible public repository with MIT licensing and reviewer instructions What we learned The most useful agent interaction is not always “do this for me.” In creative work, a person may communicate intent more naturally by demonstrating one example. WebMCP can turn that visual interaction into structured semantics without reducing it to a fragile macro. We also learned that human control works best when it is part of the product state: proposals are visible, reviewable, and separate from committed edits. The agent can reason broadly while the person keeps authorship over what becomes real. What was built during the Challenge DOGAGA existed before August 25, 2026, and the public repository history documents that prior work. During the Challenge period it was meaningfully extended with the WebMCP shared-state architecture and completed compact production path, including: page-native WebMCP registration and typed command schemas agent-safe editor state and privacy boundaries actual local-media Preview connected to shared state Cloudflare Pages deployment browser-native Export canonical multi-track video/audio editing speed, fades, split, cross-dissolves, opacity/visibility, and multi-audio mixing Project Brief and non-mutating propose_edit_plan still-image and transparent-PNG support Teach by Example semantic demonstrations the final 23-tool WebMCP surface The repository's dated commit and pull-request history distinguishes this Challenge-period work from the earlier project. What's next DOGAGA is intentionally compact. Next steps include persistent project save/relink, richer timeline positioning, waveforms, captions and lyrics, image motion, and more advanced effects. The current release focuses on a small but genuinely usable local-first editor and a clear human-agent collaboration model. Try it Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled: Live app: https://dogaga.pages.dev Source and setup instructions: https://github.com/yo4e/DOGAGA Recommended flow: load three local still images, teach one 3-second faded V2 treatment, ask the agent to do the same to the other images, review and Apply the proposed plan, then Preview or Export the shared result. Built With canvas-api cloudflare-pages html5-video mediarecorder open-source react typescript vite vitest web-audio-api webmcp Try it out dogaga.pages.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo creator.

title: Flow
pitch: Inclusive Tech for Effortless, Hands-Free Access
about_excerpt:
Inclusive Tech for Effortless, Hands-Free Access

 Inspiration 

 It started when I noticed my grandma’s hands trembling. She can no longer hold or use her phone, and watching her struggle sparked an idea—technology should adapt to people, not the other way around. Flow was built to give her, and anyone with limited hand mobility, the same freedom to use a computer as everyone else. 

 What it does 

 Flow enables complete hands-free computer control. 

 
 Facial gestures move the mouse and trigger clicks or drags. 
 Voice commands let the user type, dictate messages, send emails, or ask an AI agent questions like “What’s the weather?”—all without touching a keyboard or mouse. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Real-time face landmarking and calibration provide precise facial control. 
 LangGraph powers a multi-agent system for complex actions. 
 Airia handles multi-agent coordination and MCP (Model Context Protocol). 
 Gladia provides low-latency speech-to-text. 
 Minimax generates natural text-to-speech responses. 
 Bright Data enables WebMCP integration for external data retrieval. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Calibrating facial structure to avoid mis-cues and achieve smooth, accurate cursor control. 
 Reducing STT and TTS latency, which we solved with streaming and intelligent end-of-speech detection. 
 Designing reliable ways to bring up the AI agent exactly when the user starts speaking. 
 Creating intuitive toggles for different agent modes, such as asking a question versus dictating text. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We achieved fast, accurate face-controlled navigation and a responsive multi-agent voice interface that runs on everyday laptops without special hardware. Seeing my grandma successfully use a computer again with only her face and voice was the ultimate proof of impact. 

 What we learned 

 
 Start simple and get a working prototype before adding complexity. 
 Multi-agent systems add power but also increase build complexity and latency, which must be carefully managed. 
 Facial calibration is far harder in practice than it appears on paper. 
 

 What's next for Flow 

 Our next step is to refine the current experience, release it to real users, and gather feedback to guide updates. We’ll focus on stability, user comfort, and the features people value most before expanding to new platforms and integrations.

title: CityDefense: Fork the Future
pitch: The chat is temporary. The city remembers.
about_excerpt: The chat is temporary. The city remembers. Like Comment Story Updates The authenticated top-level page exposes exactly two WebMCP tools: get_city_context and place_stamp_bundle. One bounded WebMCP write updated the visible map and Activity Feed; the same D1-backed state survived reload. Live CityDefense in the Codex in-app browser with Site Tools READY and durable Branch v1 state. Inspiration Stateful work often outlives the AI chat that performed it. We wanted to explore a web-native collaboration model where the application—not a model-specific memory layer—owns the durable role, object identifiers, event history, and current state. A city-defense surface makes that problem visible. An agent can inspect a district and leave a canonical signal in the same live interface the human is watching. The signal remains after the interaction and after a normal page reload. What CityDefense does CityDefense is a focused, working WebMCP vertical slice. An authenticated Planner seat exposes exactly two Site Tools: get_city_context reads the active Branch, Central Ward state, current Branch Version, persistence mode, and recent activity without changing state. place_stamp_bundle performs one bounded, typed city action: placing a canonical confirmation stamp on district:CENTRAL_WARD . A successful write creates stable Event and Stamp identifiers, increments the Branch Version, updates the visible city and Activity Feed, and persists the result in Cloudflare D1. A normal reload restores the same state. Why WebMCP is a strong fit An agent should not need to infer button positions or reconstruct application state from pixels. WebMCP lets the authenticated top-level page expose the meaning of available operations, their input schemas, and stable application identifiers. The tools are bound to the same live Seat, Branch, and page state the human is viewing. Human and agent therefore work against one authoritative application state. How it improves the UX Typed inputs remove ambiguity about the target, operation, scope, and expected Branch Version. The human gets immediate visual feedback in the same page, while server-issued Event and Stamp IDs make the change auditable. Optimistic version checks prevent stale writes. A request ID prevents accidental duplicate mutation. Server-backed persistence means the result survives a normal reload instead of remaining only in the chat transcript or temporary browser state. What people and agents can now do together A human can authorize a temporary browser-agent thread to inspect a live, authenticated city Branch and perform a precisely bounded application action. The human immediately sees what the agent changed and can verify the durable record in the same interface. This establishes a reusable pattern for web applications where temporary agent sessions operate durable, human-inspectable state. How we implemented WebMCP The authenticated /play page registers two tools from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . No iframe is used. Both tools call the same server query and command paths used by the application. The server authenticates the Seat, authorizes the role and Branch, validates canonical IDs, checks the expected Branch Version, enforces request idempotency, writes the Event and Stamp to Cloudflare D1, and returns compact structured results. The flow was exercised in the Codex in-app browser: exact available tool set: get_city_context , place_stamp_bundle ; read operation invoked without mutation; one bounded write invoked; Branch changed from v0 to v1 ; visible game surface and Activity Feed updated; persisted=true ; normal reload restored the same state. Challenges The hardest part was keeping one trustworthy chain of evidence across WebMCP registration, authenticated Seat authorization, optimistic concurrency, idempotency, D1 persistence, browser-host behavior, human-visible feedback, public-source sanitization, and the deployed login path. We also had to ensure the submission described only the live vertical slice rather than future design work. Accomplishments and lessons learned We proved the complete loop: a real WebMCP host discovered the exact two-tool set; the browser agent invoked both the safe read and the bounded write; the write issued stable Event and Stamp identifiers; the visible page updated; and a normal reload restored the same D1-backed result. The key lesson is that durable human-agent collaboration is not only a model-memory problem. A web application can own continuity through authenticated roles, stable object references, typed actions, Event history, and visible state—while WebMCP connects an ordinary temporary agent session to that authoritative layer. What’s next The documented design extends this foundation with persistent Sentinel and Planner roles, structured city signals, crisis telemetry, semantic replay, owner-controlled branching, transport systems, and a data-driven crisis catalog. These are development directions, not claims about the current live submission. title: Strudel WebMCP
pitch: Live-code together.
about_excerpt: Live-code together. Like Comment Story Updates The agent isn't controlling another Strudel session. It's playing in yours. Strudel WebMCP lets a browser agent join the exact live Strudel REPL a human is already performing with. You type, select code, and drag inline sliders as normal; the agent reads and edits that same unsaved CodeMirror document, evaluates its changes in the same running scheduler, and can record what the result sounds like — under a permission dial you own. No embedded LLM, no MCP server, no WebSocket bridge, no session ID. Live demo: https://strudel-webmcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/strudel-webmcp Why WebMCP Live coding is a bad fit for every earlier agent-integration shape, because the thing an agent needs to touch — the unsaved editor buffer, the exact cursor and selection, the inline slider values, the scheduler that is playing right now — exists in one browser tab and changes every second. A file-based or bridged integration has to keep a second copy of that in sync, and the copy is stale the moment a slider moves. WebMCP has no second copy. The tool call is a method on the same page, over the same document, in the same tab the human is looking at. Nothing to install, nothing to configure, no bridge that can drift. That makes something ordinary that was previously very hard: a human dragging a filter-cutoff slider with the mouse while an agent, in the same instant, rewrites a different line of the same unsaved buffer — and neither can clobber the other's most recent change. What the agent can do Thirteen tools, registered through document.modelContext.registerTool (src/webmcp/tools.ts), all backed by one adapter over the live (src/strudel/adapter.ts): Read live context: playback state, cursor, the human's current selection, what is sounding now, the agent mode, and any pending proposal, solo or recording. Read the exact current source, unsaved edits included, optionally by line range. Apply precise range edits, or replace the whole source — in review mode both become proposals. Evaluate through Strudel's own Update path (host.editor.evaluate()), so an agent edit becomes audible exactly the way a human's does, without stopping the clock; or solo just a range; or audition a pending proposal. Play, stop, and select-and-scroll to a range so the human sees what the agent means. Record the live output — master, or one .analyze("id") voice — and get dBFS and band analysis back, plus a playable take left in the page. List and extend the sound registry the running scheduler actually resolves s("...") against. Snapshot the source as a named version; switch the editor theme. Every mutating tool requires the codeHash from a previous read, computed fresh from the live document, and is refused with STALE_CODE if anything changed since — including a slider drag, because Strudel's slider widgets rewrite the source's numeric literals directly. The human's most recent edit always wins. The permission dial has three positions. Read: the agent can look, record and point, nothing else. Review: every edit arrives as a proposal with a diff the human auditions, accepts or discards — the source is unchanged until you say so. Live: edits apply directly. What people and agents can do together You keep performing. The agent reads the exact state you're in — down to the characters you have selected — and makes structural edits to the lines you didn't ask it to leave alone, then evaluates them into the same running pattern. Both of you act through the one Strudel instance; the audio reflects both immediately because neither owns a separate copy. In review mode the agent pitches instead of acting: "swap the kick for a different one" appears as a diff you can hear before it lands. And the agent has ears: ask "is the bass too loud?" and it records four seconds of the live output, answers from measured dBFS band energy, and suggests a concrete gain change. Who this is for Live coders, algorave performers, and people learning music through code — an audience for whom the editor buffer is the whole instrument, and for whom anything that isn't that exact buffer is useless mid-performance. Today, getting an agent into that instrument means standing up an MCP server, a bridge, and usually a modified frontend before a single note changes. That is real friction for a hobbyist or student and dead weight for a performer who wants a second pair of hands for eight bars. The claim is direct: browser-native creative tools shouldn't need to embed a model or ship a dedicated connector to be legible to an agent. The page can expose the instrument the human already has open. Strudel is the proof; the pattern — unsaved live document, precise agent edits, human-owned permission dial — applies to any browser-native creative or editing tool with real-time state worth exposing. Live coding is a specialized audience, but the engine underneath it is not niche: @strudel/core , the pattern engine every Strudel-based tool depends on, drew about 30,000 npm downloads in the 30 days ending August 29, 2026, and the wider @strudel/* family this project embeds — mini-notation, transpiler, WebAudio backend, CodeMirror integration, the REPL itself — adds roughly 76,000 more over the same window. The seam this project adds is generic to any of those downstream tools, not specific to this demo's drum pattern. Compared with the existing Strudel MCP bridges Existing Strudel MCP projects drive Strudel through an MCP server, a WebSocket or SSE bridge, and often a special frontend or a session ID copied between browser and agent. They work. The difference is what it takes to start: a connector, a bridge, session synchronization, and MCP configuration on one side; opening the page on the other. Here the page publishes its own controls, and the browser agent already accompanying the user joins the REPL with no external bridge, no session ID, no agent-specific server, and no second source of truth. Why this is different from "AI + music" Most "AI + music" demos are generation: describe a vibe, get a clip, no instrument in the loop. Most WebMCP demos so far are forms and dashboards. This is neither. It is a person and a browser agent performing through the same live instrument — one typing, selecting, dragging and listening; the other reading exact state, making precise edits, evaluating, and pointing back into the source. The review-mode propose/audition/accept loop goes further: the agent gets a way to pitch a change and let the human hear it before committing, which has no analogue in a form-filling demo. How it's built A static site — no server, no bridge — wrapping the official Strudel REPL and CodeMirror editor. The adapter is the only code that touches @strudel/repl internals; the tools, schemas, registration and error helpers sit above it. Unit tests (Vitest) cover hashing, position and offset conversion, edit validation, stale-hash rejection, source-size bounds and error normalization. Playwright end-to-end tests run against the real <strudel-editor> , including one that physically moves an inline slider and confirms a stale agent write against the pre-slider hash is rejected, and a modes suite covering read denials, the proposal lifecycle, solo, both recording modes, samples, snapshots and themes. Try it Open https://strudel-webmcp.vercel.app in a WebMCP-capable browser, confirm "WebMCP ready · 13 tools" in the status strip, press Play. Then ask your agent: Keep the bass and kick exactly where I left them. Make the hats evolve over eight bars instead of staying static. Then turn the header dial to Review and ask: "Swap the kick for a different one — but let me check it first." The proposal/diff bar appears before anything sounds different. Every sound in the demo video is generated live by Strudel's own Web Audio engine from the pattern that ships in this repo (src/demo-pattern.ts) — synths and the built-in RolandTR909 drum bank, captured from the app's audio graph while it played. AGPL-3.0. title: Serendipity
pitch: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services.
about_excerpt: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Serendipity because planning a free evening in Tokyo kept turning into admin. I would find an interesting place, look for dinner nearby, check when both closed, open a map, and then discover that the route did not fit. A simple night out could leave me with ten tabs and no actual plan. The first version was a technical reservation-network demo. It worked, but it did not answer the question a normal user would ask: why would I use this? I kept the reliable parts and rebuilt the product around a simpler job. Give it the evening you have, and get back one plan whose times and prices you can check for yourself. What it does You choose Shibuya, Shinjuku, or Ikebukuro, then set the group size, time, per-person budget, walking limit, and the kind of night you want. Dinner can be included or left out. Serendipity builds one route with two or three stops. It shows when to visit, how long the walks are, what each stop should cost, and the estimated total for the group. If three stops do not fit, it says why it returned two. If nothing fits, it does not quietly loosen the request. It shows the closest option and waits for the user to approve the change. Each stop has a sources section with the publisher, checked date, published hours, official menu, and official link. This is planning from published information, not a live booking service. Serendipity does not claim a seat is available and does not send anything to a venue. Why WebMCP is a strong fit This kind of planning often starts as a conversation: “Plan a calm Ikebukuro evening for three, include dinner, and keep it under ¥4,000 each.” Then comes the follow-up: show me where the meal price came from, or change one stop. An assistant can try to operate the form like a person, but it has to interpret the layout and guess whether the page really changed. WebMCP gives it five actions instead: find a plan, show the evidence for a place, change one stop, save the plan, or delete it. Those actions use stable plan and place IDs, and the result appears on the same page the user is watching. I stopped at five tools. Finding a plan, checking evidence, and changing a stop are read-only. Saving and deleting are the only write actions, and they only affect this browser. Opening a restaurant or venue website is still a normal link the user chooses. How I built it The app is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. The planner is deterministic. It checks combinations of activities and meals against published opening hours, visit length, closing time, budget, and walking limits. Restaurant budgets use the highest price in the official menu range. Walking time is marked as a coordinate-based estimate. I reviewed 21 places across the three hubs: four activities and three meals in each area. Every place in a route needs support for its name, address, coordinates, hours, public access, and price. I wrote the short descriptions myself and used official pages instead of copying marketplace reviews or photos. Google enrichment exists behind a server flag, but it is off in the submitted version. The live app works from its reviewed data and official menu pages. The human controls and the five Site Tools call the same controller. I did not want an agent demo sitting beside a separate, less reliable product. If a request is stale, malformed, cancelled, or unsafe, both paths reject it in the same way. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the app was allowed to say. It is easy to make a schedule look convincing. It is much harder to prove that a place is actually open at that time and that the displayed price came from a menu. I spent more time removing weak data than adding new places. Parks without published hours, prices inferred as zero, stale closure calendars, and unclear reuse rights all forced changes to the data model. The UI went through several bad versions. One was two dashboards side by side. Another had oversized type and decorative cards that made the route harder to follow. Feedback on those versions was blunt, but correct. I removed most of the explanation from the main path, gave the route the full page, and kept source details behind disclosures. The agent and the human also kept finding different edge cases. A late response could overwrite a newer search. Browser Back could make the URL disagree with the plan. A damaged saved record could break reopening. Fixing those bugs led to one shared state controller instead of two implementations. Accomplishments The live app covers three Tokyo hubs, with four reviewed activities and three official-menu meals in each one. Codex discovered all five Site Tools in the ChatGPT desktop browser and used them to build a real plan and open its meal evidence on the visible page. A strict request can return an honest no-result. The app only offers a relaxed search after the server has verified it and the user chooses it. What I learned A difficult technical demo is not automatically a useful product. The first version proved that several sites could coordinate, but people still asked, “What is this for?” Rebuilding it around one understandable job made the engineering choices much clearer. Good Site Tools are closer to product actions than UI controls. The agent does not need a tool for every button. It needs a few useful verbs, clear limits, and enough evidence for the person to check the result. WebMCP worked best when the agent and the user could look at the same updated plan, not when the agent disappeared into a background workflow. What’s next I would add more neighborhoods only after reviewing them to the same standard as the current three. The next practical improvements are transit-aware travel, shareable saved plans, and an optional live Google check controlled by the user. I would not add booking or payment until a venue provides real booking authority and there is a safe way to handle the transaction.
